itineraries.title: Road Trip through Baden-Württemberg: Romantic Castles, Legendary Thermal Baths and the Enchanting Black Forest
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May–June and September–October, with temperatures of 15–24°C, ideal for castles and Black Forest hikes. Avoid July–August (heat up to 32°C, crowded sites) and December–February (cold weather, 0–5°C, short days, frequent snow at higher elevations). Bring a jacket even in summer: the Black Forest stays cool and damp year-round.

visits.text: Marvel at Heidelberg Castle, one of Germany's most romantic ruins perched high above the red-roofed old town. This magnificent Renaissance fortress, partially destroyed by French troops in the 17th century, offers breathtaking views over the Neckar Valley and houses the world's largest wine barrel. The atmospheric ruins create an unforgettable silhouette against the sky that has inspired poets and artists for centuries.

Explore the Palatinate Museum (Kurpfälzisches Museum) on the pedestrianized main street, where fascinating exhibits reveal the Celtic and Roman civilizations that inhabited this region long before the castle was built. The museum houses remarkable archaeological treasures and artwork spanning millennia of human settlement in the Neckar Valley. This cultural institution provides essential context for understanding Heidelberg's deep historical roots.

Wander through Heidelberg's enchanting old town, a maze of cobblestone streets, baroque churches and historic university buildings that make it one of Germany's most picturesque cities. The famous Alte Brücke (Old Bridge) offers postcard-perfect views of the castle reflected in the river below. Stay overnight to experience the magical atmosphere after the day-trippers have departed and the city reveals its true romantic character.

activities.text: Join a guided castle tour to discover the fascinating stories behind these evocative ruins and explore hidden chambers

visits.text: Lose yourself in the magnificent gardens of Schloss Schwetzingen, a splendid summer palace with hectares of meticulously landscaped grounds that rank among Germany's finest baroque gardens. The salmon-pink palace provides an elegant backdrop to formal parterres, romantic temples and winding woodland paths designed to delight at every turn. This princely retreat was created for the Electors Palatine as an escape from court life in Heidelberg.

Discover the garden's extraordinary follies, including a mosque, Roman temple and bath house that reflect 18th-century fascination with exotic cultures. The circular parterre and grand water features demonstrate the height of baroque garden design and horticultural artistry. If visiting in May, the town's famous white asparagus festival celebrates this prized local delicacy with culinary events throughout the region.

activities.text: Enjoy lunch at one of the charming restaurants along the road leading to the palace gardens

visits.text: Stand in awe before the Speyer Cathedral (Speyer Dom), a monumental Romanesque masterpiece that served as the principal church of the Holy Roman Empire. This UNESCO World Heritage site, one of the largest Romanesque churches in the world, houses the crypts of eight German emperors and kings beneath its soaring vaulted ceilings. The cathedral's twin towers and red sandstone facade have dominated the Rhine plain for nearly a thousand years.

Descend into the imperial crypt to pay respects at the final resting place of medieval rulers who once shaped the destiny of Europe. The atmospheric underground chambers feature simple yet powerful stone sarcophagi that connect visitors directly to the empire's medieval glory. An excellent audio guide available in multiple languages brings the cathedral's fascinating history vividly to life.

Visit the museum opposite the cathedral square to deepen your understanding of Speyer's crucial role in European history. The “Kreuz und Krone” collection presents the history of the cathedral and the diocese of Speyer through religious objects and liturgical treasures. In summer, the lively Brezelfest fills the streets with rides and traditional festival tents, while December brings a charming, comfortably sized Christmas market.

activities.text: Stroll along the historic Maximilianstrasse, Germany's oldest and longest pedestrian street

visits.text: Explore the mysterious Burg Berwartstein, a fascinating castle perched dramatically atop one of the rocky sandstone hills that characterize this border region. Once seized by notorious robber barons during the Middle Ages, this fortress is steeped in amazing myths and legends that the guided tours bring thrillingly to life. The hand-carved, candlelit tunnels beneath the castle create an atmospheric adventure unlike any other.

Discover the castle's remarkable architecture, including a small chapel adorned with medieval paintings that survived centuries of conflict and neglect. The robber baron history adds a thrilling dimension to the visit, with tales of ambushes, ransoms and dramatic escapes echoing through the stone corridors. This hidden gem remains surprisingly untouched by mass tourism, offering an authentic castle experience.

activities.text: Take the guided tour to hear the fascinating legends and explore the candle-lit underground passages

visits.text: Immerse yourself in the legendary spa culture of Baden-Baden, a spa town that has drawn visitors seeking rejuvenation for over two thousand years. The Romans first built public baths here to harness the natural hot springs, and in the 18th century the town became a glamorous haven for French nobles fleeing the revolution. The elegant promenades, grand hotels and manicured gardens retain an atmosphere of refined sophistication.

Experience the therapeutic waters of the Caracalla Therme, a modern wellness complex where warm mineral pools, saunas and relaxation areas continue the ancient bathing tradition in contemporary comfort. For a more traditional experience, the Friedrichsbad offers elaborate bathing rituals in an opulent 19th-century setting.

Explore the extensive castle ruins perched on the forested hillside above the town, offering panoramic views over the spa quarter and surrounding Black Forest peaks. The famous casino, one of the most beautiful in Europe, has attracted high society since the 1800s with its lavish interiors. Art galleries, boutiques and the elegant Trinkhalle colonnade complete Baden-Baden's appeal as one of Germany's most romantic destinations.

activities.text: Take an autumn or spring walk through the Lichtentaler Allee, a magnificent park along the Oos River

visits.text: Drive the legendary Black Forest High Road (Schwarzwaldhochstraße) from Baden-Baden to Freudenstadt, one of Germany's most scenic mountain routes. This spectacular drive takes you along the peaks of the Black Forest, with incredible views plunging down into forested valleys at every bend. Numerous viewpoints and trailheads invite you to stop, breathe the pine-scented air and absorb the magnificent panoramas.

Stop at the Mummelsee, a mystical glacial lake surrounded by dark fir forests and shrouded in local legends about water spirits and lake nymphs. Allow for a round trip within a day from Freudenstadt, followed by an uphill walk to the viewing platform on the Hornisgrinde, the highest peak in the northern Black Forest, which rewards visitors with 360-degree views extending to the Vosges mountains in France. Several hiking trails of varying difficulty lead from the road through unspoiled forest landscapes.

Arrive in Freudenstadt, home to Germany's largest market square, a vast open space surrounded by arcaded houses that give the town a distinctly Mediterranean feel. This planned Renaissance town was founded in 1599 and rebuilt after World War II damage with remarkable attention to its historic character. The unique L-shaped Protestant church and covered shopping arcades make it a pleasant base for Black Forest exploration.

activities.text: Stop for short hikes along the route to experience the Black Forest's pristine nature up close

visits.text: Step back in time at the Black Forest Open-Air Museum (Vogtsbauernhof), an extraordinary village of meticulously rescued historic farm buildings spanning 400 years of rural life. Each farmhouse, barn and mill has been carefully dismantled, transported and reconstructed on this picturesque hillside site, complete with authentic furnishings and equipment. This living museum offers an unparalleled window into the traditional way of life in the Black Forest region.

Watch craftspeople demonstrate traditional skills in the working wooden toy workshop, where hand-carved Black Forest toys are made using century-old techniques. If you're lucky, the wood-fired bread ovens will be in operation, filling the air with the irresistible aroma of freshly baked loaves. Farm animals roam the grounds, adding to the authentic atmosphere of a working agricultural community of the past.

Follow the excellent audio guide through the farmhouses to understand how families lived, worked and survived the harsh mountain winters. Interactive exhibits vividly bring agricultural techniques and domestic life to life, engaging visitors of all ages. The traditional Black Forest houses with their distinctive low-pitched roofs represent architectural solutions to the region's heavy snowfall.

activities.text: Purchase authentic Black Forest handicrafts and traditional products directly from the museum workshops

visits.text: Discover Freiburg im Breisgau, the sunniest city in Germany, where a youthful university atmosphere fills the charming medieval streets. The old town is crisscrossed by Bächle, small water channels running through the cobblestone streets and sidewalks that have cooled the city for centuries. Local legend warns that if you accidentally step in one, you're destined to marry someone from Freiburg!

Admire the magnificent Freiburg Minster (Freiburger Münster), a Gothic masterpiece built from striking red sandstone over three centuries during the Middle Ages. The cathedral's intricate spire, considered one of the finest in Christendom, rises 116 meters above the bustling market square below. The medieval stained glass windows and remarkable gargoyles showcase the extraordinary craftsmanship of medieval artisans.

Ascend the Schlossberg by funicular for panoramic city views, or take the cable car up to the 1,284-meter summit of Schauinsland for breathtaking vistas across the Black Forest, Rhine Valley and Alps. The observation tower at the top provides 360-degree views that on clear days extend to the Swiss Alps. Freiburg's position as gateway to the Black Forest makes it an ideal base for hiking and nature excursions.

activities.text: Browse the farmers' market around the cathedral, Monday to Saturday except public holidays and August 15, one of Germany's best for fresh local produce

visits.text: Relax at Titisee, one of the Black Forest's most beloved lakes nestled in a picture-perfect mountain setting. This natural glacial lake offers crystal-clear waters perfect for swimming, pedal boating or simply strolling along the scenic lakeside promenade. The surrounding forested hills and traditional Black Forest villages create postcard views in every direction.

Browse the shops along the lakefront for authentic Black Forest souvenirs, including the region's famous cuckoo clocks crafted by local clockmakers using traditional techniques. The mechanical artistry of these hand-carved timepieces represents generations of Black Forest craftsmanship passed down through families. Look for shops offering demonstrations of how these intricate clocks are assembled.

Take a boat ride across the glittering waters, either paddling yourself or aboard one of the tourist vessels that cruise the lake. The surrounding mountains are laced with hiking trails offering spectacular views of the lake and the Black Forest peaks. A visit to the Menzenschwand valley nearby reveals traditional villages and the famous Café zum Kuckuck.

activities.text: Rent a pedal boat or rowboat to explore the lake at your own pace and enjoy the mountain scenery

visits.text: Explore Konstanz on the shores of the Bodensee (Lake Constance), Germany's largest lake straddling the border with Switzerland and Austria. The lovely lakeside promenade is lined with restaurants and cafes offering views across the shimmering waters toward the Swiss Alps. The famous rotating Imperia statue at the harbor entrance completes one revolution every three minutes, a modern monument with medieval satirical roots.

Visit the fascinating open-air lake-dwelling museum in Unteruhldingen, a UNESCO World Heritage site that reconstructs Stone Age and Bronze Age settlements built on wooden stilts above the water. Allow for a round trip from Konstanz, taking the ferry to Meersburg and then continuing to Unteruhldingen. These remarkable reconstructions offer a glimpse of human life on Lake Constance more than 4,000 years ago. Archaeological finds from the lake bed vividly bring these ancient communities to life through engaging exhibitions.

Cross to Mainau Island, the famous “island of flowers” where subtropical botanical gardens, a Baroque palace and a butterfly house create a Mediterranean paradise in the heart of Europe. The gardens burst with color throughout the year, from spring tulips to summer roses and autumn dahlias. To visit Meersburg Castle, take the ferry from Konstanz to Meersburg on the opposite shore of the lake. Germany's oldest inhabited castle rises spectacularly above the lake, with some sections still occupied by the family that owns it.

activities.text: Take a boat cruise across the Bodensee to appreciate the stunning Alpine panorama from the water

visits.text: Behold Hohenzollern Castle, one of Germany's most spectacular castles and ancestral seat of the Prussian royal family whose members later became German emperors. This fairy-tale fortress, rebuilt in its current neo-Gothic splendor in 1850, crowns a dramatic conical peak rising 855 meters above the Swabian countryside. The castle rivals Bavaria's famous Neuschwanstein in beauty and surpasses it in the authenticity of its royal ties.

Tour the gloriously opulent interiors, where visitors don enormous felt slippers to protect the precious parquet floors while children can dress in royal costumes for an immersive experience. The family still uses the castle for special events, so verify opening times before your visit to avoid disappointment. The treasury displays Prussian crown jewels and personal effects of Frederick the Great.

Hike to the neighboring Zeller Horn viewpoint for the iconic photograph of the castle floating above clouds that has made Hohenzollern Castle famous worldwide. The approach road itself offers increasingly spectacular views as the castle emerges from the forested hilltop. Hot air balloon rides over the castle at sunset provide an unforgettable perspective on this architectural marvel.

activities.text: Visit Hohenzollern Castle during Advent to discover the Königlicher Winterzauber exhibition, with illuminations and Christmas decorations in the castle courtyards and rooms

visits.text: Fall in love with Tübingen, a charming university town that many consider Germany's most beautiful city. The picturesque old town features a magnificent castle, cobblestone streets lined with half-timbered houses and a picturesque waterfront along the Neckar River. The century-old university gives the town a youthful, intellectual energy that fills the winding lanes and historic squares.

Climb to Hohentübingen Castle, perched on a ridge overlooking the town, where university students attend classes in buildings that have educated scholars for over 500 years. The castle courtyard offers panoramic views over the red-tiled roofs and church towers of the old town below. The surrounding vineyards produce local wines that feature on menus throughout the town.

Experience a traditional Stocherkahn boat ride, Tübingen's version of Venetian gondolas, where flat-bottomed punts glide along the Neckar past willow-draped banks. The annual Stocherkahnrennen boat race is a beloved local tradition featuring costumed students and much hilarity. The Holzmarkt square and surrounding streets come alive on summer evenings with locals enjoying the outdoor café culture.

activities.text: Explore the old town's atmospheric squares and imagine yourself on a Harry Potter film set

visits.text: Wander through Esslingen's remarkably preserved medieval old town, home to some of Germany's finest half-timbered buildings clustered in atmospheric lanes. The town center features extraordinarily large and beautifully decorated timber-frame houses that survived centuries of war and development pressures. This architectural treasure trove just southeast of Stuttgart rewards visitors who venture beyond the capital.

Admire the historic Altes Rathaus (Old Town Hall) and the twin-spired Stadtkirche that dominate the market square, both masterpieces of medieval civic architecture. The town's wine-growing tradition continues on the steep vineyard slopes that surround the old town, producing excellent local varieties. Canal waterways threading through the center add to Esslingen's picturesque charm.

Visit during Christmas market season to experience one of Germany's most magical medieval markets. The market transforms the old town into a fairy-tale setting with medieval children's rides, torch-lit streets and the unique spectacle of betting on mice running into small numbered wooden houses. Flaming braziers and costumed performers create an authentically medieval atmosphere unlike any other Christmas market.

activities.text: Climb to the castle ruins above town for panoramic views over the half-timbered rooftops and vineyards

visits.text: Discover Schwäbisch Hall, a beautiful and charming town that was once a major center of salt production, the precious “white gold” that created its wealth. Winding streets lined with magnificent half-timbered buildings lead through the old town center to a gorgeous central market square dominated by the imposing St. Michael's Church. The covered wooden bridge spanning the Kocher River creates one of Germany's most photographed scenes.

Visit the local museum to learn about the fascinating history of salt making that gave the town its name and fortune. Salt has been extracted here since Celtic times, and the industry shaped every aspect of local life, architecture and culture. The Hällisch-Fränkisches Museum brings this heritage to life through engaging exhibits about the salt workers and merchants who built the town.

Explore the Großcomburg monastery complex perched on a hill just above the town, where 16th-century defensive walls still stand to protect the Romanesque chapel and cloister within. The monastery's peaceful courtyards and historic architecture offer a contemplative contrast to the bustling town below. Check the town's festival calendar, as Schwäbisch Hall hosts excellent cultural events throughout the year.

activities.text: Relax in the riverside park along the Kocher and admire views of the picturesque covered bridge

seo.h1_title: Road Trip through Baden-Württemberg: Romantic Castles, Legendary Thermal Baths and the Enchanting Black Forest
seo.intro_paragraph: Discover southwestern Germany, a region where fairy-tale castles overlook verdant valleys, thousand-year-old thermal baths preserve Roman rituals and dark fir forests safeguard centuries-old craft traditions. From romantic Heidelberg to the cuckoo clocks of Titisee, from the imperial ruins of Speyer to perfectly preserved half-timbered villages, this itinerary reveals the hidden gems of Baden-Württemberg.
seo.seo_hook: 10 days of wonder among imperial castles, prestigious spa towns and the mysteries of the Black Forest.

itineraries.title: Germany's Romantic Road: Fairytale Castles and Medieval Villages in Bavaria
itineraries.subtitle: From Würzburg to Füssen, 400 kilometers through Baroque palaces, medieval towns, and Alpine peaks
itineraries.climate: Best period: May-September, temperatures 15-25°C, ideal for castles and walks. Avoid December-February (frost, frequent fog, some sites closed). July-August: peak tourist crowds at Neuschwanstein.
specialties: Franconian Silvaner wine in Bocksbeutel bottles

visits.text: The Würzburg Residence, built between 1720 and 1744 under the patronage of the Schönborn prince-bishops, is Europe's most stylistically unified Baroque palace according to UNESCO, which inscribed it as a World Heritage Site in 1981. Architect Balthasar Neumann, then 33 years old, oversaw the work with the help of specialists from Vienna, Paris, Italy, and Flanders. The grand staircase houses the world's largest fresco painted as a single continuous work (32 × 19 meters), created by the Venetian artist Tiepolo in just 210 days between 1752 and 1753: it depicts the four continents known at the time paying homage to the prince-bishop. The prince-bishop had initially hired a Milanese artist, but he painted so poorly that the prince-bishop decided to bring in Tiepolo, promising him 10,000 florins—three times his Venetian salary.

Step through the doors of the Hofkirche, the Residence chapel tucked into the southwest wing. Despite its modest dimensions, it's considered one of the most perfect achievements of 18th-century sacred architecture. Five oval domes rise in succession above twisted pink marble columns crowned with gilded Corinthian capitals. Tiepolo painted the altarpieces here, while Antonio Bossi crafted the stuccowork. After the chapel, stroll through the Court Gardens (Hofgarten), laid out in terraces between 1765 and 1780, adorned with sculptures, putti, and symmetrical flower beds—they too are part of the UNESCO listing.

The Alte Mainbrücke, Würzburg's oldest bridge, has connected the city to Marienberg Fortress since the 15th century. An earlier stone bridge existed as early as 1133, but floods in 1342 and 1442 destroyed it. The current bridge, 185 meters long and comprising eight limestone arches, was rebuilt between 1476 and 1703. Since the 1720s, twelve 4.5-meter-tall Baroque sandstone statues have adorned its pillars, including Saint Kilian, the city's patron saint, who was martyred in 689, and Charlemagne. Until 1886, it was the only way to cross the Main in Würzburg. Now pedestrianized, the bridge keeps a local tradition alive: residents gather there at the end of the day for a glass of Franconian Silvaner, the region's signature grape, served in the distinctive flattened Bocksbeutel bottles.

St. Kilian's Cathedral (Dom), Germany's fourth-largest Romanesque church, has dominated the cityscape since the 11th century. It is named after the city's patron saint, an Irish missionary who was martyred in 689 alongside his companions Colman and Totnan. Inside, works by the sculptor Tilman Riemenschneider stand alongside Ottoman elements from the early 11th century and Gothic additions. The Schönborn family's funerary chapel, designed by Balthasar Neumann in 1736, can be visited in the transept.

activities.text: Settle on the Alte Mainbrücke in the late afternoon to enjoy a glass of Franconian Silvaner as the sun sets over the Marienberg fortress and the vineyard-covered hills.

visits.text: Marienberg Fortress, perched on the left bank of the Main, served as the residence of Würzburg's prince-bishops for five centuries before the Residence was built. Its origins date back to 706, when the first church was built on the site—one of the oldest in Germany. The present enclosure combines medieval fortifications with Renaissance bastions. Inside, the Main Franconian Museum (Mainfränkisches Museum) houses the world's largest collection of sculptures by Tilman Riemenschneider, a master of the late Gothic period who worked in Würzburg between 1483 and 1531 and whose limewood faces are strikingly expressive.

Climb the 247 steps along the Way of the Cross leading to the Käppele, the pilgrimage church of the Visitation, built by Balthasar Neumann between 1748 and 1750 on the Nikolausberg hill. It all began in 1640, when a fisherman from the Main placed a Pietà in his vineyard during the Thirty Years' War; miraculous healings were reported there a few years later, drawing pilgrims. The Way of the Cross, the largest in Germany, is marked by 14 chapels housing 77 life-size statues sculpted by Johann Peter Wagner. The church miraculously survived the bombing of March 16, 1945, which destroyed 90% of the city—a German soldier is said to have pretended to be out of ammunition to avoid shelling it.

The Juliusspital, a hospital founded in 1576 by Prince-Bishop Julius Echter von Mespelbrunn "for the indigent and the sick," remains operational today. It derives its income from about a hundred hectares of vineyards it has owned since the 16th century, making it one of Würzburg's three great historic wine estates alongside the Bürgerspital (founded by wealthy burghers). The arcaded inner courtyard, the 17th-century buildings restored after the war, and the bistro where you can taste Würzburger Stein are worth a stop.

On the market square, the Marienkapelle (St. Mary's Chapel) is a Gothic church recognizable by its white and red sandstone façade. Across from it, the Falkenhaus, with its magnificent yellow and white Rococo façade adorned with stucco, houses the tourist office. Franconia's first Baroque collegiate church, St. John im Haug (1670), designed by Italian architect Antonio Petrini, stands out with its two towers flanking a tall façade and an imposing dome—a Crucifixion by Tintoretto (1583) surmounts the high altar.

activities.text: Descend into the vaulted cellars of the Bürgerspital or Juliusspital for a tasting of Franconian wines. Franconia, one of Germany's 13 wine regions, is known for its dry white wines—Silvaner, Bacchus, and Müller-Thurgau—served in flattened Bocksbeutel bottles. The terraced vineyards lining the Main and overlooking the city are an integral part of the landscape.

map_keywords: St. Jakobskirche Rothenburg ob der Tauber

visits.text: Rothenburg ob der Tauber is one of Europe's best-preserved medieval towns. Perched on a plateau above the Tauber, it has remained virtually unchanged since the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648), which ruined the town but paradoxically preserved it: too poor to modernize, it retained its medieval appearance intact. Its 13th- and 14th-century ramparts still stand for 4 kilometers, punctuated by 42 towers and gates. The wall walk (Turmweg) is free to access and offers a walk of about an hour and a half at a height of 6 meters, with views looking down over the red-tiled roofs and the valley. After the bombing of March 31, 1945, destroyed more than a third of the old town, international aid enabled it to be faithfully rebuilt—the donors' names are engraved on the stones of the restored ramparts.

The Plönlein—from the Latin planum, “little square”—is Rothenburg's most photographed corner and one of Germany's most reproduced images. At the intersection of two sloping streets, a slightly crooked yellow and red half-timbered house stands between the Siebers Tower (1385) on the left and the Kobolzeller Gate on the right, which leads down toward the Tauber valley. This setting inspired the village in Disney's animated film Pinocchio. Come early in the morning to avoid crowds and enjoy the low-angle light. From there, climb the Röder Tower or the Renaissance town hall's belfry for a 360° panorama of the town.

St. James's Church (St. Jakobskirche), built between 1311 and 1484, rises above the Marktplatz with its Gothic silhouette. It houses the Holy Blood Altarpiece, a masterpiece by the sculptor Tilman Riemenschneider.

The Burggarten, at the western tip of town, occupies the site of the Hohenstaufen castle built in 1142, from which King Conrad III ruled the Holy Roman Empire. Of the double fortress, only St. Blaise's Chapel remains, now converted into a memorial. This terraced garden offers Rothenburg's finest panorama: unobstructed views of the Tauber valley, vineyards, town rooftops, and the double row of ramparts.

activities.text: Join the Night Watchman's tour (Nachtwächter), which leaves from the Marktplatz. Dressed in medieval costume, with a lantern in his hand and a halberd on his shoulder, the watchman guides visitors through the dark lanes of the old town, recounting Rothenburg's legends, scandals, and anecdotes - a tradition dating back to the Middle Ages, when watchmen patrolled to prevent fires and disturbances.

practical_info.booking: Show up at Marktplatz, tours in German and English

visits.text: The Medieval Crime Museum (Kriminalmuseum), housed in the former commandery of the Order of St. John, displays over a thousand years of the history of law and justice across four floors. Public humiliation masks, dunking cages, “shrew's fiddles” for punishing talkative women: these instruments reveal the brutal realities of medieval law enforcement. In complete contrast, the German Christmas Museum (Deutsches Weihnachtsmuseum) celebrates German holiday traditions year-round through thousands of decorations, nutcrackers, and historic Advent calendars—Rothenburg hosts one of Germany's oldest Christmas markets.

The Imperial City Museum (Reichsstadtmuseum), housed in the former Dominican convent founded in 1258, preserves an intact medieval monastic kitchen, Rothenburg's Stations of the Cross (1494)—a cycle of twelve panels painted by Martinus Schwarz—and Mayor Nusch's drinking cup, the famous 3.25-liter cup adorned with the emperor surrounded by the seven prince-electors (1616), which illustrates the Meistertrunk legend.

Fifty kilometers south of Rothenburg, Dinkelsbühl is the forgotten “little sister” of the Romantic Road—and that's precisely its charm. This former Free Imperial City, fortified by Emperor Henry V, has kept its ramparts intact thanks to an edict by King Ludwig I of Bavaria and was spared from bombings in both world wars. The walls feature about twenty towers, the oldest dating from 1370. The Wörnitztor, the town's oldest gate, opens onto streets lined with patrician houses with colorful gables, the Wine Market square (Weinmarkt), and St. George's Church, one of the finest Gothic hall churches in southern Germany, built between 1448 and 1499, with its net vaulting and St. Aurelian's reliquary.

activities.text: Try a Schneeball (snowball), Rothenburg's specialty: puff pastry rolled into a ball, fried, and dusted with powdered sugar or coated in chocolate. This Franconian pastry comes in dozens of variations at bakeries along Schmiedgasse and Herrngasse.

visits.text: Augsburg, founded in 15 BCE by the Roman legions of Emperor Augustus, is one of Germany's oldest cities. During the Renaissance, it became one of Europe's financial capitals: the Fugger and Welser dynasties of merchants and bankers lent money to Emperors Maximilian I and Charles V. It was in Augsburg that the Augsburg Confession, the founding charter of Lutheranism, was read in 1530, and that the Peace of Augsburg, which formalized the coexistence of religions within the Empire, was signed in 1555. The city is also the birthplace of Leopold Mozart, the composer's father, and of the writer Bertolt Brecht. It is the only city in Germany with its own public holiday: on August 8, the Peace Festival commemorates the end of the oppression of Protestants after the Thirty Years' War.

The Fuggerei, founded in 1521 by Jakob Fugger—considered the richest man of his time—is the world's oldest social housing complex still in operation. Behind its walls and blue-and-white-striped gate, 67 ochre-fronted houses contain 142 apartments of 60 square meters each. The annual rent, set at one Rhenish guilder in 1521, has never changed: today, it is equivalent to €0.88. In return, residents must be Catholic, originally from Augsburg, in financial need, and recite three prayers each day for the founders. A 10 p.m. curfew is still in force. Mozart's great-grandfather, the mason Franz Mozart, lived here from 1681 to 1694—a commemorative plaque recalls his stay. A model apartment and a bunker dating from 1943 are open to visitors.

The Town Hall (Rathaus), designed by the architect Elias Holl and completed in 1620, is regarded as the most important secular Renaissance building north of the Alps. Everything was destroyed by the bombing in 1944 but faithfully rebuilt.

Stroll down Maximilianstraße, the city's finest avenue, laid out along the ancient Roman Via Claudia Augusta. Three monumental bronze fountains punctuate the promenade: the Augustus Fountain (1588-1594) by Dutch sculptor Hubert Gerhard, the Mercury Fountain (1596-1599), and the Hercules Fountain (1597-1600) by Adriaen de Vries. These fountains are part of Augsburg's water management system, inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019—an ensemble of 22 hydraulic monuments spanning more than 700 years of history. At No. 36, the Fugger Palace features a Renaissance arcaded courtyard; at No. 46, the Schaezler Palace (1770) houses the most important gallery of German Baroque art and a Rococo ballroom.

Augsburg's Cathedral of Our Lady (Dom), whose oldest sections date back to 994, combines Romanesque and Gothic architecture. It preserves figurative stained-glass windows dating from the 11th century: the Prophets - Daniel, Jonah, Hosea, Moses, and David - set in the south windows of the nave. The Romanesque bronze door, considered the cathedral's oldest work of art, is displayed in the adjoining diocesan museum.

activities.text: Take a seat in one of the city-center beer halls to try Käsespätzle, fresh pasta baked with cheese, a Swabian specialty of Augsburg. Located on the border between Bavaria and Swabia, the city offers cuisine that draws on both traditions—round off your meal with Leberkäse (meatloaf) or Zwetschgendatschi (damson plum tart).

Attend a performance at the Augsburger Puppenkiste, the famous marionette theater founded in 1943. Housed in the former Holy Spirit Hospital, this string puppet theater stages fairy tales for children as well as adult productions, with an attention to detail that has made it renowned throughout Germany.

visits.text: Neuschwanstein Castle, inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2025, is Germany's most visited castle, with more than one million admissions a year. King Ludwig II of Bavaria, crowned in 1864 at the age of 18, commissioned its construction in 1869 on a rocky spur 200 meters high. He had 8 meters of rock blasted away to clear the foundations, and between 1879 and 1880 had some 465 tonnes of Salzburg marble and 400,000 bricks transported to the site. The project used the most modern technology of the era: central heating, running water on every floor, and a steel structure to support the throne room. Ludwig II lived there for only a few months in 1884 before being declared unfit to rule and dying mysteriously in Lake Starnberg on June 13, 1886. The castle was still unfinished—and would never be fully completed.

Walk up to the Marienbrücke, suspended 90 meters above the Pöllat Gorge and its 45-meter waterfall. This bridge, originally built in wood in the 1840s by Ludwig II's father as a birthday gift for Queen Marie, then reconstructed in iron in 1866, offers THE classic photo of Neuschwanstein: the castle stands out in its entirety against a backdrop of forests and Alpine peaks. This silhouette inspired Walt Disney for Sleeping Beauty's castle at the first Disneyland, opened in 1955 in California—it later became the Disney studios logo. The walk up from the Hohenschwangau parking lot takes about 40 minutes.

Hohenschwangau Castle, below Neuschwanstein, was the home where Ludwig II spent his childhood. His father, Maximilian II, had it restored in the neo-Gothic style from 1832 onwards. The rooms, richly decorated with tapestries depicting medieval legends—including that of Lohengrin, the Swan Knight—fired the future king's imagination from an early age. Seeing Wagner's opera Lohengrin in 1861, at the age of 15, was a revelation for Ludwig: the swan would become his emblem, appearing throughout Neuschwanstein. The castle overlooks the Alpsee, whose turquoise waters invite a stroll along the trail that circles the lake.

activities.text: Walk the circuit around the Alpsee, a 5-kilometer trail hugging turquoise waters framed by conifer forests and the rocky faces of the Alps. The panorama of the two royal castles from the south shore is spectacular. The trail is flat and accessible, perfect for unwinding after visiting the castles.

visits.text: The Hohes Schloss (High Castle) in Füssen, the summer residence of the prince-bishops of Augsburg from the late 15th century onwards, is one of the largest and best-preserved Gothic castles in Swabia. Its trompe-l'oeil painted façades—false windows, false battlements, and false oriel windows—are unique in Germany and date from the reign of Bishop Friedrich von Zollern (1486–1505). The Rittersaal (Knights' Hall), with its carved coffered ceiling, is worth the climb. The Bavarian State Gallery, housed in the former reception rooms, displays late Gothic paintings and sculptures from the 15th and 16th centuries.

Below the castle, St. Magnus's Benedictine Monastery (Kloster St. Mang), founded in the 8th century and rebuilt in Baroque style between 1697 and 1726, houses one of Europe's finest collections of antique lutes and violins—Füssen is considered one of the cradles of European luthiery. The cultural heritage museum also presents Jakob Hiebeler's “Dance of Death” (1602), Bavaria's oldest mural representation of a danse macabre. The monastery's splendid Baroque halls offer a glimpse of the institution's former wealth.

Wander through Füssen's pedestrianized old town along Reichenstraße, lined with houses with painted façades and following the route of the ancient Via Claudia Augusta, the Roman road that connected Italy to Germania. The luthiers' fountain recalls the town's historic role in the manufacture of stringed instruments. On Schrannenplatz, the site of the former grain hall, historical parades enliven the town in summer. Perched at an altitude of 800 meters at the foot of the Alps, the town has more than 2,000 years of history—its colorful Baroque houses, narrow streets, and mountain views make it a spectacular end point for the Romantic Road.

activities.text: Walk down to Lechfall, the Lech waterfall, 10 minutes from the center of Füssen. The Lech River, which rises in Austria, plunges into a narrow gorge here through a series of natural cascades. The bridge spanning the gorge offers spectacular views of the turquoise water and rocks sculpted by erosion.

Embark on a cruise on the Forggensee, Bavaria's fifth-largest lake by surface area. Boats operate from early June to mid-October and offer panoramas of Neuschwanstein and Hohenschwangau castles, Füssen's old town perched on its hill, and the surrounding Alpine peaks. Evening cruises at sunset are particularly recommended.

practical_info.booking: Navigation from June to mid-October only

seo.h1_title: Germany's Romantic Road: Fairytale Castles and Medieval Villages in Bavaria
seo.intro_paragraph: The Romantic Road stretches 400 kilometers from Franconia to the Bavarian Alps, from Würzburg's Baroque palace—listed by UNESCO for the world's largest fresco, painted by Tiepolo—to Neuschwanstein Castle, a fairytale fortress inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2025. In between, Rothenburg ob der Tauber retains its 4 kilometers of intact medieval walls and 42 towers, Dinkelsbühl reveals half-timbered houses that have survived every war, and Augsburg is home to the Fuggerei, the world's oldest social housing complex, where the annual rent is still €0.88. Seven days of rich history, changing landscapes, and discoveries around every bend.
seo.seo_hook: From Tiepolo's giant fresco to the castle that inspired Disney: 400 kilometers through medieval towns, intact ramparts, and the Bavarian Alps.
featured_list: Neuschwanstein Castle, a UNESCO World Heritage Site and the model for Disney's castle

The Bavarian Alps and the Marienbrücke suspended above Pöllat Gorge
Dinkelsbühl, an intact medieval gem that has survived every war

itineraries.title: Bavaria Road Trip: Complete Tour from Munich to the Bavarian Alps
itineraries.climate: Best period: May-September, temperatures 18-26°C in lowlands, 15-22°C in mountains. Avoid winter (December-February): alpine roads closed, freezing temperatures, frequent fog in lowlands. Watch for afternoon thunderstorms in summer across the Bavarian Alps.

visits.text: Discover Munich, Germany's third-largest city and the vibrant capital of Bavaria. This cosmopolitan metropolis will captivate you with its sumptuous palaces, majestic parks and churches with iconic bell towers. The convivial atmosphere of the famous beer gardens and the richness of its architectural heritage make it an essential destination to begin your exploration of Bavaria.

Stroll around Marienplatz, the beating heart of the old town, where the imposing New Town Hall features its famous mechanical glockenspiel. Admire the Gothic architecture of the Frauenkirche with its iconic twin towers, then lose yourself in the picturesque lanes of the historic center where every facade tells the story of centuries of Bavarian history.

Explore the Munich Residenz, one of Europe's largest urban palaces and former seat of the Dukes and Kings of Bavaria. Its 130 sumptuously decorated rooms, Renaissance courtyards and treasury will immerse you in the splendor of the Bavarian monarchy. The nearby English Garden, one of the world's largest urban parks, offers an ideal green retreat.

activities.text: Stroll through the Schwabing district and its art galleries
Visit the Deutsches Museum, the world's largest science museum

visits.text: Delve into Augsburg's thousand-year history, one of Germany's oldest cities, founded by the Romans. During the Renaissance, this city was a world-renowned financial and commercial center, rivaling Venice and Florence. Its exceptional architectural heritage bears witness to this glorious era when the powerful Fugger and Welser families dominated European trade.

Admire the sumptuous Renaissance Town Hall, a masterpiece by Elias Holl, whose Golden Hall dazzles with its coffered ceilings adorned with gold leaf. The three monumental fountains on Maximilianstraße, dedicated to Roman deities, form a unique ensemble listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Visit the Fuggerei, the world's oldest social housing complex, in continuous operation since 1521. This picturesque neighborhood with ochre facades and cobblestone lanes offers a fascinating glimpse into Renaissance philanthropy and the social organization of the era.

activities.text: Discover Augsburg Cathedral and its 11th-century Romanesque stained glass windows

visits.text: Discover Lake Constance, nestled where Germany, Austria and Switzerland meet. This inland sea, with its deep blue waters, offers an exceptional natural setting, bordered by terraced vineyards and overlooked by Alpine peaks. The Mediterranean microclimate even allows exotic fruits to be grown along its shores.

Explore Lindau, the pearl of the German shore, whose historic center occupies a picturesque island linked to the mainland. Its iconic harbor, guarded by a Bavarian lion and a lighthouse, offers one of Germany's most photographed views. The patrician houses with painted facades and medieval lanes create an atmosphere of rare elegance.

Wander along the lakeside promenades lined with palm trees and magnolias, where the panorama of the Swiss Alps creates a postcard-perfect setting. Numerous cruise options allow you to discover the charming towns of Constance and Meersburg from the lake's crystal-clear waters.

activities.text: Panoramic cruise on Lake Constance

visits.text: Admire Neuschwanstein Castle, Bavaria's ultimate jewel. This fairy-tale fortress, perched on a rocky spur facing the Alps, served as the model for Walt Disney's Sleeping Beauty Castle. Its extravagant architecture, blending Romanesque and Gothic styles, rises from the fir forests like a medieval dream come true.

Enter the sumptuous apartments where King Ludwig II of Bavaria brought to life his romantic fantasies inspired by Wagner's operas. The throne room, never completed, was meant to rival the Palatine Chapel of Byzantium, while the illuminated artificial grotto evokes the legends of Tannhäuser. Each room reveals the eccentric and visionary personality of this solitary monarch.

Admire Hohenschwangau Castle, Ludwig II's childhood home, whose romantic frescoes depicting Germanic legends profoundly influenced the future king's imagination. The view from the gardens over both castles and Lake Alpsee forms a panorama of surreal beauty.

activities.text: Hike to Marienbrücke bridge for the iconic view of Neuschwanstein

visits.text: Visit Linderhof Palace, the most intimate of Ludwig II's palaces and the only one he saw completed in his lifetime. This rococo gem nestled in an Alpine valley enchants with its hilly park dotted with gushing fountains, sculpted groves and exotic pavilions. The Venus Grotto, artificially lit, recreates a scene from the opera Tannhäuser with a navigable underground lake.

Discover Ettal Abbey, a masterpiece of Bavarian Baroque founded in 1330 by Emperor Louis IV. Its monumental dome, one of Germany's largest, houses celestial frescoes of breathtaking magnificence. The Benedictine monks still perpetuate the tradition of monastic brewing and liqueur distillation to this day.

Wander through the lanes of Oberammergau, a village world-famous for its facades painted with biblical frescoes and fairy-tale scenes. This tradition of Lüftlmalerei, trompe-l'oeil painting on plaster, transforms every house into a work of art. The village has also hosted the famous Passion Play every ten years since 1634.

activities.text: Discover the local craft of woodcarving

visits.text: Conquer the Zugspitze, Germany's highest point at an elevation of 2,962 meters. Accessible by modern cable car or historic cogwheel train, this summit offers a dizzying panorama over four countries and more than 400 Alpine peaks. On clear days, the view stretches from the Italian Dolomites to the Bavarian plains in a magnificent natural spectacle.

Marvel at Lake Eibsee, an emerald lake with crystal-clear waters nestled at the foot of the Zugspitze. This natural jewel, dotted with eight small islands, offers a mountain setting of exceptional purity. The 7-kilometer trail circling it allows you to appreciate its multiple shades of blue and green depending on the light.

Explore Garmisch-Partenkirchen, a world-renowned Alpine resort that hosted the 1936 Winter Olympics. This twin town with authentic charm preserves its traditional houses with painted facades and cobblestone lanes. It's the ideal starting point for countless Alpine hikes and mountain activities.

activities.text: Panoramic cable car ascent to the Zugspitze

visits.text: Climb the Herzogstand, a hikers' paradise rising to 1,731 meters between two strikingly beautiful lakes. This iconic peak offers one of Bavaria's most beautiful panoramas, taking in the Kochelsee with its steely reflections and the turquoise waters of the Walchensee in a single view. A cable car makes access easier, but reaching the summit requires walking from the upper station.

Discover the Walchensee, one of Germany's deepest and purest Alpine lakes. Its intensely blue waters, often compared to tropical lagoons, contrast magnificently with the surrounding snow-capped peaks. This naturally dammed lake served as the setting for numerous films and remains a well-kept secret among Bavarians.

Contemplate the Kochelsee, a more peaceful and accessible lake bordered by green meadows and traditional villages. It was here that painter Franz Marc, a major figure of German Expressionism, found inspiration for his famous works. The Franz Marc Museum in the nearby village pays tribute to this master of color.

activities.text: Panoramic ridge hike on the Herzogstand

visits.text: Savor the beauty of Tegernsee, a lake prized by the Bavarian aristocracy as a vacation destination for centuries. Nestled at the foot of the Alps amid wooded mountains, this lake with pure waters has elegant towns with geranium-bedecked houses along its shores. The refined atmosphere and unspoiled setting make it a destination of choice for Munich residents seeking nature.

Visit the Baroque church of the former Benedictine abbey of Tegernsee, founded in the 8th century, whose brewery continues a thousand-year-old tradition. Remodeled in the 17th century, the church houses remarkable artistic treasures.

Ascend the Wallberg by panoramic cable car, then continue on foot to the summit for a 360-degree view of the Bavarian Alps. At an elevation of 1,722 meters, the panorama takes in the entire Tegernsee, the Austrian mountain ranges and, on a clear day, reaches as far as Munich. A panoramic terrace offers views of this spectacle in every season.

activities.text: Lakeside walk and discovery of the villages of Bad Wiessee and Rottach-Egern

visits.text: Sail on the Chiemsee, nicknamed the Bavarian Sea with its surface area of 80 km². Bavaria's largest lake and Germany's third-largest, this majestic body of water bordered by the Alps harbors several islands, each concealing unique treasures. The panorama of snow-capped peaks from the lake's calm waters forms a picture of absolute serenity.

Discover Herrenchiemsee Palace on Men's Island, Ludwig II's grandiose tribute to Versailles. This unfinished castle surpasses its French model through the splendor of its Hall of Mirrors, longer than the original. The French-style gardens, monumental fountains and royal apartments bear witness to the poetic megalomania of the king who built it.

Explore Fraueninsel (Women's Island), a charming fishing village dominated by a Benedictine convent founded in the 8th century. The nuns still produce liqueurs and marzipan according to centuries-old recipes today. The flower-lined lanes, fishermen's houses with colorful shutters and Romanesque church create a timeless atmosphere.

activities.text: Boat crossing to the islands of Chiemsee

visits.text: Behold the Königssee, the absolute jewel of German lakes, set between 1,800-meter vertical cliffs in the heart of Berchtesgaden National Park. This fjord-like lake with exceptionally pure emerald-green waters can only be explored by silent electric boats, perpetuating a century-old ecological tradition.

Sail to St. Bartholomew's pilgrimage church, a Baroque gem with red onion domes set on a peninsula at the foot of the dizzyingly steep rock face of the Watzmann. The legendary echo of the captain's trumpet resounding seven times off the cliffs is a magical moment of the crossing. This site of surreal beauty ranks among Germany's most photographed.

Hike in Berchtesgaden National Park, Germany's only Alpine national park, classified as a UNESCO biosphere reserve. This natural sanctuary is home to chamois, marmots and golden eagles in a setting of jagged peaks, tumultuous waterfalls and flowering alpine meadows. The town of Berchtesgaden itself charms with its preserved Bavarian authenticity.

activities.text: Electric boat cruise on Königssee

visits.text: Discover Passau, the Bavarian Venice, a spectacular city built at the confluence of three waterways: the blue Danube, the green Inn and the black Ilz. This unique geographical setting creates a fascinating spectacle of colors where waters of different colors are slow to mix. The old town on its peninsula offers romantic views at every turn of its lanes.

Visit St. Stephen's Cathedral, an Italian Baroque masterpiece housing the world's largest cathedral organ with its 17,974 pipes. Daily organ concerts make this monumental instrument resonate beneath vaults adorned with gilded stucco and celestial frescoes. The exceptional acoustics of this sanctuary make it a major center of European sacred music.

Stroll through the old town with its typically Italian pastel facades, a legacy of master builders from the peninsula after the fire of 1662. The elegant squares, vaulted passages and picturesque staircases bear witness to Passau's historic role as a commercial crossroads between Central Europe and Italy.

activities.text: Walk along the quays at the confluence of the three rivers

visits.text: Explore Ratisbon (Regensburg), Bavaria's first capital, listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. This city with 2,000 years of history contains more than 1,500 listed historic buildings, together forming Germany's best-preserved medieval architectural ensemble. The patrician towers competing in height bear witness to the power of medieval merchant families.

Cross the Stone Bridge, a masterpiece of 12th-century medieval engineering that served as the model for Prague's Charles Bridge. At 310 meters long and supported by 16 arches, this bridge offers a splendid panoramic view of the old town skyline dominated by the spires of the Gothic cathedral. It was once the only stone bridge over the Danube between Ulm and Vienna.

Admire St. Peter's Cathedral, the only example of pure French Gothic in Bavaria, whose medieval stained glass windows rank among Germany's finest. The old town abounds with architectural treasures: the old town hall where the Diet of the Holy Roman Empire sat, the colorful patrician houses and Renaissance inner courtyards.

activities.text: Walk along the Danube quays at sunset

visits.text: Immerse yourself in the history of Nuremberg (Nürnberg), Bavaria's second-largest city and an imperial city of crucial importance in the Middle Ages. This powerful city where the Diets of the Holy Roman Empire were held and where the imperial crown jewels were kept retains an authentic medieval atmosphere behind its imposing walls. Its Christmas market, the Christkindlesmarkt, is Germany's most famous.

Visit the Kaiserburg, the imperial fortress dominating the city from its rocky promontory. This complex castle, enlarged over the centuries, was the residence of all the emperors of the Holy Roman Empire. The view from its ramparts encompasses the red roofs of the old town, the church towers and the meanders of the Pegnitz River.

Discover the old town rebuilt after the destruction of 1945, where half-timbered houses stand alongside the Gothic churches of St. Sebaldus and St. Lawrence. The Nuremberg Trials courthouse, Albrecht Dürer's house and the Documentation Center on Nazism bear witness to both the dark and bright chapters in the history of this city of art and culture.

activities.text: Visit the Germanic National Museum, the largest museum of German art and culture
Stroll through the medieval lanes of the artisans' quarter

visits.text: Marvel at Bamberg, one of Germany's most beautiful cities, listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. This thousand-year-old city, miraculously spared by bombing, has more than 2,300 listed historic buildings. Built on seven hills like Rome, it harmoniously blends medieval, Baroque and Rococo architecture into an exceptionally cohesive whole.

Photograph the Altes Rathaus, the old town hall built on an artificial island in the middle of the Regnitz River, Bavaria's most iconic monument. Its trompe-l'oeil frescoes adorning the half-timbered facades create the illusion of three-dimensional sculptures. According to legend, when the bishop refused to cede land, the burghers created this island to build their town hall.

Visit the four-towered Imperial Cathedral, a Romanesque masterpiece housing the tomb of Emperor Henry II and the famous Bamberg Horseman, the first life-size equestrian statue of the Middle Ages. Bavaria's Little Venice, the former fishermen's quarter with colorful houses reflected in the river, completes this enchanting picture.

activities.text: Tasting Rauchbier, a smoked beer and local specialty

visits.text: Admire the Würzburg Residence, one of Europe's most beautiful Baroque palaces, listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. This architectural masterpiece commands respect from the moment you reach the grand ceremonial staircase, covered by the world's largest fresco, painted by Tiepolo and depicting the four continents. The 340 sumptuously decorated rooms rival Versailles in magnificence.

Explore Würzburg, an elegant city in the heart of Bavaria's Franconian wine country. Dominated by Marienberg Fortress perched on its hill, this episcopal city abounds with Baroque churches with dazzling interiors. The Old Main Bridge, adorned with monumental statues of saints, offers a romantic view of the terraced vineyards.

Discover the renowned Franconian vineyards producing excellent white wine served in the characteristic flat bottles called Bocksbeutel. The wine region stretches along the Main River in a hilly landscape punctuated by picturesque wine villages and castles overlooking the hillsides.

activities.text: Walk across the Old Bridge and Franconian wine tasting

map_keywords: St. Jakobskirche Rothenburg ob der Tauber

visits.text: Enter Rothenburg ob der Tauber, Germany's most beautiful medieval city, comparable to Carcassonne in its exceptional preservation. This fortified town seems frozen in the Renaissance with its intact ramparts, watchtowers and cobblestone lanes lined with half-timbered houses adorned with flowering geraniums. Time stopped here in the 16th century.

Walk along the covered wall walk, which offers unique views of the red roofs and flower-filled courtyards. The 42 towers punctuating the walls and the monumental fortified gates bear witness to the power of this Free Imperial City. The Plönlein, a picturesque junction between two towers, is the most photographed view in Bavaria.

Visit St. James's Church housing the Altar of the Holy Blood, a masterpiece by Tilman Riemenschneider, and the Medieval Crime Museum displaying torture and justice instruments of the era. The Christmas Museum open year-round perpetuates the tradition of Käthe Wohlfahrt's handcrafted decorations, famous worldwide.

activities.text: Nighttime guided tour with the night watchman in period costume

itineraries.title: Southern Germany Road Trip: Castles, Forests & Medieval Towns
itineraries.subtitle: From the Romantic Road to the Bavarian Alps, from the Black Forest to the Roman baths of Trier: 8 days through the landscapes and history of southern Germany.
itineraries.climate: Best period: May-June and September, temperatures 15-22°C, ideal for castles and hiking. Avoid July-August (heat and tourist crowds at popular sites, frequent thunderstorms in the mountains). Alpine roads may be snowy until May.
specialties: Schwarzwälder Kirschtorte (Black Forest cake with cherries and kirsch)

map_keywords: Marktplatz Rathaus Rothenburg ob der Tauber
St. Jakobskirche Rothenburg ob der Tauber
Mittelalterliches Kriminalmuseum Rothenburg ob der Tauber

visits.text: Start at the Plönlein early in the morning—before 8am if possible, as tour buses don't arrive until after 9am. This small Y-shaped intersection is framed by two 14th-century towers: the Siebersturm on the left (1385) and the Kobolzeller Tor on the right. The yellow-and-red half-timbered house standing prominently between them is said to have inspired the village setting in Disney's Pinocchio. The composition is perfect in the slanting morning light.

Continue along the rampart walkway—4 kilometers punctuated by 42 towers, free to explore. Rothenburg survived the Thirty Years' War almost intact thanks to a colorful legend: in 1631, General Tilly, having seized the town, promised to spare it if a local notable could drain a 3.25-liter tankard of wine in one go. Former mayor Nusch took up the challenge. Every Pentecost, locals reenact the scene during the Meistertrunk.

Then head to the Marktplatz, the town's heart since medieval times. The town hall (Rathaus) combines two styles side by side: a Gothic 14th-century facade facing north, and a Renaissance facade facing the square. Climb the 60-meter belfry for a view over red-tiled roofs and the Tauber valley. On the 1683 clock, figurines come to life every hour between 11am and 3pm to reenact the Meistertrunk scene.

Then step inside St. James's Church (Sankt Jakobskirche), built between 1311 and 1484. It houses two key works: the Holy Blood Altarpiece carved by Tilman Riemenschneider around 1499–1505, considered one of the masterpieces of German late Gothic art, and the Twelve Apostles Altarpiece by Friedrich Herlin (1466). Also look at the choir's stained-glass windows, dating from the 14th century.

At the end of the day, make your way to the Burggarten (castle garden), which occupies the site of the Hohenstaufen fortress built in 1142 and destroyed by an earthquake in 1356. Only St. Blaise Chapel survives. The garden offers a panorama over the Tauber valley and the vineyards below—this is the best time to have it almost to yourself.

The Medieval Crime Museum (Mittelalterliches Kriminalmuseum) houses its collections in the former commandery of the Knights of St. John. Over 50,000 objects related to medieval European justice: instruments of public humiliation, shame masks, cages, law books and seals. An unsettling museum, often overlooked by visitors in a hurry.

activities.text: Rothenburg can be explored on foot within its compact area of about 1 km². A nighttime guided tour starting from the Marktplatz with the Night Watchman in medieval costume is available - a different way to discover the town once the daytime groups have left.

visits.text: Neuschwanstein Castle perches on a rocky spur 200 meters above the valley. Ludwig II of Bavaria had it built starting in 1869 as a "worthy temple" dedicated to his friend Richard Wagner—the interior frescoes illustrate the composer's operas. The king spent only 172 nights in his castle before being removed by the government in 1886, then found dead in Lake Starnberg three days later. Book your ticket well in advance: 6,000 visitors daily in summer.

Next, climb to the Marienbrücke bridge, built above the Pöllat gorge, for the postcard view of Neuschwanstein - the one that inspired Sleeping Beauty Castle at Disneyland in 1955. Walt Disney explicitly referred to Neuschwanstein when designing the castle. In winter, the bridge may be closed for safety reasons in snowy or icy conditions.

Descend to Hohenschwangau Castle, Ludwig II's childhood residence, restored by his father Maximilian II starting in 1833 in neo-Gothic style. This is where young Ludwig grew up surrounded by murals illustrating medieval legends that would nourish his imagination for life. Combined ticket available with Neuschwanstein.

In late afternoon, head to Füssen to visit the old town and the Hohes Schloss, the former summer residence of the Prince-Bishops of Augsburg. The town marks the southern terminus of the Romantic Road, just a few hundred meters from the Austrian border. The historic core with its painted facades and cobbled lanes deserves an hour of wandering.

activities.text: Lake Alpsee, directly below the two castles, lends itself to a short stroll along its shores. Ludwig II himself walked these banks. In summer, rowboats are available for rent.

visits.text: The Bavarian Forest National Park (Bayerischer Wald) is Germany's oldest national park, created in 1970. It covers 24,000 hectares along the Czech border, continuous with Šumava National Park on the Bohemian side—together they form the largest protected forest area in Central Europe.

Start at the Tierfreigelände in Neuschönau, a 250-hectare natural enclosure where 45 animal species live in conditions close to their wild habitat: wolves, brown bears, lynx, European bison, otters, beavers, deer and large raptors. A 7-kilometer trail winds through the site—allow 3 to 4 hours. Bring binoculars, as some animals keep their distance. Entry is free.

Then head to Rachelsee, a mountain lake at an altitude of 1,071 meters, surrounded by century-old beeches and spruces. Local legend says its name derives from the devil's grandmother and tells of an evil woman who was the last to travel across its waters, her coffin accompanied by a flock of black ravens. The trail from Spiegelau is well marked.

Stop at the Hans-Eisenmann-Haus visitor center in Neuschönau, which presents the park's history and wildlife. It's also the starting point for the Baumwipfelpfad, a 1,300-meter aerial walkway that winds through the forest canopy.

activities.text: Hike the marked trails of the park from Riedlhütte or Neuschönau. Over 500 kilometers of paths crisscross the park, some passing through “primeval forest” zones where no human intervention has been permitted for decades. The areas around Lusen and Großer Rachel are the wildest.

visits.text: Start with the Partnachklamm, a 700-meter gorge carved by the Partnach River, with walls rising up to 80 meters in places. Designated a natural monument as early as 1912, it's accessible via a path carved into the rock alongside the glacial torrent. In winter, the waterfalls transform into spectacular frozen cascades. Allow 25 minutes on foot from the Olympic stadium.

Then head back up to Partenkirchen's Ludwigstrasse for a stroll through the historic heart. Garmisch and Partenkirchen were two separate municipalities for centuries before being forcibly merged by Hitler in 1935, ahead of the 1936 Winter Olympics. Their character remains distinct: Garmisch is more modern, while Partenkirchen retains its houses with painted trompe-l'oeil facades, a Bavarian decorative style called Lüftlmalerei.

Spend the afternoon on the Zugspitze, Germany's highest point at 2,962 meters, on the Austrian border. In clear weather, the panorama stretches as far as Italy. A 90-year-old cogwheel train connects Garmisch to the glacial plateau at 2,600 meters, from where a 1,000-meter cable car ascends to the summit.

activities.text: Walk around Lake Eibsee, with its turquoise waters surrounded by limestone rocks and pine forests, at the foot of the Zugspitze. The complete loop is about 7 kilometers. In summer, rowboats can be rented on site.

to_next_leg.road_type: mountain pass

map_keywords: Wallfahrtskirche Maria in der Tanne Triberg

visits.text: Start with the Triberg waterfalls: the Gutach River drops 163 meters in seven successive cascades through the granite rocks of the Black Forest. The site is illuminated until 10 p.m. Come on a weekday or early in the morning - the main path can get busy in peak season. The admission ticket includes access to the Black Forest Museum.

Continue to the Schwarzwaldmuseum, established in 1873, which showcases regional crafts and traditional life across 1,600 m²: clockmaking, folk costumes including the famous Bollenhut with red or black pompoms (indicating the woman's marital status), and a collection of mechanical music boxes and orchestrions. Triberg has been at the center of the Clockmakers' Route since the 18th century.

Make a detour to Triberg station, starting point for the Schwarzwaldbahn discovery trail. This historic line connecting Offenburg to Singen passes through Triberg with its 37 tunnels and a 700-meter elevation gain over 149 kilometers—an engineering feat when built between 1863 and 1873.

activities.text: Hike one of three marked trails around the waterfalls: the Kaskadenweg (45 minutes), the Kulturweg (1 hour) or the Naturweg (1 hour 30 minutes). All offer different perspectives on the falls and surrounding forest. After the ascent, continue on forest paths above the waterfalls to reach the small Bergsee lake.

visits.text: Take the Schwarzwaldhochstrasse (B500) to reach Baden-Baden through the uplands—60 kilometers of forests and ridges, this is the scenic route through the northern Black Forest. Join it from the south when arriving from Triberg.

Next, head down into the old town to see the ruins of the Roman baths. Baden-Baden's springs rise from a depth of 2,000 meters at temperatures between 56 and 68 degrees - 800,000 liters a day flow from twelve artesian springs that are 12,000 to 17,000 years old. The Romans called the town Aquae Aureliae.

Then book a session at the Friedrichsbad, built between 1869 and 1877 by architect Karl Dernfeld. Inspired by Roman baths and Irish baths, it offers 17 bathing stations beneath a 17.5-meter dome. Mark Twain stayed there and wrote: “After 10 minutes, you forget time; after 20 minutes, the world.” The bathing tradition here is mixed-gender and without swimsuits.

End the day with a walk along the Lichtentaler Allee, which follows the Oos River for 2.3 kilometers between the town center and the Cistercian abbey of Lichtenthal founded in 1245. This avenue lined with century-old trees was Europe's open-air salon in the 19th century—Napoleon III, Queen Victoria, Dostoevsky and Brahms all stayed here.

activities.text: The modern Caracalla Therme, opened in 1985 and covering 5,000 m², allows you to enjoy the thermal waters in a swimsuit. Several pools at temperatures between 18 and 38 degrees, an outdoor pool open year-round, saunas and steam baths. More accessible than the Friedrichsbad, with or without a reservation.

visits.text: Begin with the Porta Nigra, whose construction began in 169–170 AD as the northern entrance gate of the Roman city of Augusta Treverorum. Its 7,200 sandstone blocks, weighing up to 6 tonnes each, are assembled without mortar, held by iron clamps secured with lead. It owes its name to the dark color the stone has taken on over the centuries. It survived thanks to the hermit Simeon, who settled there in the 11th century: Bishop Poppo had the gate transformed into a church in his honor in 1040, thus sparing it from demolition. Napoleon had the medieval additions removed during his visit in 1804.

Next, head to the Basilica of Constantine (Konstantinbasilika), the former imperial throne room: 67 meters long, 27 wide and 33 high. Trier was one of the largest cities in the Roman Empire, described as a “second Rome” at the end of the 3rd century. Constantine the Great lived there for six years in the early 4th century. The basilica's acoustics, with a 7-second echo, now make it a concert venue.

Continue to St. Peter's Cathedral, Germany's oldest, built in the 4th century on the site of a palace from Constantine's era. The cathedral-Liebfrauenkirche ensemble has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986. The Liebfrauenkirche, completed around 1260, is the first entirely Gothic church in Germany.

Next, visit the Imperial Baths (Kaiserthermen), begun under Constantine in the early 4th century. They were never completed - the building was converted into military barracks and later a quarry. Go down into the underground passages where slaves fed the hypocausts (underfloor heating systems).

Trier's amphitheater, built in the 2nd century, could accommodate 20,000 spectators—one of the best-preserved Roman amphitheaters north of the Alps. Descend into the underground cellars where gladiators and animals waited to enter the arena.

Finish with a walk along the Moselle riverbanks and through the old town. Karl Marx was born in Trier in 1818—his birthplace is now a museum. To leave the city, Frankfurt is about 2 hours by train, Luxembourg 50 kilometers away.

activities.text: The Moselle Valley around Trier is one of Germany's most renowned wine regions, specializing in Riesling grown on steep slate slopes. Several estates offer tastings in the surrounding villages.

seo.h1_title: Southern Germany Road Trip: Castles, Forests & Medieval Towns
seo.intro_paragraph: Rothenburg ob der Tauber with its intact ramparts, Neuschwanstein perched on its rocky spur, the Bavarian Forest with its wolves, the glacial gorges of Garmisch, the waterfalls of Triberg, the Roman baths of Baden-Baden, and Trier, Germany's oldest city. 8 days through the deep south.
seo.seo_hook: Neuschwanstein, medieval Rothenburg, the Black Forest, the Bavarian Alps: 8 days of contrasts in southern Germany, from fairy-tale castles to Roman baths.
featured_list: Neuschwanstein: the castle that inspired Disney
Garmisch: the Zugspitze and its glacial gorges

Trier: the Rome of the North
