itineraries.title: German Alpine Road: Lake Constance to Königssee
itineraries.subtitle: Five days along the Deutsche Alpenstraße from Lindau Island on the Bodensee to the emerald waters of Königssee, via Neuschwanstein, the Zugspitze, and Herrenchiemsee Palace.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May-June and September-October, with temperatures of 15 to 23°C, ideal for Alpine scenery and castles. Avoid July-August (severe afternoon thunderstorms in the mountains, heavy tourist crowds).

visits.text: Begin the route on Lindau Island on Lake Constance (Bodensee). The old town occupies a 70-hectare island that's been linked to the mainland by a railway bridge since 1853. Two iconic guardians stand at the harbor entrance: the Mangturm, a former 13th-century lighthouse 37 meters tall that guided boats on the lake from 1230, and the new white lighthouse built between 1853 and 1856—Bavaria's only lighthouse. The 6-meter sandstone statue of the Bavarian lion, the work of sculptor Johann von Halbig unveiled in 1856, completes the scene.

Stroll down Maximilianstrasse, the old town's main artery, lined with burgher houses in varied architectural styles—Gothic, Renaissance, and Baroque—forming a surprisingly harmonious row. Along the way, stop at Reichsplatz to see the 15th-century Altes Rathaus with its fresco-painted facade. Lindau was a free imperial city from 1275 to 1805 and hosted several Diets of the Holy Roman Empire at this town hall.

Continue east along the Deutsche Alpenstraße—Germany's oldest tourist route, inaugurated in 1933, which links Lindau to Berchtesgaden over 450 km along the Alps. The first major stop is Bad Hindelang and its Oberjochpass: 106 bends over 5 km to climb 300 meters, including 9 hairpins winding spectacularly above the village. Built in 1895, the Jochstraße was already a feat of road engineering—in 1662, 15,850 barrels of salt passed through here each year on the backs of 300 horses. Allow for a round trip within the day from Lindau to Bad Hindelang and the Oberjochpass.

Halfway up the Oberjochpass, stop at the Kanzel, a viewpoint offering a panoramic view of the Ostrach valley, Bad Hindelang and Bad Oberdorf below, with the Nagelfluhkette and the 2,224-meter Nebelhorn in the background. It is one of the best viewpoints accessible by car in the Bavarian Alps. Allow for a round trip within the day from Lindau to reach this viewpoint.

activities.text: Take a ferry from Lindau harbor along the shores of the Bodensee toward Bregenz (Austria) or Friedrichshafen. From the water, the silhouette of the island's old town, with its two lighthouses and colorful facades, comes fully into view—it is from out on the lake that Lindau truly reveals itself.

A self-guided walk at the Aussichtspunkt Kanzel on the Oberjochpass, with a short path from the parking lot leading to the viewpoint in 2 minutes. In fine weather, the panorama extends to the Austrian ranges. Allow for a round trip within the day from Lindau for this walk.

to_next_leg.road_type: mountain pass

visits.text: Neuschwanstein Castle rises on a rocky outcrop 200 meters above Hohenschwangau village. Ludwig II of Bavaria laid its first stone on September 5, 1869, as a “worthy temple” dedicated to his friend Richard Wagner—the interior frescoes directly illustrate the composer's operas. The king spent only 172 nights here before being deposed by the government for “insanity” in June 1886, then found dead in Lake Starnberg three days later. The castle opened to the public seven weeks after his death and now attracts over a million visitors annually. Book your guided tour slot well in advance.

Then climb to Marienbrücke, a bridge spanning the Pöllat gorge, for a view looking down on Neuschwanstein—this is the angle that inspired Walt Disney's Sleeping Beauty Castle at Disneyland in 1955, and later the studio logo. The bridge is closed in winter due to ice.

Descend to Hohenschwangau Castle, Ludwig II's childhood residence, restored in neo-Gothic style by his father Maximilian II from 1833. The murals depict medieval legends of the Swan Knight and the Nibelungen - a backdrop that shaped the future king's imagination. Available as a combined ticket with Neuschwanstein.

In the late afternoon, head to Füssen to see the Hohes Schloss, the former summer residence of the prince-bishops of Augsburg overlooking the old town. Its exterior facade is adorned with trompe-l'oeil paintings imitating Gothic windows and carved balconies—an exceptional illusionistic decoration. The castle now houses a gallery of the Bavarian State Collections.

Continue to the Lechfall, an artificial cascade built in the 18th century to prevent Füssen from flooding. The Lech River, with the turquoise waters characteristic of Alpine limestone torrents, plunges 12 meters in several tiers into a narrow gorge. From the König-Max-Steg bridge (1895), named after King Maximilian II, the view of the falls is striking.

activities.text: Walk around the Alpsee, the lake directly below both castles. A flat trail follows the shore for about 4 km. Ludwig II himself walked here regularly. In summer, rowboats are available for rent.

visits.text: Start your morning at the Partnachklamm, a 700-meter gorge carved up to 80 meters deep by the Partnach River through limestone cliffs south of Garmisch. A path hewn into the rock follows the glacial torrent - the water, flowing from Zugspitze glaciers, maintains an intense blue-green tint. Designated a natural monument in 1912, the gorge is a 25-minute walk from the Olympic stadium.

Continue to Lake Eibsee, its turquoise waters framed by limestone rocks and pine forests at the foot of the Zugspitze. From its shores, the cable car inaugurated in 2017 ascends to the summit, holding three world records: tallest support tower (127 m), greatest elevation difference (1,945 m), and longest unsupported span in the world.

activities.text: Ascend the Zugspitze, Germany's highest peak at 2,962 meters on the Austrian border. The 90-year-old cogwheel train climbs from Garmisch to the glacier plateau at 2,600 meters, where a second cable car reaches the summit. On clear days, the panorama extends to the Dolomites and the Swiss Alps. Allow half a day and book ahead in season.

visits.text: Board a boat from Prien-Stock harbor to reach Herreninsel Island on Chiemsee, Bavaria's largest lake. The crossing takes about 20 minutes. In 1873, Ludwig II purchased the entire island for 350,000 florins from an industrialist who planned to clear its entire forest. Construction of the palace began in 1878 under the direction of Georg von Dollmann.

Tour Herrenchiemsee Palace, Ludwig II's final and most lavish construction project—and the one where he spent the least time: just 16 days. The king spent more money on this single construction than on Neuschwanstein and Linderhof combined. At his death in 1886, 50 rooms remained unfinished. The Great Hall of Mirrors, inspired by the one at Versailles, measures 98 meters—25 meters longer than its French model. To illuminate it, 70 servants had to light 33 candelabras and 52 chandeliers.

After the palace, take the boat to Fraueninsel (Women's Island), where the Frauenwörth Benedictine convent has existed for 1,200 years—one of Germany's oldest monastic communities still in operation. Walk around the small island (one hour on foot) among fishermen's houses and monastery gardens. The nuns produce a renowned local spirit.

activities.text: At the end of the day, back in Prien, stroll along the shores of Chiemsee on the Priener Uferweg. Enjoy the sunset over the lake with the Alps in the background.

visits.text: Board one of the Königssee's electric boats at Schönau to explore this lake, protected since 1978 within Berchtesgaden National Park. The lake, 8 km long and 190 meters deep, is enclosed by vertical limestone walls. Halfway along, the skipper plays a trumpet toward the rock face to demonstrate the exceptional echo.

Disembark at St. Bartholomä, a peninsula accessible only by boat. The baroque pilgrimage church, built from 1134 onward and remodeled in the early 18th century, is recognizable from afar by its red onion domes. The church and former royal hunting lodge, silhouetted against the east face of the Watzmann (1,800 meters of vertical rock face), form one of Germany's most famous photographic subjects.

Continue by boat to Salet to walk to the Obersee—a flat 15-minute walk from the dock. This smaller lake, with no boats whatsoever, has absolutely clear water and perfect reflections of the surrounding rock walls. Since commercial fishing ended in 1978, the lake has returned to its wild state.

Then board the Jennerbahn to reach the Jenner summit at 1,800 meters. The view takes in the entire Königssee, the east face of the Watzmann, and the Berchtesgaden Alps on the Austrian side. Salzburg is 30 km away—this area is the natural endpoint of the circuit for those returning their car in Austria.

activities.text: Hike the Malerwinkel-Rundweg, a scenic forest trail above the Königssee offering the classic view of the lake from above. In 2015, this spot was ranked Germany's 12th tourist attraction. Allow 1 to 2 hours depending on your pace.

seo.h1_title: German Alpine Road: Lake Constance to Königssee
seo.intro_paragraph: The medieval island of Lindau on the Bodensee, the 106 bends of the Oberjochpass, Neuschwanstein perched on its rocky spur, the Zugspitze and its glaciers, Herrenchiemsee Palace and the Königssee enclosed by its limestone walls. Five days on the Deutsche Alpenstraße, Germany's oldest tourist route.
seo.seo_hook: From Lindau to Königssee, 450 km through the Bavarian Alps: Neuschwanstein, Herrenchiemsee, glacial lakes and Ludwig II's castles along the Deutsche Alpenstraße.

itineraries.title: Saxony Road Trip, Germany: Dresden, Leipzig and Saxon Switzerland
itineraries.subtitle: From baroque Dresden to the Bastei cliffs, via Meissen porcelain and Seiffen's toys
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May to September, with temperatures of 18–25°C, ideal for visiting Dresden and hiking in Saxon Switzerland. Avoid December–February: damp cold (0–5°C), frequent gray skies, and less accessible sites. Moderate rainfall year-round; bring a raincoat.

visits.text: The Zwinger is Dresden's most iconic monument. Built from 1709 by Matthäus Daniel Pöppelmann for Augustus the Strong, Elector of Saxony and King of Poland, it began as an orangery and princely festival arena. Its official inauguration took place in 1719 for the marriage of Augustus's son to Archduchess Maria Josepha of Austria. Six pavilions linked by galleries enclose a vast interior courtyard with fountains and lawns—Augustus the Strong had himself depicted as Hercules above the Wallpavillon. The Kronentor, the gate crowned by a golden crown carried by four eagles, is the complex's most photographed image.

The Old Masters Picture Gallery, housed in the Semper Wing built between 1847 and 1855, contains over 700 paintings from the 15th to 18th centuries. Its greatest treasure is Raphael's Sistine Madonna, painted around 1512 and acquired by Augustus III in 1754 for the colossal sum of 25,000 ducats. Rubens, Vermeer, Rembrandt, Titian, Giorgione, and Botticelli are also represented. The paintings had been evacuated before the 1945 bombings—they were found hidden in underground mines and returned by the USSR in 1955 after being held in Moscow for ten years.

The Zwinger Porcelain Collection houses some 20,000 pieces of Chinese, Japanese, and Meissen porcelain. Augustus the Strong was so obsessed that in 1717 he traded a regiment of 600 Prussian soldiers for 151 Chinese porcelain vases—these pieces are still on display here. The collection also illustrates how the discovery of European porcelain at Meissen in 1708 arose from a royal commission for alchemy: Augustus wanted gold, his chemists invented porcelain.

The Semperoper, standing on Theaterplatz facing the Zwinger, is one of Europe's most renowned opera houses. The first building was designed by Gottfried Semper and inaugurated in 1841, then destroyed by fire in 1869. The second, also designed by Semper but completed by his son Manfred, reopened in 1878—the elder Semper was then banished from Saxony for participating in the 1849 insurrection. Razed by the February 13, 1945 bombings, it was rebuilt to match the original and reopened on February 13, 1985, exactly forty years after its destruction. Richard Strauss premiered several of his operas here, including Der Rosenkavalier in 1911.

activities.text: Walk or electric scooter ride along the Elbe to admire Dresden's reconstructed skyline
Observation platform at the Frauenkirche for views over the city

visits.text: The Residenzschloss, palace of the prince-electors and kings of Saxony, is one of Dresden's oldest buildings. Its construction dates to 1220; it was remodeled in Renaissance style between 1548 and 1556, then partially destroyed in 1945 and gradually rebuilt from 1986. It now houses several major museums. The Historic Green Vault (Historisches Grünes Gewölbe) presents 3,000 examples of baroque goldsmithing in their original 18th-century display cases—one of Europe's largest treasure collections. On November 25, 2019, thieves broke a window at 5 a.m. and stole several sets of diamond jewelry from the collection: the case caused a scandal throughout Germany.

The Fürstenzug stretches 102 meters along the outer wall of the Stallhof, the palace stable courtyard. This monumental mural depicts the procession of the 35 rulers of the House of Wettin, from Conrad I in 1127 to King George I in the early 20th century, accompanied by soldiers, artists, and scholars. Originally painted between 1871 and 1876 to celebrate 800 years of the dynasty, it was replaced between 1904 and 1907 by approximately 23,000 Meissen porcelain tiles to withstand the weather—it's the world's largest porcelain artwork. Despite the 1945 bombings, only 200 tiles had to be replaced during restoration.

The Frauenkirche, standing on the Neumarkt, is the symbol of Dresden's resurrection. Built between 1726 and 1743 by municipal architect Georg Bähr, the church has a 96-meter stone dome—the largest north of the Alps—which withstood Prussian cannonballs in 1760 as they bounced off it. The church collapsed, however, on February 15, 1945, two days after the Allied bombings, from the accumulated heat in the sandstone. The ruins remained a memorial for 45 years under the GDR. Reconstruction, financed by donations from around the world, lasted from 1994 to 2005: 3,643 original stones blackened by fire were reintegrated into the new edifice, identifiable by their dark color among the light blocks. The golden cross at the top was donated by British donors, including the son of one of the pilots who had bombed the city.

activities.text: Ascent to the Frauenkirche observation gallery for a panoramic view of Dresden's rooftops, the Elbe, and surrounding hills. Access is via an interior staircase to the dome lantern, 67 meters above ground.

practical_info.booking: Separate ticket, reservation recommended in high season

visits.text: The Neustadt, on the right bank of the Elbe, is Dresden's artistic quarter—it survived the 1945 bombings better than the Altstadt, and its Art Nouveau streets from the early 20th century have kept their character. The Kunsthofpassage, a series of five interconnected courtyards, is the best-known example of this creativity: each courtyard was entrusted to different artists. The most famous is the Court of Elements, whose blue facade is covered with gutters shaped like trumpets and funnels that transform rain into music.

The Brühlsche Terrasse, nicknamed "the balcony of Europe" by Goethe, is a 500-meter elevated promenade along the Elbe above the old ramparts. Developed in the 18th century on medieval fortifications by Count Brühl, it offers the classic view of the Altstadt silhouette with its domes and steeples. It's from this terrace that Romantic painters—notably Canaletto and Caspar David Friedrich—immortalized Dresden's panorama.

The Albertinum houses the Gallery of New Masters, covering painting and sculpture from the 19th century to the present. The collection includes works by Caspar David Friedrich, including Two Men Contemplating the Moon, as well as Impressionist and Expressionist paintings. The building itself, a 19th-century neo-Renaissance arsenal, was flooded during the 2002 Elbe floods—the works had to be urgently carried to upper floors to be saved.

Moritzburg Castle rises in the middle of a vast artificial pond, its silhouette with four round towers topped by copper roofs reflecting in the water—the image is striking, especially in misty weather. The first hunting lodge was built here between 1542 and 1546 by Duke Moritz of Saxony, whose name the castle bears. Augustus the Strong had it completely rebuilt in Baroque style from 1703, with the help of Pöppelmann, architect of the Zwinger. The interiors of its more than 200 rooms are lined with painted leather depicting hunting scenes—unique 18th-century pieces—and house the world's largest collection of deer trophies. Napoleon stayed here in 1806, on the occasion of the coronation of his ally the King of Saxony. In winter, the castle hosts the Three Nuts for Cinderella exhibition, named after the 1973 Czechoslovak fairy-tale film that was shot here and remains a cult classic throughout Central Europe.

The Fasanenschlösschen, the little pheasant palace, is located 2.5 km from the main castle at the end of a long vista laid out through the forest. This bright pink rococo pavilion, built between 1769 and 1782, was used as a secondary residence during hunting parties. Its miniature harbor with a jetty and Saxony's only lighthouse—a pink lighthouse, too—served as the setting for reenacted naval battles that the princes organized on the ponds.

activities.text: Walk around the pond to see the castle from all angles. The promenade around the lake is about 3 km and takes 45 minutes. The most impressive view of the castle is from the opposite shore.

visits.text: The Albrechtsburg dominates Meissen from a rocky promontory above the Elbe. This late Gothic castle, begun in 1471 by architect Arnold of Westphalia, is considered one of Germany's first residential palaces—designed as a princely residence rather than a fortress. In 1710, Augustus the Strong installed Europe's very first porcelain manufactory here, under the direction of alchemist Johann Friedrich Böttger, who had promised to make gold and discovered porcelain instead. The manufacturing secret was so well guarded that workers were not allowed to leave the castle. Production remained here until 1863, when it was transferred to new buildings below. The interior walls are covered with 19th-century frescoes illustrating Saxony's history.

The Cathedral of Saints John and Donatus, adjoining the Albrechtsburg on the same promontory, was built from 1250 on the ruins of a 10th-century Romanesque church. Construction continued until the end of the 15th century. It houses 14th-century Gothic sculptures depicting Emperor Otto I and his wife Adelaide of Burgundy, as well as paintings by Lucas Cranach the Elder.

The Meissen Porcelain Manufactory, in its current buildings at the foot of the hill, houses the most comprehensive museum on the history of European porcelain. The demonstration workshops allow you to watch the different stages of production—modeling, wheel throwing, glazing, hand painting—carried out according to methods unchanged since the 18th century. The trademark of two crossed blue swords, created in 1722, is one of the oldest trademarks still in use in the world.

activities.text: Porcelain painting workshop at the Meissen Manufactory. The workshops offer introductory sessions where visitors paint a design on a piece of porcelain themselves, supervised by an artist from the manufactory.

practical_info.booking: Reservation required on the manufactory website

visits.text: The Karl May Museum occupies two buildings: Villa Shatterhand, where the writer lived from 1895 until his death in 1912, and Villa Bärenfett, a Wild West-style log cabin built next door. Karl May—who had never set foot in America when he wrote his novels about Winnetou—owned a collection here of over 800 Native American ethnographic objects from the 18th and 19th centuries. His study, library, and Oriental drawing room are preserved exactly as they were in Villa Shatterhand. May is the most-read German novelist of all time, with 200 million copies sold worldwide.

The vineyards of Radebeul cover the slopes above the town, facing due south on terraces supported by stone walls. This 507-hectare region is one of Germany's northernmost—vines have been cultivated here since at least the 12th century. The dominant grape varieties are Riesling, Müller-Thurgau, and Pinot Blanc. Wackerbarth Palace, a state-owned wine estate founded in 1728, is the best-known in the valley.

activities.text: Hiking in the Radebeul vineyards with views over the Elbe valley. Marked trails cross the vineyard terraces to the Bismarckturm at the hilltop. Allow about 2 hours for a complete circuit with views of Dresden in the distance.

Saxon wine tasting at a Radebeul winery. Local winemakers offer guided tastings in the cellar or on the terrace with views over the vines—Riesling, Pinot Blanc, and Goldriesling are the region's flagship wines.

visits.text: Pillnitz Castle is actually an ensemble of three palaces set in a 28-hectare park on the banks of the Elbe, 15 km southeast of Dresden. Augustus the Strong had received it from a disgraced former mistress—the Countess of Cosel—and decided to make it a pleasure palace “in the Indian style,” meaning exotic. Between 1720 and 1724, architect Pöppelmann built the Wasserpalais and Bergpalais, two symmetrical buildings with characteristic pagoda roofs, framing a Baroque courtyard. A wide staircase descends from the Wasserpalais to the Elbe, where royal gondolas docked directly. In 1791, it was here that the Emperor of Austria and the King of Prussia signed the Declaration of Pillnitz, threatening military intervention in France if the French royal family were mistreated—which precipitated the declaration of war.

The New Palace, built between 1819 and 1826 after the fire of 1818 destroyed the Renaissance wing, closes off the eastern side of the courtyard. Its Classical dome is the only one of its kind in Dresden. The park also contains a Chinese pavilion from 1804 and a Neoclassical English pavilion from 1780. The garden's camellia, imported from Japan around 1780 and planted in 1800, stands 8.9 meters tall and produces up to 35,000 carmine-red flowers between February and April.

activities.text: Stroll in Pillnitz Park between the three palaces, French gardens, English garden, and greenhouses. You can also walk along the Elbe on the landscaped banks below the Wasserpalais.

visits.text: Pirna is the gateway to Saxon Switzerland—and a medieval town worth a stop in itself. Its lanes around the Marktplatz have remained almost intact since the 16th century, with Renaissance facades with Gothic porticoes and houses with Baroque elements in adjacent streets (Schmiedergasse, Schössergasse). The painter Bernardo Bellotto, known as Canaletto, worked there in the 1750s and left several paintings of the town that show how little it has changed—some are visible at the Residenzschloss in Dresden.

The Marienkirche, whose steeples dominate the Marktplatz, is a Gothic church built from the 14th to 16th centuries. Its interior, modified in the Baroque era, retains Gothic ribbed vaults and a Renaissance altarpiece.

Sonnenstein Castle dominates the town from a rocky spur. Built from the 13th century for the Margraves of Meissen, it became a psychiatric hospital in 1811—the first establishment of this type in Saxony. Between 1940 and 1941, as part of the Nazi euthanasia program Aktion T4, more than 13,700 people with mental and physical disabilities were gassed in its cellars. A memorial on the site documents these crimes and honors the victims. The castle now houses the district administrative headquarters.

The Bastei is Saxon Switzerland's iconic rock formation—sandstone columns sculpted by erosion over a million years, rising 194 meters above the Elbe from a plateau at an altitude of 305 meters. The Bastei Bridge, built in sandstone in 1851 to replace the original wooden bridge of 1826, links several of these rocky pinnacles over 76.5 meters with its seven arches. Caspar David Friedrich painted the rocks as early as 1822. In season, crowds are dense from 10 a.m.—arrive early for the best views over the Elbe's meanders.

The ruins of Neurathen Castle, on the Bastei rocks themselves, are the remains of the largest rock castle in Saxon Switzerland. Built by the Sorbs along 700 meters of the top of the ridge, it was conquered and burned in 1469. View the rocks and remains from outside, along the Bastei Bridge route: the metal walkways within the ruins have been closed since September 2023 and no longer allow access for visits.

activities.text: Hike from the village of Rathen to the Bastei Bridge and surrounding rocks. The route starts on the right bank of the Elbe after a ferry crossing (a few minutes), followed by a climb of about 40 minutes through the forest. Several trails offer different routes back.

visits.text: Königstein Fortress occupies 9.5 hectares on a sandstone plateau rising 240 meters above the Elbe—it's one of Europe's largest mountain fortresses. Never taken by storm, it was nicknamed the “Bastille of Saxony”: a state prison from 1591 to 1922, it notably housed Johann Friedrich Böttger, inventor of European porcelain, who was imprisoned there to try to recreate his secret formula. During World War II, it served as a prisoner-of-war camp for Allied officers—General Henri Giraud escaped on April 17, 1942, by descending a rope made of knotted sheets, an action that sent Hitler into a fury. The well dug between 1563 and 1569 to supply the garrison is 152.5 meters deep—the deepest in Saxony.

activities.text: Walk around the fortress ramparts (1.7 km) with panoramic views of the Elbe valley, Saxon Switzerland National Park, and Bohemia. A panoramic elevator provides access to the plateau from below.

visits.text: Bautzen perches on a meander of the Spree, surrounded by its medieval towers—eighteen are still standing. It's the cultural capital of the Sorbs, Germany's smallest ethnic minority: about 60,000 people still speak Upper Sorbian in this Upper Lusatia region. Their migrations from Eastern Europe brought them here in the 6th century. Bilingual German-Sorbian signs line the entire city. The Sorbian Museum traces their history, traditional costumes, and living culture.

St. Peter's Cathedral is Germany's oldest and largest shared church—used by both Catholics and Protestants. Since the Reformation in 1524, the choir has belonged to Catholics and the nave to Protestants, separated by a grille forming a rood screen. Each of the two denominations holds its services according to its own calendar. The Gothic part dates back to the 13th century; the Baroque dome of the tower was added in 1664 after the fire of 1634. The Baroque altar in Saxon marble (1723) is surmounted by a painting by Giovanni Antonio Pellegrini.

The Reichenturm, Bautzen's leaning tower, tilts 1.44 meters from the vertical—a foundation defect from the 14th century that was never corrected. It's visible from the market square and offers a beautiful view over the roofs from its summit.

activities.text: Walk on the old town ramparts above the Spree. The path runs along several medieval towers and offers views over the river and gardens below.

visits.text: Görlitz is Germany's best-preserved city—more than 4,000 listed historic buildings in the center, covering five centuries of architecture from late Gothic to Art Nouveau, because the city emerged intact from World War II. Its prosperity in the 15th century rested on cloth manufacturing and trade in woad, a highly prized blue pigment. The Untermarkt, the lower square, is the heart of the old town: its colorful Renaissance and Baroque facades, wrought-iron balconies, and vaulted passages form one of Saxony's most beautiful ensembles. The city serves so often as a film location it's called "Görliwood"—Wes Anderson's The Grand Budapest Hotel, Inglourious Basterds, and The Reader were filmed here.

The Görlitzer Warenhaus, the former Art Nouveau department store from 1913 on Demianiplatz, is the building used as the hotel lobby in The Grand Budapest Hotel. Its large glass-roofed interior courtyard and multi-level shopping galleries are striking—the building was threatened with demolition before the filming saved it.

The Schönhof, dating from 1526, is one of Germany's oldest Renaissance burgher houses still preserved in their original state. It houses the Silesian Museum, which documents the history and art of Silesia, a region shared between Germany, Poland, and the Czech Republic.

The Church of St. Peter and Paul stands directly on the banks of the Neisse, the border with Poland. Its Baroque "sun organ," built in 1703 by Eugenio Casparini, is one of Saxony's most remarkable instruments—its monumental case has remained intact since its creation.

activities.text: Cross the Old Town Bridge (Altstadtbrücke) to Zgorzelec, the Polish side. The pedestrian bridge rebuilt in 2004 bears a European Union plaque at its center. You can stroll for a few minutes on the Zgorzelec side—the two municipal councils have jointly managed many facilities since the symbolic reunification of the two banks.

visits.text: The Thomaskirche is Leipzig's musical heart. Johann Sebastian Bach was cantor here from 1723 until his death in 1750—he composed the St. Matthew Passion, the Christmas Oratorio, and more than 150 cantatas here. His tomb stands before the altar. The Thomanerchor, founded in 1212, is one of the world's oldest choral ensembles and still performs motets every Friday and Saturday. Martin Luther himself preached from this pulpit.

The Gewandhaus Orchestra, founded in 1743 by Leipzig's merchant bourgeoisie—a clean break from the tradition of princely or ecclesiastical orchestras—is one of the world's oldest symphony ensembles. Felix Mendelssohn was its director and it was under his direction that Bach's St. Matthew Passion was rediscovered in 1829, after a century of oblivion. Richard Wagner is a native of Leipzig, Robert Schumann lived and composed here. More than 500 composers have reportedly resided in the city.

The Nikolaikirche, a Gothic church remodeled in the 16th century with a green and white palm-themed neoclassical interior, is the church of the Peaceful Revolution of 1989. It was here that the Monday demonstrations (Montagsdemonstrationen) began, with prayers for peace organized every week since 1982. On October 9, 1989, 70,000 people marched through Leipzig's streets—it was the turning point that precipitated the fall of the Berlin Wall.

The Völkerschlachtdenkmal, inaugurated in 1913 for the centenary of the Battle of the Nations, is Germany's largest monument: 91 meters high, an interior staircase of 500 steps, colossal sandstone statues of warriors in the Wilhelmine monumental tradition. The October 1813 battle, which pitted Napoleon against the allied Prussian, Austrian, Russian, and Swedish forces, left 90,000 dead in four days at Leipzig's gates—one of the Napoleonic era's deadliest.

activities.text: BMW factory tour

visits.text: The Spinnerei, in the Plagwitz district in the west of the city, is a former cotton mill built in 1884 that employed up to 3,500 workers. Since the 1990s, its 10 hectares of industrial buildings have been converted into artist studios, galleries, cafes, and cultural spaces—more than 100 artists work there. The “Neue Leipziger Schule,” a figurative painting movement influential in global contemporary art in the 2000s, was born here.

The Mädlerpassage, one of the historic covered passageways in central Leipzig, houses Auerbachs Keller in its cellars—a tavern whose origins date back to 1525. Goethe frequented it during his Leipzig student years and made it the setting for a scene in Faust: Mephistopheles makes wine gush from a wooden table. Two groups of statues at the entrance depict the scene.

activities.text: Concert or motet at the Thomaskirche. Friday evening and Saturday afternoon motets with the Thomanerchor are free and open to all—it's one of Germany's most authentic musical experiences.

visits.text: Chemnitz was renamed Karl-Marx-Stadt in 1953 by the GDR and regained its historic name in 1990 after reunification. The Karl Marx Monument, inaugurated in 1971, is a colossal bust weighing 40 tonnes, carved from Siberian granite and placed on a 13-meter pedestal. The locals call it the “Nischel,” a local dialect term for “skull.” In 2025, Chemnitz is European Capital of Culture under the slogan “C the Unseen”—150 projects and 1,000 events distributed throughout the city and 38 surrounding municipalities, in converted former industrial buildings.

The Kaßberg district is one of Germany's largest continuous ensembles of Gründerzeit and Art Nouveau architecture—about a hundred blocks from the late 19th century with their sandstone facades and sculpted ornaments. It had largely escaped the 1945 bombings that devastated the center.

The municipal art collections (Kunstsammlungen Chemnitz) feature works by Karl Schmidt-Rottluff - the Expressionist painter was a native of the city. The museum also includes an important collection of 19th-century paintings and contemporary art.

Seiffen is the iconic village of the Ore Mountains (Erzgebirge), nestled at an altitude of 700 meters on the Czech border. When the region's mines were exhausted in the 18th century, inhabitants turned to woodworking. In the 19th century, the village established itself as the world center for miniature toys and Christmas decorations. There are more than a hundred craftspeople and around forty shops. The wood-turning technique called “Reifendrehen”—a log slice is turned then cut like a pie to obtain dozens of identical animal silhouettes—is unique to Seiffen and inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list.

The Seiffen Toy Museum traces the village's history and its craftsmanship since the 18th century. Christmas pyramids—those wooden candle carousels that rotate by thermal convection—are displayed in historical versions. Nutcrackers shaped like Saxon soldiers, whose first version was created in the region to ridicule authority figures, are the other local specialty. The tradition of the miner's angel and the Schwibbogen, the illuminated wooden arch placed in windows, is also explained here: these objects recall the candles that miners placed at the mine entrance on Christmas Eve.

activities.text: Hiking in the Ore Mountains from the village. Marked trails cross conifer forests and ridges with views over the Czech border. In winter, the cross-country ski trail network is one of Germany's densest.

Travel on a historic steam train on the Fichtelbergbahn, the narrow-gauge railway that has linked Cranzahl to Oberwiesenthal since 1897. First drive to Cranzahl, approximately 54 km from Seiffen, a 55-minute drive, then take the train. The historic steam locomotives pass through the villages and forests of the Ore Mountains.

visits.text: Gera is the birthplace of Otto Dix (1891-1969), one of the most important German painters of the 20th century. Born into a working-class family in the village of Untermhaus, he studied decorative arts in Dresden before leaving for war in 1914. His paintings of the Great War—The Trench, the War Cripples—are among the rawest and most disturbing visual testimonies of that conflict. In 1937, the Nazis confiscated 170 of his works as "degenerate art." The Otto Dix House and the Orangery of the Princes of Reuss, dedicated to him, house a selection of paintings and engravings including the famous Der Krieg (The War) series from 1924.

Gera's market square is one of Thuringia's most beautiful, with its Baroque town hall, whose mansard roof and entrance tower were built after the 1686 fire. The neighboring Church of the Savior (Salvatorkirche) is a Thuringian Baroque masterpiece with its frescoed ceiling and ornate galleries.

The Höhler are a network of vaulted cellars dug under the old town in the 17th and 18th centuries to store beer. Since the late 1980s, a section has been open as a museum. In October, the cellars host the Höhler Festival, one of Thuringia's largest folk festivals.

The Krämerbrücke is Europe's longest inhabited bridge—120 meters spanning the Gera River with 32 half-timbered houses built on both sides along the entire length of the deck. You don't realize you're on a bridge until you look from the banks. First mentioned in 1156, rebuilt in sandstone in 1325, it still has residents and artisan shops today. In June, the Krämerbrückenfest attracts hundreds of thousands for a medieval market.

St. Mary's Cathedral and St. Severus Church together form the Gothic ensemble dominating Domplatz from their twin hills. The cathedral, whose origins go back to the 8th century, is famous for the Gloriosa—the world's largest free-swinging medieval bell, weighing 11 tonnes, cast in 1497 by the Dutchman Geert van Wou. It rings only eight times a year and can be heard for several kilometers. It was in this cathedral that Martin Luther was ordained a priest in 1507.

The Augustinian Monastery, built in 1300, is where Luther took his monastic vows in 1505 after surviving a violent storm. He spent five years here before being sent to Wittenberg. The cell where he studied theology is preserved. In 2023, the Old Synagogue and its 13th-century mikveh were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List—the medieval treasure discovered in the walls in 1998 contained 3,141 gold and silver coins, Europe's largest medieval Jewish treasure.

activities.text: Visit Erfurt's Jewish treasure in the synagogue cellar, featuring Gothic goldwork and silverwork

seo.h1_title: Saxony Road Trip, Germany: Dresden, Leipzig and Saxon Switzerland
seo.intro_paragraph: Dresden and its palaces, the Bastei cliffs, Görlitz on the Polish border, Meissen porcelain, Leipzig, and the wooden toys of Seiffen.
seo.seo_hook: Baroque Dresden, the Bastei cliffs, Meissen porcelain and Seiffen's toys: Saxony between palatial grandeur and spectacular nature.

Bastei: rock formations
Meissen: porcelain heritage
Görlitz: beauty on the border

itineraries.title: Thuringia, Germany Road Trip: Cities and Nature
itineraries.subtitle: From Luther's Wartburg to Saalfeld's porcelain, through Hainich's primeval forest, Erfurt, Weimar, and Jena: Thuringia unites three UNESCO sites and a thousand years of German cultural history.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May–September, with temperatures of 15–25°C, ideal for visiting cultural cities and exploring Hainich's natural surroundings. Avoid December–February (harsh winter, 0 to −5°C, frequent snow, short days). Continental climate with possible summer thunderstorms.

visits.text: Wartburg Castle rises from a rocky spur 411 meters above Eisenach, in the Thuringian Forest. Founded around 1067 by Count Ludwig the Springer, its name springs from legend: upon first seeing the hill, the count allegedly shouted “Warte, Berg - du sollst mir eine Burg tragen!” (“Wait, mountain - you shall bear my castle!”). The Romanesque palace (Palas), built between 1156 and 1162, is the oldest preserved residential building of its kind in Germany. The complex was extensively remodeled in the 19th century under architect Hugo von Ritgen at the behest of Grand Duke Karl Alexander—a restoration whose images directly inspired Ludwig II of Bavaria for Neuschwanstein. The castle has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1999. In 1817, student associations gathered here to demand a German constitution: the “Wartburgfest” is considered one of the founding acts of the German liberal-national movement.

In the Lutherstube, a small vaulted chamber in the Vogtei, Martin Luther lived from May 1521 to March 1522 under the alias Junker Jörg—“Knight George.” Declared an outlaw after refusing to recant at the Diet of Worms, he had been kidnapped by fake brigands dispatched by Elector Frederick the Wise to protect him. In ten to eleven weeks, he translated the New Testament from ancient Greek into German—a version that did as much to standardize the German language as to spread the Reformation. Luther called Wartburg his “Patmos,” referring to the Greek island where the apostle John wrote the Book of Revelation. The museum also preserves works by Lucas Cranach the Elder and objects related to Saint Elizabeth of Hungary, who lived here from 1211 to 1228.

activities.text: Panoramic view over the Thuringian Forest from Wartburg's ramparts. On clear days, the vista extends to the Rennsteig - the ridgeline that once separated Saxony from Franconia, and during the Cold War, the two Germanys.

visits.text: Hainich National Park is Germany's largest contiguous deciduous forest with its 13,000 hectares. Established on December 31, 1997, it is Thuringia's only national park. Its uniqueness stems from its military past: vast sectors were restricted zones during the Cold War, leaving them to develop freely for decades. The forest has thus returned to an almost primeval state, with old trees, abundant deadwood, and more than 1,600 identified fungus species. The 1,573-hectare core zone has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2011 as part of the “Primeval Beech Forests of Europe.” A 9.5 km World Heritage trail traverses the core zone.

The Baumkronenpfad—canopy walkway—starts at the park center in Thiemsburg. Over 540 meters, the walkway gradually rises to a height of 24 meters, level with the tops of the beech trees, then climbs to an observation platform at 44 meters, with an unobstructed view over the whole Hainich and the Thuringian Basin. Panels at each level explain life in the canopy and the diversity of species.

The national park center features an interactive exhibition on Hainich's limestone geology, forest fauna, and conservation challenges. A reconstructed «root cave» illustrates subterranean life. The center also provides information on the wildcat - an emblematic species visible at the dedicated village of Hütscheroda, a few kilometers away.

activities.text: A hike along the World Heritage trail, a 9.5 km circuit through the primeval beech forest. The path runs alongside areas of deadwood, skirts forest pools, and crosses clearings where the black woodpecker—Europe's largest woodpecker—excavates its nesting cavities in old trunks.

visits.text: Bad Langensalza owes its medieval prosperity to the trade in woad—a blue dye it shared with only four other Thuringian cities—which enabled burghers to build large churches and travertine ramparts. Later, the exploitation of mineral springs made it a spa town. Today, the city is known for its ten themed parks and gardens arranged along the spa promenade. The Japanese garden “Kofuku no Niwa” (“garden of happiness”) combines two classical pavilions, a koi carp pond, a dry garden, a bamboo grove, and cherry trees that blossom in spring.

Bad Langensalza's rose garden is one of Thuringia's most significant. It showcases collections of antique and modern roses organized in themed beds, complemented by a small rose museum tracing this flower's cultural history.

The arboretum brings together trees and shrubs of rare or spectacular species, both native and exotic, planted in themed collections. Next to it, the botanical garden displays medicinal plants and plants used in pharmaceutical preparations, recalling the town's spa tradition.

Bad Langensalza's old town is one of Thuringia's best-preserved: an almost entirely preserved medieval wall, half-timbered houses from the 15th and 16th centuries restored since 1990, and several large churches testifying to the past wealth of the woad trade.

activities.text: Relaxation at the Friederiken Therme, a thermal spa fed by Bad Langensalza's sulfurous and saline springs. The complex features indoor and outdoor pools and several themed saunas.

practical_info.booking: Recommended on weekends and in summer

visits.text: Erfurt's St. Mary's Cathedral dominates Domplatz from a raised terrace, flanked by the collegiate Church of St. Severus—together forming one of Central Europe's most impressive religious architectural ensembles. The current cathedral was begun around 1280 with a vast Gothic choir. Its glory is the Gloriosa: cast in 1497, it's the world's largest free-swinging medieval bell. It's rung only on major occasions to protect the structure. The cathedral also houses the “Wolfram,” a 12th-century bronze candelabrum, and Gothic stained glass in the choir.

Fischmarkt is Erfurt's central square, surrounded by Renaissance merchants' houses, some dating from the 16th century. The neo-Gothic town hall, built 1870-1874, overlooks the square with its murals of local legends. Erfurt miraculously survived World War II bombing, explaining the density of its historic fabric - the city is often called «the preserved medieval metropolis».

The Krämerbrücke—“grocers' bridge”—is Central Europe's longest inhabited bridge: 120 meters long, with 32 half-timbered houses built directly on its structure. First mentioned in 1156, its current stone form dates from the 14th century. It recalls Florence's Ponte Vecchio or Venice's Rialto, except that its houses are inhabited and occupied by shops even today.

Erfurt's Old Synagogue, built around 1094, is Central Europe's best-preserved medieval synagogue. Its walls remained intact because after the pogrom of March 21, 1349—when about 900 of the city's Jews were massacred—it was converted into a warehouse and fell into oblivion, which protected it during Kristallnacht. The synagogue, mikveh, and Stone House complex has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2023. In the cellar, the Erfurt Treasure—discovered in 1998 in the wall of a neighboring cellar—has been permanently displayed since 2009: 3,141 silver coins, 14 ingots, and more than 700 pieces of 14th-century Gothic goldsmiths' work. The centerpiece is a gold ring adorned with a miniature temple bearing the Hebrew inscription “mazal tov.” The treasure was exhibited at the Musée de Cluny in Paris and the Metropolitan Museum in New York before joining the permanent collection.

activities.text: A visit to Erfurt's medieval Jewish treasure in the Old Synagogue's cellar. Looking through the Gothic goldsmiths' work—gem-studded brooches, gold rings, ceremonial tableware—gives a sense of Erfurt's Jewish community at its height, before its annihilation in 1349.

map_keywords: Goethe Gartenhaus Park an der Ilm Weimar

visits.text: Tiefurt Palace is a small summer residence on the banks of the Ilm east of Weimar. Originally a modest manor from the mid-16th century enlarged in 1765, it became Duchess Anna Amalia's favorite retreat from 1781 until her death in 1807. Despite its seven rooms per floor, it hosted literary and musical soirées bringing together Goethe, Wieland, and Corona Schröter, making Tiefurt a pastoral «Museion». The music room and the duchess's apartments are restored to their late 18th-century state with original furniture. Tiefurt is part of the UNESCO site «Classical Weimar».

activities.text: Stroll through Tiefurt's English landscape park along the Ilm River. Open meadows, century-old trees, and small monuments punctuate the main avenue: an artificial grotto, a temple of the muses, a Japanese-style wooden bridge. The park was designed in the spirit of 18th-century «natural» English gardens.

visits.text: The Bauhaus was founded in Weimar on April 12, 1919, by architect Walter Gropius, who merged the city's Academy of Fine Arts and School of Applied Arts. His manifesto proclaimed that “the aim of all visual art is building.” Among the recruited masters: Paul Klee, Wassily Kandinsky, László Moholy-Nagy, and Oskar Schlemmer. The school left Weimar in 1925 under pressure from a conservative regional government and moved to Dessau, before being closed by the Nazis in 1933. The Bauhaus Museum Weimar, opened in 2019 for the centenary, holds the world's oldest Bauhaus collection—started by Gropius himself—with 13,000 objects spread across three floors. The Bauhaus sites in Weimar have been UNESCO World Heritage Sites since 1996.

Goethe's House at Frauenplan is the residence the poet occupied for 50 years, from 1782 to his death in 1832. It is preserved as he left it: his study with the mineral collection carefully arranged on shelves, his 5,000 volumes, the bed in which he died. It's the world's most important museum dedicated to Goethe. The house is part of the UNESCO site «Classical Weimar» inscribed in 1998.

Schiller's House is the dwelling the poet occupied during his last three years of life, from 1802 to his death in 1805. It's here that «The Bride of Messina» and «William Tell» were written. The study is preserved with the inclined desk at which Schiller worked standing, his cane, the manuscripts. The modest rooms contrast with the grandeur of the works born there.

The Duchess Anna Amalia Library is housed in the Renaissance “Green Palace” (1562–1565), converted into a library in 1761. Goethe was its director from 1797 to 1832 and doubled the holdings to reach 80,000 volumes. The three-story oval Rococo hall, built of wood, is one of Germany's most photographed interiors. On September 2, 2004, a fire destroyed 50,000 volumes and damaged 118,000—a national tragedy. After restoration, the library reopened in 2007. It preserves the world's largest collection of Goethe's Faust.

The House of the Weimar Republic (Haus der Weimarer Republik), opened in 2019, traces the history of Germany's first democracy. In 1919, the National Constituent Assembly met in Weimar's German National Theater—Berlin was deemed too dangerous amid revolution—and adopted the Constitution of August 11, 1919, instituting universal suffrage and social rights that were pioneering for the time. The permanent exhibition illuminates the birth, crises, and fall of this Republic.

activities.text: Bauhaus walking tour through Weimar's streets to discover buildings linked to the school: the Haus am Horn (1923), a Bauhaus housing prototype built for an exhibition, and Henry van de Velde's buildings where the school had its first workshops. Specialist guides offer guided tours.

practical_info.booking: Guides available at the tourist office

visits.text: Schiller's Garden House in Jena is the modest dwelling the poet occupied from 1797, when he was teaching at the university. It's in this pastoral setting that he began his creative collaboration with Goethe - who had brought him to Jena - and started «Wallenstein». The original building is preserved with some period furniture.

The Zeiss-Planetarium, inaugurated on July 18, 1926, is the oldest continuously operating projection planetarium in the world. It was designed by Carl Zeiss engineer Walther Bauersfeld, who simultaneously developed the thin-shell concrete dome—an architectural invention that revolutionized construction in the 20th century. The dome measures 25 meters in diameter. Current projections use a Zeiss Velvet full-dome laser system. The original idea dates back to 1913, when the founder of the Deutsches Museum approached Zeiss for a “Himmelsschau”—a representation of the sky.

The JenTower is a 160-meter cylindrical tower built during the GDR era to serve as a Zeiss research center—hence its local nickname “Keksrolle” (roll of cookies). At 128 meters high, the panoramic platform offers views over the deeply incised Saale Valley and the surrounding limestone hills.

The Kunstsammlung Jena (Jena Art Collection) brings together more than 5,000 works ranging from the Middle Ages to the present, with a particular focus on German Expressionism. The museum is housed in several buildings in the historic city center.

activities.text: A hike along a section of the SaaleHorizontale, a 91 km trail that follows the limestone ridges overlooking the Saale River around Jena. The cliffs rising sheer above the river offer views down into the valley and over the city. Several possible starting points from the city center.

visits.text: Leuchtenburg overlooks the Saale Valley from an altitude of 395 meters and is nicknamed “the Queen of the Saale Valley.” Its first documented mention dates to 1221, when it was a military base of the Lords of Lobdeburg. It changed hands frequently and became the administrative center of the Wettin villages in 1396. In 1553, an 80-meter-deep well was dug into the rock—Thuringia's second-deepest at the time. After its administration closed in 1705, it served in turn as a prison, a poorhouse, and an asylum. Between 1920 and 1997, Thuringia's first youth hostel operated there. The castle was purchased at auction in 2007 by the Leuchtenburg Foundation and restored, and a new permanent exhibition opened in 2014.

Porzellanwelten Leuchtenburg traces 800 years of Thuringian porcelain history in the castle's halls. The exhibition explores the art, technology, and culture of this craft, for which the town of Kahla, at the foot of the castle, is a historic center. Modern installations deliberately contrast with the medieval walls.

The Mythos Burg exhibition presents the castle's medieval history and legends linked to Leuchtenburg. The keep, accessible by a steep staircase, offers a 360-degree panorama over the Harz, the Thuringian Forest, and the deeply incised Saale Valley.

activities.text: Panoramic view from Leuchtenburg's keep: on clear days, the vista extends to the Harz in the north and the Thuringian Forest in the south. The ascent is via a path or stairs from parking areas below.

A hike along a section of the Hohenwarte Reservoir trail, a 74.4 km circuit that follows the reservoir through the dense forest of the Thuringian Slate Mountains. In places, the paths overlook the Saale's deeply incised meanders from rocky cliffs, creating a landscape evoking Norwegian fjords—hence the nickname “Thuringian Sea” for this region.

practical_info.difficulty: Moderate to challenging on some sections

activities.text: A walk in the Naturpark Thüringer Schiefergebirge/Obere Saale, which covers the Thuringian Slate Mountains and the upper reaches of the Saale. The nature park protects landscapes of heathland, conifer forests, and deep valleys typical of this slate mountain range.

visits.text: Saalfeld's Feengrotten—“fairy grottoes”—are the galleries of a former alum mine worked from 1530. After closing in 1850, the mine was rediscovered in 1910, and the third chamber—the “Fairy Realm”—was discovered in 1913. The grottoes opened to the public on May 31, 1914. In 1993, the Guinness Book of World Records designated them “the most colorful grottoes in the world”: the mineral formations—stalactites, stalagmites, concretions—display hues ranging from blue to red, including yellow, due to the oxidation of iron phosphate (diadochite), a rare mineral. Since 1914, more than 20 million visitors have traversed the three chambers connected by galleries.

Since 1937, a gallery of Saalfeld's grottoes has housed Germany's first “Emanatorium”—a gallery used for treatment by inhaling underground air. The gallery's microclimate (constant temperature, mineral-rich air) was used to treat respiratory conditions. This therapeutic gallery is Germany's oldest.

The Grottoneum, an interactive museum adjacent to the grottoes, presents the site's geological and mining history along with exhibitions on the region's minerals and crystals. Children's activities are offered.

activities.text: Forest adventure trail near Saalfeld's Feengrotten, with family-friendly routes through the woods above the grottoes.

visits.text: Kochberg Castle is a moated castle (Wasserschloss) built around 1600 in Renaissance style, surrounded by a moat. It's known worldwide for its connection to Goethe and Charlotte von Stein. The von Stein family acquired the estate in 1733. Goethe was a regular guest of Charlotte von Stein from 1775 to 1788—it was at Kochberg that he met Friedrich Schiller for the first time on September 7, 1788, before inviting him to Jena. He wrote the dates of his visits in ink on the castle's secretary desk, where they are still visible today. More than 1,700 letters from Goethe to Charlotte von Stein testify to this thirteen-year relationship. The museum reconstructs the period's apartments with original furniture, portraits, and handwritten documents.

The six-hectare landscape park was transformed by Carl von Stein (Charlotte's son) between 1800 and 1840, from a Baroque garden into a Romantic English park. Under imposing old trees, winding paths lead to a canvas hut, a ruined tower, a grotto with a burial site, a swimming lake, and the flower garden with its floral staircase.

The Liebhabertheater is a 75-seat private theater built around 1800 by Carl von Stein, modeled on Weimar's court theater. It's a jewel unlike any other in the world: the classical columned portico, the auditorium with its hand-marbled wallpaper and floral friezes, the stage, and the orchestra pit are fully restored. It belongs to the “European Route of Historic Theatres” and hosts operas, chamber concerts, and theatrical performances every weekend from May to October.

activities.text: Performance at Kochberg's Liebhabertheater: Baroque opera or chamber concert in this 75-seat theater, in the authentic atmosphere of the 18th century. Productions are conceived specifically for this space and employ historically informed performance practices.

seo.h1_title: Thuringia, Germany Road Trip: Cities and Nature
seo.intro_paragraph: From Luther's UNESCO-listed Wartburg to Hainich's primeval forest, from Erfurt and its medieval Jewish treasure to Weimar, capital of Classicism and the Bauhaus, and on to Saalfeld's grottoes and Kochberg Castle, where Goethe visited Charlotte von Stein. Thuringia offers an extraordinary concentration of cultural and natural heritage over 8 days.
seo.seo_hook: Luther's Wartburg, the Weimar of Goethe and the Bauhaus, Guinness-record colorful grottoes: three UNESCO sites and Germany's cultural heart in Thuringia.
featured_list: Wartburg: Luther and Wagner's medieval castle, a UNESCO World Heritage Site
Weimar: world capital of Classicism and the Bauhaus
Erfurt: inhabited 14th-century bridge and Jewish treasure rediscovered in 1998
Saalfeld: the world's most colorful grottoes according to Guinness

highlights: Wartburg: UNESCO site founded in 1067, where Luther translated the New Testament in 1521
Classical Weimar and Bauhaus: two UNESCO inscriptions in the same city
Erfurt's Old Synagogue: a UNESCO site since 2023, with the 14th-century Jewish treasure
Saalfeld's Feengrotten: designated world's most colorful grottoes by Guinness in 1993
