itineraries.title: Berchtesgaden in 4 Days: Königssee, Salt, and Summits
itineraries.subtitle: In 4 days, travel from the Bad Reichenhall saltworks to Königssee, Jenner, and the Zauberwald in Ramsau.
itineraries.notes: The Kehlsteinhaus, devastated by a fire on October 23, 2026, is excluded from the itinerary until a reopening is announced. All four nights are spent in Berchtesgaden; boats serve Salet from late April to mid-October, and the Jennerbahn shuts down for maintenance in November.
itineraries.climate: Aim for June through September: in Schönau am Königssee, average highs range from around 20 to 26 °C, and boats serve Obersee from late April to mid-October. Pack a rain jacket, as July and September average more than 140 mm of precipitation. Avoid November: the Jennerbahn shuts down for maintenance then, and both the Alte Saline and Dokumentation Obersalzberg close for several days.

visits.text: The roar of water follows you into the underground passages of the Alte Saline in Bad Reichenhall. Rebuilt on the orders of King Ludwig I after the fire of 1834, the saltworks still runs waterwheels measuring 13 m in diameter, which pump brine to the surface. The underground route covers approximately 400 m and 270 steps: wear sturdy shoes, then finish with the five rooms of the Salzmuseum.

If the air feels salty in the Königlicher Kurgarten, look toward the Gradierhaus. Along this structure, 160 m long and 13 m high, brine trickles through bundles of blackthorn and evaporates into a fine mist that you breathe as you walk. From April to October, spend 30 minutes walking alongside it on the side sheltered from the wind; admission to the park, designed in 1868, is free.

The Münster St. Zeno is a reminder that Bad Reichenhall does not depend on salt alone. Consecrated in 1228, this Romanesque basilica with a nave and two side aisles is 90 m long and is considered the largest Romanesque church in southern Bavaria. Allow around 20 minutes outside service times, as the building remains an active place of worship.

activities.text: Since July 1, 1928, the Predigtstuhlbahn has linked Bad Reichenhall to Predigtstuhl with its appearance unchanged. It is considered the oldest large-cabin cable car preserved in its original condition and climbs more than 1,100 m in approximately 8 minutes 30 seconds. Have lunch on the terrace of the historic restaurant at the upper station, then walk a few minutes to the Almhütte Schlegelmulde.

practical_info.tip: Tiroler Tor / Predigtstuhlbahn bus stop; check the day’s schedule on the operator’s website, as times change in winter and in bad weather.

to_next_leg.road_type: B20 via Bischofswiesen

visits.text: Plan your afternoon around the guided tours of Königliches Schloss Berchtesgaden: they are the only way to see the interior. The former Augustinian monastery, later a Wittelsbach residence, opens 30 of its 214 rooms to visitors, featuring two altarpieces by Tilman Riemenschneider and three armories. Arrive a few minutes before the tour starts, then finish in the rose garden overlooking the Berchtesgaden Alps.

A 19th-century Romanesque Revival facade conceals a medieval core: the Stiftskirche St. Peter und Johannes, next to the castle, is much older than it looks. The first church on the site was consecrated in 1122, and the 14th-century Gothic choir stalls feature a lion, a pelican, a unicorn, and a stag, all Christian symbols. The Romanesque cloister is accessed from Schlossplatz rather than the nave: look for its entrance on the square.

Follow the ramp through “Vertikale Wildnis” at the Haus der Berge: the exhibition climbs from the depths of Königssee to the summits of the Watzmann, moving from water to forest, then to alpine pasture and rock. At the end, the slats of a large display window open to reveal the real Watzmann. Open daily from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., the national park center has also reassembled the Lahner-Kaser, an alpine pasture hut dating from 1848, in its garden.

activities.text: Locals call it the “Arschpfeifenrössl”: a little wooden horse with a whistle for a tail. Berchtesgadener Handwerkskunst sells it on the ground floor of the Alte Fronveste, built around 1510 between Marktplatz and Schlossplatz and once the prince-provosts’ prison. Each piece is carved and painted by hand; come on a weekday if possible, as the shop opens only in the morning on Saturdays.

practical_info.tip: Open Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to noon and 2 to 6 p.m., and Saturday from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m.

visits.text: St. Bartholomä stands on a peninsula formed by sediment deposited by the Eisbach, beneath the Watzmann’s east face. Rebuilt in 1697–1698 on the site of a chapel consecrated in 1134, the church has three red domes crowning its trefoil-shaped choir, with a layout reminiscent of Salzburg Cathedral. Admission is free; on the Saturday after August 24, pilgrims arrive on foot from Maria Alm via the Steinernes Meer.

activities.text: There is no engine noise: since 1909, electric boats have crossed Königssee between cliffs that plunge almost vertically into a lake nearly 190 m deep. Halfway to St. Bartholomä, the boatman plays a few notes facing the Echowand, and the cliff echoes the melody once, rarely twice. Buy a ticket to Salet, allowing about 1 hour 45 minutes for the round-trip boat ride, and board before 10:30 a.m. on fair-weather days.

practical_info.tip: Boats serve Salet from late April to mid-October; the rest of the year, they run to St. Bartholomä unless the lake is frozen. There are no restrooms or refreshments on board.

activities.text: Get off at Salet, the last stop on Königssee, and walk 15 minutes to Obersee. The trail then follows its shore, with a railing along the rock face, to Fischunkelalm; beyond it, Röthbachfall drops about 470 m, making it Germany’s highest waterfall. Allow for a 5.5 km round trip, wear shoes with good traction, and keep an eye on the last boat’s departure time.

practical_info.tip: Fischunkelalm serves food and drinks only in summer. There is no other way back from Salet after the last boat.

activities.text: The best shot of Königssee is taken at Malerwinkel, reached on foot, rather than from a boat deck. This viewpoint takes in the entire lake, with St. Bartholomä on its peninsula and the 2,653 m Schönfeldspitze in the background. The Malerwinkl-Rundweg loop covers 5 km, takes about 1 hour 30 minutes, and includes 160 m of ascent: save it for late in the day, after your boat ride.

practical_info.tip: The loop starts in Schönau am Königssee and is freely accessible, with no ticket required.

to_next_leg.road_type: Ascent via Salzbergstraße

visits.text: Hitler began vacationing on the Obersalzberg in 1923; after 1933, this mountainside became the second center of Nazi power after Berlin. Dokumentation Obersalzberg traces this history first through the “Idyll und Verbrechen” exhibition, which opened in 2023 and features around 350 objects and documents, then through a network of period bunkers. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours and wear sturdy shoes: the tunnel floors are uneven in places.

activities.text: Next, take the Roßfeld-Panoramastraße from Klaushöhe on the Obersalzberg: billed as Germany’s highest scenic toll road, it reaches nearly 1,600 m. Along the ridge, it runs through Austrian territory for about 1.5 km, while the Salzach Valley and Salzburg unfold a thousand meters below. Set aside €9.50 for the toll and descend on the northern side toward Oberau.

practical_info.tip: The road is open year-round; several parking areas along the ridge offer places to stop.

to_next_leg.road_type: Roßfeld toll road, then Oberau

visits.text: If you choose just one underground visit, make it Salzbergwerk Berchtesgaden, a mine in continuous operation since 1517. Dressed in miners’ coveralls, you ride a small train 1,400 m into the mountain, then descend a wooden slide and cross the Spiegelsee, an illuminated underground brine lake, by boat. The temperature stays at 12 °C year-round: bring a jacket and book online to avoid waiting.

activities.text: Berg- und Enzianbrennerei Grassl in Unterau has distilled gentian since 1692 and describes itself as Germany’s oldest gentian distillery. The gentian roots, dug up by hand at elevations above 1,000 m, are processed in five mountain distilling huts, including the one at Priesbergalm on the Jenner. The tour and tasting of more than 40 spirits and liqueurs are free: choose a designated driver before raising a glass.

practical_info.tip: Closed Sundays; from November to April, open weekdays from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. and Saturdays from 9 a.m. to noon.

map_keywords: Jennerbahn valley station Schönau am Königssee

activities.text: The Jenner is well worth a morning: from its summit, Königssee stretches out some 1,200 m below, opposite the Watzmann. The glass-sided ten-person gondolas, in service since June 2019, reach the station at 1,800 m in about 20 minutes. From there, a trail equipped with safety features leads to the summit cross at 1,874 m in 20 minutes. Aim for the first ride up at 9 a.m., as the summit gets very busy.

practical_info.tip: The Jennerbahn closes for maintenance from November 9 to December 4, 2026. The “vom See zum Gipfel” combination ticket (€56) also includes the boat to St. Bartholomä.

activities.text: Next, follow the 360° Panoramaweg, a 400 m loop around the upper station and Jenneralm. Just 15 minutes on this easy, marked trail, dotted with photo spots, brings changing views from the Watzmann to the Steinernes Meer. Before heading down, stop at the national park information point, with step-free access just outside the gondola exit.

practical_info.tip: Hiking shoes are recommended: the Jenner’s trails cross alpine terrain.

to_next_leg.road_type: B305 toward Ramsau

visits.text: The murmur of the Ramsauer Ache accompanies the view that made Ramsau famous: the Pfarrkirche St. Sebastian, framed from the Malerwinkel with the Ertlsteg in the foreground and the Reiter Alm in the background. Construction of the church began in 1512 under Prince-Provost Gregor Rainer. Its pews still bear the nameplates of village families, whose seats were assigned starting in 1615. The church is always open: step inside after taking your photo.

Keep four euros handy for the Wimbachklamm, reached from the Wimbachbrücke parking lot: buy your ticket from the machine at the gorge entrance. For about 200 m, wooden walkways and bridges follow the rock walls as water gushes from the rock and tumbles down in cascades. The gorge is open from late April to early November; on hot days, it is the coolest stop of the day.

activities.text: About 3,500 years ago, part of the Hochkalter collapsed: some 15 million m³ of rock blocked the valley and created the Hintersee. The Zauberwald grew among this jumble of boulders; explore it along the Naturlehrpfad (3.3 km, 1 hour 15 minutes), then follow the lakeshore. In the early 19th century, Carl Rottmann and other painters set up their easels here; park at the Zauberwald parking lot in Seeklause.

practical_info.tip: Free access year-round; the path from the Zauberwald to the Hintersee is cleared of snow in winter.

seo.h1_title: Berchtesgaden in 4 Days: Königssee, Salt, and Summits
seo.intro_paragraph: This 4-day itinerary uses Berchtesgaden as a base, with every night spent there. It takes in the saltworks and cable car in Bad Reichenhall, a full day on the Königssee continuing to the Obersee, the salt mine and the Dokumentation Obersalzberg, followed by the Jenner and the trails of Ramsau.
seo.seo_hook: Berchtesgaden in 4 days: Bad Reichenhall saltworks, an electric boat on the Königssee, the salt mine, a gondola ride up the Jenner, and Ramsau’s Zauberwald.
featured_list: Bad Reichenhall: 13 m waterwheels in the Alte Saline
Königssee: the Echowand’s echo and the red-domed church of St. Bartholomä
Obersee: trail to the Röthbachfall, Germany’s highest waterfall
Obersalzberg: around 350 objects and bunkers in the 2023 exhibition
Salzbergwerk: a small train, a slide, and an underground brine lake
Jenner: the summit cross at 1,874 m, facing the Watzmann
Ramsau: St. Sebastian Church, the Zauberwald, and the Wimbachklamm

itineraries.title: Munich and Its Lakes in 5 Days: In the Footsteps of Ludwig II
itineraries.subtitle: In 5 days, explore Munich on foot, then head to Lake Starnberg, Andechs, and the islands of Lake Chiemsee.
itineraries.notes: The first three days are spent on foot and by public transportation in Munich; a car is only useful for days 4 and 5, and the final night is spent in Prien am Chiemsee, which has train connections to Munich and Salzburg. Avoid scheduling day 3 on a Monday, when the Alte Pinakothek is closed, and aim for April through mid-October, when the Nymphenburg pavilions and the Votivkapelle in Berg are open to visitors.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May through September, with average highs of 19 to 25 °C in Munich. June through August are also the rainiest months, with frequent thundershowers, so keep rain gear handy for days on the lakes. From November through March, highs drop to between 4 and 10 °C and castle opening hours are shorter: save this season for Munich’s museums. On days with foehn winds, the dry air clears the view of the Alps from the old town’s towers.

visits.text: Tiny on the outside, immense within: the Asamkirche, officially St. Johann Nepomuk, occupies a plot measuring 22 m by 8 m. The Asam brothers built it between 1733 and 1746 as a private church, and Egid Quirin could see the altar from a window in his neighboring house. Look up at the high altar’s four twisted columns, a nod to Bernini’s above the tomb of St. Peter in Rome. Admission is free, but visits pause during services.

The thread running through this trip begins with a tomb, and that feels entirely fitting. In the Wittelsbach crypt of St. Michael, a church completed in 1597, Ludwig II rests among some thirty members of his family. Above, the barrel vault spans more than 20 m without a single pillar, a span exceeded at the time only by St. Peter’s in Rome. Budget €3 for the crypt, which is closed on Sundays.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from St Michael Munich to Frauenkirche Munich
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

visits.text: “Teufelstritt,” the devil’s footprint: this is what Munich locals first point out at the Frauenkirche, a footprint in the paving at the entrance. According to legend, the devil thought the church had no windows and stamped his foot while laughing; from this spot, no windows were visible between 1620 and 1858. The two towers, nearly 99 m tall, received their onion domes around 1525. The south tower is open to visitors: after about 90 steps, an elevator takes you up to 80 m, with tickets sold only on-site.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Frauenkirche Munich to Marienplatz Munich
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

visits.text: If you reach Marienplatz shortly before noon, find a spot facing the Neues Rathaus: the Glockenspiel and its 43 bells reenact a wedding tournament from 1568, followed by the coopers’ dance, at 11 a.m. and noon, plus 5 p.m. from March through October. This neo-Gothic backdrop was only completed in 1905, after nearly forty years of construction. Afterward, two elevators take you to the top of the 85 m tower, with 20-minute time slots starting at €7.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Marienplatz Munich to Alter Peter Munich
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

activities.text: About 300 steps and no elevator: reaching the bell tower of St. Peter, known to Munich locals as “Alter Peter,” takes some legwork. This is the city’s oldest parish church, and its viewing platform at 56 m looks straight toward the Neues Rathaus; on days with foehn winds, the Alps appear on the horizon. Tickets cost €5 and cannot be reserved: check the sky before climbing, since the view depends on visibility.

practical_info.tip: From April through October, the tower is open for climbs from 9 a.m. to 7:30 p.m. (last entry at 7 p.m.); in winter, from 9 a.m. to 6:30 p.m. on weekdays and until 7:30 p.m. on weekends.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Alter Peter Munich to Viktualienmarkt
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

activities.text: Cut flowers, cheeses, draft beer: let your nose lead the way through the Viktualienmarkt. King Max I Joseph moved part of the market here in 1807, and more than a hundred vendors now have stalls around the maypole and fountains honoring Munich comedians such as Karl Valentin. At the beer garden, the city’s six major breweries take turns supplying the beer; bring your own food if you like, but drinks must be purchased on-site.

practical_info.tip: The market runs Monday through Saturday, with no stalls on Sunday; each vendor sets its own hours, and Saturday trading ends around 3 p.m.

visits.text: You’ll spend the afternoon at the Deutsches Museum, founded in 1903 on an island in the Isar, and you’ll need the time. The renovated half, reopened in July 2022, features 19 permanent exhibitions: the first diesel engine, the laboratory table used in nuclear fission experiments, musical instruments, and a large model railroad. The temporary entrance is in the glass pavilion on the Corneliusbrücke side; the museum opens from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., with last admission at 4:30 p.m.

The Residenz grew over more than six centuries, and your legs will remember it. The highlight is the Antiquarium, a Renaissance hall nearly 66 m long, completed in 1571: it is the palace’s oldest space and one of the largest halls of its style north of the Alps. Next come reception rooms from every era of Wittelsbach rule. Get the combined ticket with the Schatzkammer for €15, and allow nearly two hours for the museum alone.

Next, head to the Residenz’s Schatzkammer: more than 1,200 pieces of jewelry and precious objects, spanning late antiquity to neoclassicism, made of rock crystal, gold, enamel, and ivory, including the crown of the kings of Bavaria. It all began with Duke Albert V’s decision in 1565 to prohibit the dispersal of the family treasury. Arrive at least an hour before closing: last entry is at 5 p.m. in summer and 4 p.m. in winter.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Residenz Munich to Theatinerkirche Munich
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

visits.text: Egg-yolk yellow outside and white stucco inside, the Theatinerkirche St. Kajetan brightens Odeonsplatz. Elector Ferdinand Maria and Henriette Adelaide of Savoy had it built starting in 1663 to give thanks to heaven for the birth of their heir, Max Emanuel; Agostino Barelli drew inspiration from Sant’Andrea della Valle in Rome, and the dome rises to about 70 m. Admission to the church is free; the princes’ crypt opens only at set times.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Theatinerkirche Munich to Hofgarten Munich
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

visits.text: Eight paths converge on the Dianatempel, the central pavilion of the Hofgarten, laid out beginning in 1613 for Duke Maximilian I in the style of Italian Renaissance gardens. Enter from Odeonsplatz through the Hofgartentor, designed by Leo von Klenze in 1816; admission is free. Cross the garden from west to east: its paths lead toward the Haus der Kunst and the southern end of the Englischer Garten.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Hofgarten Munich to Eisbachwelle
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

activities.text: There’s no ocean or beach, yet surfers wait their turn on Prinzregentenstraße: the Eisbachwelle, a standing wave on the Eisbach, forms at the southern edge of the Englischer Garten, near the Haus der Kunst. The city reopened it for surfing on May 8, 2026, for experienced surfers only, with leashes required and no surfing after 10 p.m. Watch from the bridge, stay well away from the banks, and leave your bike farther away: the passage is narrow.

practical_info.tip: Free to watch year-round; swimming in the Eisbach is prohibited.

visits.text: Next, head up toward the Monopteros along the Schwabinger Bach, where the Japanisches Teehaus, built for the 1972 Olympics, regularly hosts tea ceremonies. Leo von Klenze’s small round temple, about 16 m tall and completed in 1836, crowns its hill and offers a sweeping view of the city. The path up has a grade of more than 6% and is not wheelchair accessible.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Monopteros Munich to Chinesischer Turm Munich
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

activities.text: The 25 m wooden pagoda of the Chinesischer Turm watches over Munich’s second-largest beer garden, with seating for about 7,000. Built in 1789–1790 and destroyed by fire in July 1944, it was rebuilt to match the original in 1952. End the day here with a Maß of beer and a pretzel, preferably before sunset so you can find a table near the tower.

practical_info.tip: For the trip back, Universität and Giselastraße stations (U3, U6) serve the western side of the park.

to_next_leg.road_type: By rail or public transit: Chinesischer Turm → Münchner Freiheit → Schloss Nymphenburg
to_next_leg.justification: Marche ou correspondance depuis le Jardin anglais, puis transports urbains vers Nymphenburg et marche finale.

visits.text: One room alone would justify the trip: the three-story Steinerner Saal at Nymphenburg Palace has retained its Rococo stucco and ceiling painted by Johann Baptist Zimmermann since 1758. Farther on, Ludwig I’s Schönheitengalerie displays portraits of beauties painted by Joseph Stieler, including Lola Montez, while a bedroom hung with green silk recalls that Ludwig II was born here on August 25, 1845. Arrive at opening time: 9 a.m. in summer and 10 a.m. in winter.

Finish your tour of the interiors at the Marstallmuseum in the palace’s south wing: more than forty carriages and sleighs, including carriages used by Ludwig II, as gilded as you might imagine. Upstairs, the displays feature Nymphenburg porcelain from the 18th through the 20th centuries. Buy the combined ticket for the palace, Marstallmuseum, and pavilions from the outset; it costs less than separate admissions.

activities.text: Weather permitting, set aside 45 minutes for Nymphenburg Park: 229 hectares of landscaped grounds, a canal about 3 km long between two paths, and scattered pavilions, including the Rococo Amalienburg. Entry to the park is free from 6 a.m., and from April through the end of October, gondolas glide along the canal in fair weather.

practical_info.tip: The park’s pavilions (Amalienburg, Badenburg, Pagodenburg, Magdalenenklause) are open from April through October 15; the palace and Marstallmuseum remain open in winter, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.

to_next_leg.road_type: By rail or public transit: Schloss Nymphenburg → tram 17 → Stiglmaierplatz → Glyptothek
to_next_leg.justification: Marche vers l’arrêt du tramway 17, trajet vers Stiglmaierplatz puis marche jusqu’à la Glyptothèque.

visits.text: Asleep for more than two thousand years, the Barberini Faun stretches out in a room with barely plastered brick walls: the Glyptothek, on Königsplatz, is Munich’s oldest public museum, built by Leo von Klenze and opened in 1830. The frescoes were lost during the war, and the museum’s 1972 reopening retained these austere walls, which showcase the pediments from the Temple of Aphaia on Aegina. On Sundays, admission drops to €1.

You’ll spend the afternoon facing Rubens’s Last Judgment, a canvas more than six meters tall hanging on the top floor of the Alte Pinakothek. Opened in 1836 in a building by Leo von Klenze, the museum displays more than 700 paintings, including Dürer’s self-portrait in a fur coat; a lower gallery also presents around 90 works from the Neue Pinakothek, from Goya to Klimt, while that museum undergoes renovation. Admission is €1 on Sundays, and the museum stays open until 8 p.m. on Tuesdays and Wednesdays.

activities.text: “Stammtisch”: at the Hofbräuhaus, the word refers to more than 125 groups of regulars, and 616 lockers keep their personal beer steins under lock and key. Founded in 1589 by Duke William V, the brewery moved to Platzl in 1607; only the ground-floor Schwemme survived the bombings of 1945. To round off this day of museums, take a seat in this hall with room for a thousand guests, where a band plays daily: reservations are not accepted.

practical_info.tip: Open daily from 11 a.m. to midnight; only the Bräustüberl on the second floor accepts reservations.

activities.text: The wooden cross standing in Lake Starnberg, a few meters from the shore at Berg, marks the spot where Ludwig II and his psychiatrist Bernhard von Gudden were found dead in the water on the evening of June 13, 1886. The circumstances remain unexplained. From the village, a woodland path leads to the Romanesque Revival Votivkapelle, consecrated in 1900 at the initiative of Prince Regent Luitpold, on the slope above the lake. Allow 1 hour on site, including the walk.

practical_info.tip: The chapel is open from April through October, Tuesday through Sunday from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m., with the interior viewed through a grille; the cross in the lake can be seen year-round.

to_next_leg.road_type: Via Starnberg, north of the lake

visits.text: At an elevation of around 700 m, with a 60 m onion-domed bell tower, Kloster Andechs crowns the Heiliger Berg above Lake Ammersee. Behind the Gothic walls of the pilgrimage church, whose construction began in 1423, Johann Baptist Zimmermann created a Rococo interior completed in 1755. Benedictine monks have lived here since 1455, and composer Carl Orff is buried in a side chapel, the Schmerzhafte Kapelle. The church opens daily from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m.

activities.text: Prayer and hops go hand in hand here: without church tax revenue, Kloster Andechs supports itself through its brewery. At the Bräustüberl, pair a Hell or a Doppelbock Dunkel with a Schweinshaxe, out on the terrace if the weather allows. If you’re driving, leave the Doppelbock, a strong beer by definition, to your passengers.

practical_info.tip: The Bräustüberl is open from 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. on weekdays and from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. on weekends; a large free parking lot at the foot of the Heiliger Berg is a few minutes’ walk from the monastery.

visits.text: You’ll then head to northern Munich for BMW Welt, which opened in October 2007 to designs by the firm Coop Himmelb(l)au and welcomes more than three million visitors a year. Admission is free: you can wander among the models on display beneath the immense roof. The south exit of Olympiazentrum station leads directly to BMW Welt and Olympiapark.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from BMW Welt to BMW Museum
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

visits.text: Even if you’re not a car enthusiast, the BMW Museum is worth a detour for its building: a silver bowl nicknamed the “salad bowl,” designed by Viennese architect Karl Schwanzer and opened in 1973 at the foot of the four-cylinder-shaped headquarters. Renovated from 2004 to 2008, it displays around 120 exhibits across 5,000 m² and traces the brand’s history from 1916. Admission costs around €10, unlike neighboring BMW Welt.

activities.text: If the sky is clear in the late afternoon, climb Olympiaberg, the freely accessible hill in Olympiapark. From the top, the view takes in Frei Otto and Günter Behnisch’s tensile roofs, designed for the 1972 Games, the Olympic lake, and the city’s rooftops. The park covers 85 hectares: head back down along the lakeshore to reach the Olympiazentrum U-Bahn station.

practical_info.tip: The park and Olympiaberg are free to visit; only tours of the stadium and its roof require a fee.

to_next_leg.road_type: A8 toward Salzburg

visits.text: Galleys locked in battle on the ceiling of a town church: in Prien’s Pfarrkirche Mariä Himmelfahrt, rebuilt in the Baroque style from 1734 to 1738, Johann Baptist Zimmermann painted the Battle of Lepanto amid his stuccowork. He is the same artist who worked at Nymphenburg and Andechs, making this a logical conclusion. Visit late in the day, then head down to Stock harbor, where the paddle steamer Ludwig Fessler, built in 1926, still sails.

activities.text: You’ll board at Stock harbor in Prien am Chiemsee, on this lake of approximately 80 km² that Bavarians call the “Bavarian Sea.” Boats depart every 30 minutes in summer and every hour in winter, reaching Herreninsel in 15 minutes. If arriving by train, get off at Prien station: the Chiemsee-Bahn, a short steam railway opened in 1887, connects it to the harbor from mid-May to mid-September.

practical_info.tip: The Chiemsee-Bahn also runs on Saturdays, Sundays, and public holidays from early May to mid-May and from mid-September to mid-October.

to_next_leg.road_type: By ferry: Prien → Prien-Stock → Herreninsel
to_next_leg.justification: Accès terrestre au quai de Prien-Stock puis bateau régulier vers Herreninsel ; hors temps d’attente au départ.

visits.text: Ninety-eight meters of mirrors and 33 glass chandeliers: the Hall of Mirrors at Neues Schloss Herrenchiemsee is longer than its model at Versailles. Ludwig II laid the foundation stone on May 21, 1878, but slept here for only a few days in September 1885; when he died, 50 of the 70 rooms remained unfinished. The state rooms can only be seen on a guided tour lasting approximately 40 minutes: book your time slot as soon as you arrive on the island.

More intimate than the gilded salons, the König-Ludwig-II-Museum has occupied the south wing of Herrenchiemsee Palace since 1987. Its twelve rooms trace the king’s life from his christening gown to his death mask, connecting the stops on this journey, from Nymphenburg to Berg and St. Michael. You can explore at your own pace; in winter, the last admission is at 3:45 p.m.

Less gilding, greater consequences: at Herrenchiemsee’s Altes Schloss, a former monastery of Augustinian canons founded shortly before 1130, representatives of eleven West German states and West Berlin drafted, between August 10 and 23, 1948, the text that formed the basis of the Basic Law. The Constitution Museum shares the building with the restored Kaisersaal and a gallery of painters from Lake Chiemsee. Open year-round, with hours of 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. from April through October 24.

activities.text: From the Herreninsel landing, you can reach the Neues Schloss on foot in about 20 minutes across the island, or by horse-drawn carriage from April to October. Walkers have an even better option: an 8 km trail circles the entire island, with 4 and 6 km alternatives. Leave plenty of time to catch the next boat, especially in winter, when it runs only once an hour.

practical_info.tip: The palace is open from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. from April through October 24, then from 10 a.m. to 4:45 p.m. (last guided tour around 4 p.m.); closed January 1, Shrove Tuesday, and December 24, 25, and 31.

to_next_leg.road_type: Boat to Fraueninsel, 10 minutes

visits.text: The freestanding octagonal bell tower of the Münster on Fraueninsel, topped with a Baroque onion dome in 1626, is a landmark throughout the Chiemgau. Frauenwörth Benedictine Abbey, founded in the 8th century by Duke Tassilo III, is still home to a community of nuns: pass beneath the Carolingian Torhalle before entering the church, where the chapel of Blessed Irmengard, an abbess who died in 866, draws couples hoping for a child. Be discreet; the convent is still very much in use.

activities.text: Water lapping against the fishermen’s docks accompanies the entire walk: explore Fraueninsel on foot along a waterfront path of approximately 1.4 km. Around 200 residents live on these 15.5 hectares, and six families still earn their living from fishing. Try fish from Lake Chiemsee at an island inn, then stop at the monastery shop for its handmade marzipan: the convent has also been distilling spirits since at least 1470.

practical_info.tip: From Gstadt, on the northern shore, the crossing to Fraueninsel takes about 10 minutes; from Prien-Stock, allow 30 minutes.

seo.h1_title: Munich and Its Lakes in 5 Days: In the Footsteps of Ludwig II
seo.intro_paragraph: This 5-day trip devotes three full days to Munich, from the Residenz to the Deutsches Museum, followed by two days focused on the lakes and a final evening on the shores of Lake Chiemsee. The thread running through the journey is Ludwig II of Bavaria: his birth at Nymphenburg, his tomb at St. Michael, his death at Berg, and his unfinished Versailles on Herreninsel. Along the way, a stop at Andechs Abbey is a reminder that in Bavaria, beer sustains a monastery.
seo.seo_hook: Munich and Its Lakes in 5 Days: Residenz, Nymphenburg, and Deutsches Museum, then Berg, Andechs, and Herrenchiemsee in the footsteps of Ludwig II.
featured_list: Munich: Residenz expanded over more than six centuries, with the Antiquarium dating from 1571
Nymphenburg Palace: Ludwig I’s Gallery of Beauties and the room where Ludwig II was born
Deutsches Museum: 19 renovated exhibitions, reopened in July 2022
Berg: cross in Lake Starnberg, where Ludwig II was found in 1886
Andechs: Rococo church and monastery brewery on the Heiliger Berg
Herrenchiemsee: 98 m Hall of Mirrors and Ludwig II Museum

itineraries.title: Berlin and Potsdam in 5 Days: Reichstag, Wall, and Sanssouci
itineraries.subtitle: In 5 days, explore Berlin from the Reichstag to the Wall on Bernauer Straße, then discover Potsdam’s Prussian palaces.
itineraries.notes: Start on a Tuesday or Wednesday: most Berlin museums and Potsdam palaces close on Mondays, while the Humboldt Forum, Neues Palais, and Museum Barberini close on Tuesdays. Book the Reichstag dome in advance, with free admission upon registration, along with your time slot for Sanssouci Palace.
itineraries.climate: Aim for May through September: average highs range from about 20 °C in May and September to 25 °C in July. July is also the wettest month, so keep a raincoat handy; in January, highs hover around 3 °C and nighttime temperatures fall below freezing. The Chinese House and Sanssouci Picture Gallery are only open from May through October.

visits.text: The best introduction to Berlin starts on the roof of the Reichstag. Norman Foster’s glass dome, completed in 1999, crowns the federal parliament building, and its 230 m ramp offers panoramic views of the government district, accompanied by an audio guide lasting about twenty minutes. Admission is free with online registration confirmed at least two hours in advance: bring an original ID document, as copies are not accepted. During some weeks, only the rooftop terrace remains accessible; check the calendar at bundestag.de.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Reichstag to Brandenburger Tor Berlin
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

visits.text: In 1806, Napoleon took the Quadriga atop the Brandenburg Gate to Paris; it did not return to Berlin until 1814. Built between 1788 and 1791 by Carl Gotthard Langhans, the 26 m-high gate features twelve Doric columns and five passageways. The Wall ran along its western side, and the passage through the gate only reopened on December 22, 1989. Walk through toward Pariser Platz, then return after dark: access is free at all hours.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Brandenburger Tor Berlin to Denkmal Fuer Die Ermordeten Juden Europas
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

map_keywords: Denkmal für die ermordeten Juden Europas Berlin

visits.text: Head down into the Ort der Information, the information center beneath the eastern corner of the Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe: after the abstract stelae, the focus shifts to individual lives. In the Room of Names, the names of Jewish victims are read aloud using data from Yad Vashem. Admission is free, Tuesday through Sunday from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., with last admission 45 minutes before closing; a free guided tour in English starts at 2 p.m. on the first Sunday of the month.

activities.text: The ground undulates, the concrete blocks grow taller, and the city’s noise fades within a few steps. Designed by Peter Eisenman and inaugurated in May 2005, the Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe consists of 2,711 stelae spread across nearly 2 hectares, ranging from 20 cm to 4.7 m in height. Walk through several aisles without looking for a set route: each changes your perspective. This is a place of remembrance; climbing and picnicking are not allowed.

practical_info.tip: The field of stelae is freely accessible; the information center’s audio guide costs €3.

to_next_leg.road_type: On foot via Potsdamer Platz

visits.text: The Topography of Terror occupies a restrained building on a large open site near Potsdamer Platz. From 1933 to 1945, this was home to the Gestapo and its prison, the SS leadership, and the Reich Security Main Office. The documentation center, opened in 2010, traces their crimes, while an outdoor trail with 15 stations follows a surviving stretch of the Wall about 200 m long. Admission is free, daily from 10 AM to 8 PM; allow more than 1 hour.

to_next_leg.road_type: On foot via Zimmerstraße

visits.text: Touristy to the point of parody, yet steeped in history, Checkpoint Charlie was the only crossing between East and West Berlin open to foreigners, diplomats, and Allied military personnel. In late October 1961, ten Soviet tanks and ten American tanks faced off here about a hundred meters apart. Today’s guardhouse is a replica; the original is preserved at the Allied Museum. Take your photo, then save your time for the neighboring museum.

Packed with exhibits and somewhat disorganized, the Mauermuseum Haus am Checkpoint Charlie is most worthwhile for its escape artifacts. Opened in 1963 beside the border crossing, it displays an armored car, a homemade hot-air balloon, and a miniature submarine powered by a bicycle motor, all designed to reach the West. Open daily from 10 AM to 8 PM; at €18.50 for adult admission, it is best suited to Cold War enthusiasts.

to_next_leg.road_type: On foot via Friedrichstraße

visits.text: More than two years of construction, from October 2022 to March 2025, restored Gendarmenmarkt’s 14,000 m² of cobblestones, now fully wheelchair accessible. Laid out in 1688, the square features Schinkel’s Konzerthaus (1821) between two matching churches, the Französischer Dom and Deutscher Dom, whose domed towers date to 1785. Here, “Dom” refers to the dome, not a cathedral. Return toward the end of the day, when the square empties out.

activities.text: Climb to the Französischer Dom’s panoramic platform, 40 m above Gendarmenmarkt, for a 360° view of the historic center. The tower also houses the Huguenot Museum, recalling the French community that built the church between 1701 and 1705. Tickets cost €8, or €10 with an audio guide; access is by stairs only, Tuesday through Sunday.

practical_info.tip: Hours vary with the season and sunset; last admission is 30 minutes before closing.

to_next_leg.road_type: On foot via Bebelplatz and Unter den Linden

visits.text: Old brickwork, faded frescoes, and contemporary spaces play off one another at the Neues Museum, which reopened in October 2009 after its reconstruction by David Chipperfield. The bust of Nefertiti, sculpted around 1345 BC and unearthed at Amarna in 1912, takes pride of place here; its left eye was never given an iris. Before leaving the floor devoted to prehistory, see the Berlin Gold Hat, whose decoration can be read as a calendar. Reserve a time slot online and arrive right at 10 AM; the museum is closed on Mondays.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Neues Museum Berlin to Alte Nationalgalerie
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

visits.text: The Alte Nationalgalerie rises like a Roman temple, with an equestrian statue of Frederick William IV at the top of its staircase. Completed in 1876, it houses Caspar David Friedrich’s The Monk by the Sea, Adolph Menzel’s The Iron Rolling Mill, and paintings by Manet and Monet. Allow 1 hour for the highlights; if you are visiting several museums on the island, buy the day ticket covering them all. Closed on Mondays.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Alte Nationalgalerie to Berliner Dom
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

visits.text: More imperial than contemplative, Berlin Cathedral embraces the grandeur envisioned under Wilhelm II. Inaugurated in 1905, it is Germany’s largest Protestant church. Beneath the nave, the Hohenzollern Crypt reopened in March 2026 after about six years of renovation. It contains 91 coffins spanning five centuries, including the Great Elector’s sarcophagus, which weighs 8 to 10 tonnes. Buy your ticket online for around €15; visits pause during services.

activities.text: Climb the roughly 270 steps to the Kuppelumgang, the outdoor gallery around Berlin Cathedral’s dome. From the top, views stretch across the Lustgarten, Museum Island, and the Spree. The climb is included in paid admission; skip it if you are afraid of heights or if winds are strong.

practical_info.tip: Visiting hours are 9 AM to 6 PM on weekdays, 9 AM to 5 PM on Saturdays, and noon to 5 PM on Sundays, with last admission 1 hour before closing.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Berliner Dom to Humboldt Forum
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

visits.text: A Baroque palace completed in 2020: the Humboldt Forum reconstructed three facades of the former Berlin Palace, demolished by East Germany in 1950, and paired them with a decidedly modern east facade designed by Franco Stella. The Ethnological Museum and the Museum of Asian Art occupy the third and fourth floors. Several areas are free, including the sculpture hall; a day ticket costs €14. Open from 10:30 AM to 6:30 PM, except Tuesdays.

activities.text: If the sky is clear, head up to the Humboldt Forum’s rooftop terrace, 30 m above the ground: roughly 1,800 m² with views of Berlin Cathedral, Alexanderplatz, and Marienkirche. An elevator takes you there from the ground floor. Admission costs €5, and reserving a time slot online avoids the wait.

practical_info.tip: Like the rest of the building, the terrace is closed on Tuesdays.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Humboldt Forum to Nikolaiviertel
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

visits.text: Dating back to around 1200, the Nikolaiviertel was destroyed during World War II, then rebuilt for Berlin’s 750th anniversary in 1987: reconstructed houses stand alongside prefabricated apartment buildings. At its center, the Nikolaikirche, begun around 1230 and rebuilt from 1980 to 1987, houses a museum devoted to its history. Stroll through the lanes and along the Spree in the late afternoon before dinner at one of the neighborhood’s traditional restaurants.

Berliners call the cross of light that sunlight casts on the Fernsehturm’s sphere “the Pope’s revenge”: the tower was erected by an East German state that was removing crosses from churches. Standing 368 m tall, the tower opened on October 3, 1969, and whisks visitors up to around 203 m in about 40 seconds. Standard tickets start at €20. Head up at sunset: the observation deck stays open until 11 p.m.

to_next_leg.road_type: Subway from Alexanderplatz

visits.text: Walk along Bernauer Straße: the Berlin Wall Memorial follows the former border strip for 1.4 km, with a 70 m section of the original Wall, its patrol road, and a watchtower. The Window of Remembrance brings together portraits of 130 people killed at the Wall, and the Chapel of Reconciliation replaces the church demolished with explosives in 1985 because it stood in the border zone. The outdoor exhibition is free and open daily from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m.

Seen from above, the no man’s land comes into chilling focus. From the five-story observation tower at the Berlin Wall Memorial’s Documentation Center, you look down on the preserved border strip opposite; inside, the exhibition “1961 | 1989. The Berlin Wall” recalls how the border encircled West Berlin for 155 km. Admission is free, Tuesday through Sunday from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., with the last ascent at 5:45 p.m.

to_next_leg.road_type: S-Bahn from Nordbahnhof to Friedrichstraße

visits.text: The Tränenpalast owes its name, “Palace of Tears,” to the farewells between visitors from the West and loved ones who remained in the East. From 1962 to 1989, this hall at Friedrichstraße station was used exclusively for departures to West Berlin; the permanent exhibition “Site of German Division” tells the story of the country’s division. Admission is free, Tuesday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m., and weekends from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

to_next_leg.road_type: S-Bahn from Friedrichstraße to Ostbahnhof

activities.text: More colorful than moving, and all the more valuable for it, the East Side Gallery stretches for 1,316 m along the Spree, painted in spring 1990 by 118 artists from 21 countries. Dmitri Vrubel’s kiss between Brezhnev and Honecker draws every camera; the paintings were redone in 2009. Walk from Ostbahnhof toward the Oberbaumbrücke, staying on the Mühlenstraße sidewalk.

practical_info.tip: You can walk freely along the Wall without a ticket; Ostbahnhof station is served by the S-Bahn.

visits.text: The Oberbaumbrücke spans the Spree on two levels: the roadway below and the subway above, beneath pointed brick Gothic arches. Completed in 1896 by Otto Stahn, the bridge became a pedestrian crossing reserved for West Berlin residents in December 1963. Walk across toward Kreuzberg, then board the U1 at Schlesisches Tor.

to_next_leg.road_type: U1 from Schlesisches Tor toward Hallesches Tor

visits.text: If there is one building in Berlin that speaks through its architecture, it is Daniel Libeskind’s Jewish Museum, opened in 2001: a zigzag intersected by voids around 20 m high. The Holocaust Tower, a 24 m concrete silo, is lit only by a slit, while the Garden of Exile features 49 pillars topped with Russian olive trees. The permanent exhibition is free; reserve a time slot online and arrive before 5 p.m., the last admission time. The museum is closed on Mondays.

to_next_leg.road_type: By rail or public transit: Jüdisches Museum → Berlin Hauptbahnhof → Potsdam Hbf
to_next_leg.justification: Marche et transport urbain vers une gare berlinoise, puis train régional ou S-Bahn jusqu’à Potsdam.

visits.text: Climb the vineyard terraces to Sanssouci Palace, the summer palace Frederick the Great had built from 1745 to 1747 to live “without a care.” Its ten main rooms retain their 18th-century decor, on the scale of a private retreat rather than a royal court. The €14 ticket requires a timed entry: book online, download the free SANSSOUCI app, and bring your own headphones, as none are provided. Closed on Mondays.

The Sanssouci Picture Gallery, built starting in 1755 to house Frederick II’s paintings, is described as Germany’s oldest surviving gallery building. Caravaggio’s The Incredulity of Saint Thomas, painted around 1601, hangs alongside seven works by Rubens. It is open only from May through October: individual admission costs €8, or is included in the €22 sanssouci+ ticket, valid for one day at Potsdam’s palaces.

A summer residence on paper, a display of power in reality: the New Palace, built from 1763 to 1769 following the Seven Years’ War, has more than 200 rooms and over 400 sandstone statues. Among its highlights are the Grotto Hall, encrusted with shells, quartz, and semiprecious stones, and the two-story Marble Hall. Choose the €14 Grand Tour ticket; the palace is closed on Tuesdays, and also on Mondays from January through March.

End the day in the Holländisches Viertel: 134 red brick houses built in the 1730s to attract Dutch craftspeople to Potsdam. The Soldier King, Frederick William I, commissioned them from Jan Bouman, and his son Frederick the Great completed the neighborhood after 1740. Walk there along Brandenburger Straße, the pedestrian street that starts at Potsdam’s Brandenburg Gate: the city has its own, with two facades in different styles.

activities.text: It was not until 1991 that Frederick the Great was laid to rest where he had wished: in the crypt on the highest terrace of Sanssouci Palace, buried at night without pomp, as stipulated in his will. Then descend the terraces, planted with grapevines beginning in 1744, to take in the park’s parterre. Admission to Sanssouci Park is free, daily from 8 a.m. until dusk.

practical_info.tip: Avoid the park during severe weather alerts: branches weakened by drought may fall.

activities.text: The gold of the Chinese House’s columns and statues emerges between the trees as you round a bend on a path in Sanssouci Park. The park covers nearly 300 hectares, crossed by an east–west axis more than 2 km long; Johann Gottfried Büring’s pavilion, built from 1755 to 1764 on a trefoil plan, can be admired along the way. The interior is open only from May through October (€5), but you can admire the exterior year-round.

practical_info.tip: Follow the main axis west to the New Palace: more than 2 km, or a good 30 minutes on foot without stops.

visits.text: The Museum Barberini makes Potsdam a destination for Impressionism: 34 paintings by Claude Monet are on permanent display among more than 100 works collected by Hasso Plattner. The museum opened in 2017 on the Alter Markt, in a palace reconstructed on the model of Rome’s Palazzo Barberini, and refreshes its displays with three exhibitions a year. Avoid Tuesdays; admission is €16 on weekdays, €18 on weekends, and €10 from 5:30 p.m.

On February 10, 1962, U-2 pilot Gary Powers was exchanged here for Soviet spy Rudolf Abel: the Glienicker Brücke, which connects Potsdam to Berlin-Wannsee across the Havel, witnessed two more exchanges of agents in 1985 and 1986. Steven Spielberg drew on this history for his 2015 film Bridge of Spies. Walk across this bridge, built in 1907 and reopened to pedestrians on the evening of November 10, 1989.

activities.text: Climb the 223 steps of Schinkel’s Nikolaikirche to the gallery encircling its dome, 42 m above the ground: the Alter Markt unfolds at your feet, with its 16 m obelisk, the Altes Rathaus topped by a gilded Atlas, and the Landtag, whose facade replicates that of the former palace. The climb costs €5; hours vary depending on services and concerts.

practical_info.tip: The organ is often played between 11:15 a.m. and noon: a good time to stop in the nave before the climb.

to_next_leg.road_type: By rail or public transit: Potsdam Hbf → Wannsee → Berlin-Charlottenburg → Schloss Charlottenburg
to_next_leg.justification: Train de Potsdam via Wannsee vers Charlottenburg, puis transport urbain ou marche vers le château.

visits.text: For Prussian splendor, Charlottenburg Palace rivals anything in Potsdam. Built around 1700 for Sophie Charlotte, wife of Frederick I, the Old Palace houses a Porcelain Cabinet with thousands of pieces; in the New Wing, the Golden Gallery and White Hall rank among Europe’s finest Rococo creations, according to the Prussian Palaces and Gardens Foundation. The charlottenburg+ ticket (€19) covers both wings; closed Mondays.

activities.text: Weather permitting, continue into the gardens of Charlottenburg Palace, laid out beginning in 1697 in the Baroque style by Siméon Godeau and bordered by the Spree. At the end of the paths, Queen Louise’s mausoleum, built in 1810–1812 in a Neoclassical style, houses her tomb. Allow 30 minutes for a stroll, longer if you continue to the riverbank.

practical_info.tip: Buy your palace ticket online: admission to the Old Palace is timed.

to_next_leg.road_type: Bus to Adenauerplatz

activities.text: Head east along Kurfürstendamm, from Adenauerplatz to Breitscheidplatz: this 3.5 km boulevard was West Berlin’s premier shopping showcase during the economic miracle. Beginning in 1875, Bismarck had it developed into a 53 m-wide avenue along an old road leading to the Grunewald hunting lodge. Save some energy for KaDeWe, which opened in 1907, and its sixth-floor gourmet food department.

practical_info.tip: KaDeWe is a few minutes’ walk from Breitscheidplatz.

visits.text: “Der hohle Zahn,” the hollow tooth: this is Berliners’ nickname for the ruined tower of the Kaiser Wilhelm Memorial Church, left standing at 71 m after the bombing of November 22, 1943. At its foot, Egon Eiermann’s church (1959–1963), which they compare to a tube of lipstick and a powder compact, is bathed in blue light from 21,292 stained-glass windows by Gabriel Loire, inspired by Chartres. Sit for a few minutes in the octagonal nave; open daily from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

seo.h1_title: Berlin and Potsdam in 5 Days: Reichstag, Wall, and Sanssouci
seo.intro_paragraph: This 5-day trip explores Berlin on foot and by subway, from the government district to Museum Island, then follows the traces of the Wall from Bernauer Straße to the East Side Gallery. A day and a half in Potsdam connects Sanssouci, the New Palace, and Museum Barberini, before a finale at Charlottenburg and along Kurfürstendamm.
seo.seo_hook: The Reichstag dome, Museum Island, the Wall along Bernauer Straße, and Sanssouci Palace: Berlin and Potsdam in 5 days, on foot and by S-Bahn.

itineraries.title: Nuremberg and Bamberg in 3 Days: Castle, Trials, UNESCO
itineraries.subtitle: In 3 days, go from Nuremberg’s Kaiserburg to Courtroom 600, then explore Bamberg, a UNESCO-listed city.
itineraries.notes: Start on a Wednesday or Thursday: the Germanisches Nationalmuseum is closed on Mondays, the Memorium on Tuesdays, and St. Michael’s Church in Bamberg is open only Friday through Sunday. You can do everything without a car, on foot, by streetcar, subway, and train (35 to 41 minutes between Nuremberg and Bamberg).
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May through September, with average highs of 20 to 25 °C in Nuremberg. July, the sunniest month, is also the wettest, so keep an umbrella handy for thundershowers. In December, the Christkindlesmarkt draws crowds despite highs around 4 °C: dress warmly and book your accommodations early. Bring comfortable walking shoes, as both old towns have cobblestone streets and slopes.

visits.text: The best place to start exploring Nuremberg is at the top, at the Kaiserburg. Louis IV of Bavaria stayed here 74 times, and the Golden Bull of 1356 required every new ruler to hold his first assembly, the Hoftag, in Nuremberg. The €10 combination ticket gives you access to the Palas and its two-level chapel, the museum, the Tiefer Brunnen—a well more than 50 m deep cut into the rock and presented during a guided demonstration—and then the Sinwellturm, where peregrine falcons nest. Arrive at opening time (9 a.m. from April through September, 10 a.m. afterward): tickets are sold only on-site.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Kaiserburg Nuremberg to Albrecht Duerer Haus
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

visits.text: Then head downhill along the city walls to the Albrecht-Dürer-Haus, a house built around 1420 that the painter bought in 1509 and where he died in 1528. The museum describes it as the only surviving Renaissance artist’s home outside Italy: a kitchen, living quarters, a room displaying copies of his major paintings, and a workshop where a press reconstructed from a drawing by Dürer still produces prints. Allow 1 hour. Admission is €7.50; the museum is closed on Mondays except from July through September and during the Christkindlesmarkt.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Albrecht Duerer Haus to St Sebald Nuremberg
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

visits.text: The hush of stone, then the gleam of bronze: inside the Sebalduskirche, Nuremberg’s oldest parish church, the Sebaldusgrab stands over the grave of the city’s patron saint. Peter Vischer the Elder and his sons cast this tomb, shaped like a small building, between 1508 and 1519. Damaged by bombing from 1940 to 1945, the church was reconsecrated in 1957, but many of its furnishings survived after being moved to safety in time. Allow 20 minutes; avoid service times.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from St Sebald Nuremberg to Hauptmarkt Nuremberg
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

visits.text: If you reach the Hauptmarkt just before noon, look up at the Frauenkirche: as soon as the hour strikes, seven prince-electors circle Charles IV three times. This Männleinlaufen clock, completed in 1509, commemorates the Golden Bull; the church, built from 1352 to 1362, stands on the site of a synagogue destroyed during the pogrom of 1349. On the same square, the Schöner Brunnen rises 19 m, adorned with forty painted figures. From November 27 to December 24, 2026, the Christkindlesmarkt fills the square: arrive as early as 10 a.m.

activities.text: Ask for “Drei im Weggla” at the counter: three Nürnberger Rostbratwürste tucked into a roll with mustard. These grilled, marjoram-seasoned sausages measure just 7 to 9 cm and weigh around twenty grams, and their name is protected throughout the European Union by a geographical indication. Eat them standing at a kiosk near the Hauptmarkt: you still have a busy afternoon ahead.

practical_info.tip: Downtown kiosks serve “Drei im Weggla” to go, a quicker option than a sit-down meal before an afternoon of museums.

visits.text: Weißgerbergasse has Nuremberg’s largest collection of historic artisans’ houses: colorful half-timbered facades, oriel windows, and window boxes. The tanners who gave the street its name grew wealthy here during the Middle Ages, and many houses had their own well and garden. The tanneries have given way to cafés, stores, and workshops; stroll along the street at your own pace, then head to the Pegnitz via Maxplatz.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Weissgerbergasse Nuremberg to Henkersteg Nuremberg
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

visits.text: Charming in photos, sinister in history: the Henkersteg, a covered footbridge over the Pegnitz, takes its name from the executioner who lived there, employed by the city but kept apart from society. From the 15th to the 19th century, the executioner lived in the neighboring tower; one of them, Franz Schmidt, recorded 361 executions between 1578 and 1617. In 1595, a flood brought down the footbridge, killing eight onlookers. Photograph it from the south bank, with the half-timbered Weinstadel; the Henkerhaus, a museum of judicial history, is open from April through December, Tuesday through Sunday, from noon to 5 p.m.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Henkersteg Nuremberg to St Lorenz Nuremberg
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

visits.text: Walk up to the choir of the Lorenzkirche and look up: Veit Stoß’s Englischer Gruß, a wooden Annunciation measuring 3.72 m by 3.20 m, encircled by 55 gilded roses and carved in 1517–1518, floats above you. The work fell in 1817 and was almost completely shattered before being restored. Nearby, Adam Kraft’s Sakramentshaus, a sandstone tabernacle nearly 20 m tall, carved from 1493 to 1496, soars toward the vault; Kraft included a depiction of himself in it. Allow 35 minutes, and bring binoculars if you have them.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from St Lorenz Nuremberg to Germanisches Nationalmuseum
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

visits.text: Around 1.3 million objects, with some 25,000 on display: founded in 1852 and built around a former Carthusian monastery, the Germanisches Nationalmuseum is Germany’s largest museum of cultural history. Don’t look for America on Martin Behaim’s Erdapfel, the oldest surviving terrestrial globe, completed in 1492 before Columbus returned. Dürer, Veit Stoß, Rembrandt, and remnants of the original Schöner Brunnen round out the visit. Admission is €10; closed Mondays, with extended hours on Wednesdays until 8:30 p.m. and free admission from 5:30 p.m. (excluding temporary exhibitions).

Dani Karavan’s Straße der Menschenrechte transforms Kartäusergasse, in front of the museum entrance, into a manifesto in white concrete. Each of its 27 pillars bears an article of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in German and another language. In the city of the Nazi rallies and the 1945–1946 trial, the symbolism carries considerable weight. Read a few columns as you leave the museum: the street is freely accessible.

to_next_leg.road_type: Tram 8 or replacement bus from the Hauptbahnhof

visits.text: The most intense moment of the trip unfolds in an unsettling setting: the Dokumentationszentrum Reichsparteitagsgelände occupies the north wing of the never-completed Kongresshalle, pierced diagonally by Günther Domenig’s glass-and-steel “stake.” The hall was intended to hold 50,000 party activists; its walls reach only 39 m instead of the planned 68.5 m. The new permanent exhibition, opened in 2026 across 1,600 m², can be explored with a 90-minute French audio guide, included in the €7.50 admission. Opens at 9 a.m. on weekdays and 10 a.m. on weekends.

to_next_leg.road_type: On foot around the Dutzendteich

activities.text: Continue around Dutzendteich lake, following the German- and English-language signs leading from the Kongresshalle to the Zeppelintribüne. Designed by Albert Speer and built from 1935 to 1937, this 360 m grandstand overlooked grounds that could hold some 320,000 people; the swastika that crowned it was blown up on April 20, 1945. Today, the stone is crumbling, and a long-term conservation program is underway. Walking through stations 1 to 9 of the route takes about 1 hour 30 minutes.

practical_info.tip: The site has 23 information panels; to cover more of them, VAG-Rad bike-share bicycles are available near the documentation center.

to_next_leg.road_type: By rail or public transit: Zeppelinfeld → Dutzendteich → Nürnberg Hbf → Bärenschanze
to_next_leg.justification: Accès à Dutzendteich, train urbain puis métro U1 via le centre jusqu’à Bärenschanze et marche.

visits.text: A heavy silence falls as soon as you enter Courtroom 600: at the Memorium Nürnberger Prozesse, the International Military Tribunal tried 21 Nazi leaders from November 20, 1945, to October 1, 1946, over 218 hearings, and handed down twelve death sentences. The courtroom remained in judicial use until 2020; the “Zeitreise Saal 600” installation now recreates the trial there. Admission is €7.50, with a free multimedia guide in French; closed to visitors on Tuesdays. Take subway line U1 to Bärenschanze.

to_next_leg.road_type: By rail or public transit: Bärenschanze → Nürnberg Hbf → Bamberg Hbf → Altes Rathaus
to_next_leg.justification: Métro U1 jusqu’à Nürnberg Hbf, train vers Bamberg puis trajet local à pied vers l’ancien hôtel de ville.

visits.text: The legend is false, but more appealing than the history: Bamberg’s Altes Rathaus supposedly arose in the middle of the Regnitz because a bishop refused to grant the townspeople any land, although the boundary actually ran along the foot of the Domberg. First mentioned in 1387, the town hall was remodeled in Baroque and Rococo styles from 1744 to 1756, and its facades were painted in 1755. On the east side, look for the cherub’s leg that seems to protrude from the fresco. Walk around via the Obere Brücke and Untere Brücke, and don’t miss the half-timbered Rottmeisterhäuschen attached to the bridge tower.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Altes Rathaus Bamberg to Klein Venedig Bamberg
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

visits.text: Walk upstream along the opposite bank on the Am Leinritt path: according to the tourist office, this is where Klein Venedig looks its best. The former fishermen’s quarter in the Inselstadt lines the Regnitz with half-timbered houses that seem to lean against one another, complete with small gardens and moored boats. During Sandkerwa, Bamberg’s major annual festival, the facades are decorated and illuminated. The path has no steps and is wheelchair accessible; sightseeing boats pass right alongside the houses.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Klein Venedig Bamberg to Schlenkerla
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

activities.text: In the Franconian dialect, “Schlenkern” describes walking with a swinging motion of the arms: it became the nickname of Andreas Graser, the owner in 1875, and later the name of the Schlenkerla tavern. Its history dates back to 1405, the brewery to 1678, and the establishment passed from the Graser family to the Trum family. Order the Rauchbier, a smoked beer that divides opinion around the table from the first sip, in the Dominikanerklause, beneath a painted Gothic vault restored by the Germanisches Nationalmuseum in the 1920s. Open daily from 9:30 a.m. to 11:30 p.m.; food is served from 11 a.m. to 10 p.m.

practical_info.tip: The beer garden in the Dominican courtyard is open from Easter to early October, weather permitting.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Schlenkerla to Bamberger Dom
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

visits.text: Bamberg Cathedral, consecrated in 1012, then rebuilt and reconsecrated in 1237, rises above the Domberg with four towers approximately 81 m tall. Inside, the Bamberger Reiter, a stone horseman carved around 1225–1237, keeps his secret: no one knows for certain whom he represents. Also see the tomb of Henry II and Cunigunde by Tilman Riemenschneider (1499–1513), the tomb of Clement II, the only pope buried north of the Alps, and the altarpiece by Veit Stoß, carved for Nuremberg. On Sundays, visits begin at 1 p.m.; sightseeing pauses during services.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Bamberger Dom to Dioezesanmuseum Bamberg
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

visits.text: Pass through the cathedral and its Adamspforte to reach the adjoining Diözesanmuseum. The highlight is the Sternenmantel, Henry II’s star-studded cloak, displayed alongside other medieval imperial garments and pontifical vestments; the cathedral cross exhibited here weighs 600 kg. Admission is €7; the museum is closed on Wednesdays and opens only at noon on Sundays. Allow 45 minutes.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Dioezesanmuseum Bamberg to Alte Hofhaltung Bamberg
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

visits.text: In 1003, the Alte Hofhaltung was simply the palace of the Duke of Bavaria, the future Emperor Henry II; in 1007, it became the bishops’ residence. Step through the Schöne Pforte, a Renaissance portal carved in 1573 by Pankraz Wagner, where Henry and Cunigunde hold a model of the cathedral. The courtyard, surrounded by Gothic half-timbered buildings with galleries, hosts the Calderón festival in summer, with performances held here since 1973. The Historisches Museum, in the Renaissance wing, opens Friday through Sunday from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Alte Hofhaltung Bamberg to Neue Residenz Bamberg
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

visits.text: After the cathedral’s restraint, the Neue Residenz embraces Baroque extravagance, and is all the better for it. Its wings, built from 1697 to 1703 to designs by Leonhard Dientzenhofer for Prince-Bishop Lothar Franz von Schönborn, conceal the Kaisersaal, where Melchior Steidl painted sixteen emperors larger than life-size from 1707 to 1709. Guided tours of the prince-bishop’s apartment run every half hour in German; the other rooms can be explored independently. Admission is €7 and free for visitors under 18.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Neue Residenz Bamberg to Rosengarten Bamberg
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

visits.text: The fragrance reaches you before the view: some 4,500 rosebushes bloom each summer in the Neue Residenz’s Rosengarten, designed by Balthasar Neumann and framed by linden trees. Statues by Ferdinand Tietz, carved in 1760–1761, punctuate the paths, and the terrace looks out toward the Michaelsberg and the old town’s rooftops. Open from 9 a.m. to 6:45 p.m. from April through September, and from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. the rest of the year; the pavilion houses a café.

Fourteen years of work and some €43 million: St. Michael’s Church, closed in 2012 after a piece of plaster fell from the vault, reopened on April 25, 2026. Founded in 1015, the Benedictine abbey crowns the Michaelsberg; behind Leonhard Dientzenhofer’s Baroque facade, look up at the Himmelsgarten, a ceiling where restorers have identified 585 plants, then seek out the tomb of Saint Otto. Admission is free, Friday through Sunday and on public holidays, from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. only.

activities.text: Then head down through the Michaelsberg’s terraced gardens, Baroque grounds of the former monastery planted with old fruit varieties. A vineyard was replanted here for the 2012 Bavarian horticultural show, a nod to a city that grew wine grapes until the 18th century. From the rows of vines, the view stretches toward the cathedral; the garden café invites you to take a break.

practical_info.tip: Outside winter, the Michaelsberg gates remain open all day; the “Benediktinerweg” trail crosses the former Baroque gardens.

visits.text: The Obere Pfarre, the Church of Our Lady in the upper town, is Bamberg’s only purely Gothic church, according to the tourist office. The foundations of its choir date to 1375, the nave followed some fifty years later, and flying buttresses support the lofty choir. Stop at the bridal portal with its Gothic statues, then look inside for Tintoretto’s Assumption, a particularly valuable work. In December 2026, the “Poetischer Krippenweg” is performed here on the 12th, 19th, and 23rd at 3:30 p.m.

to_next_leg.road_type: On foot via the Altes Rathaus and the Inselstadt
to_next_leg.justification: Ce parcours se fait à pied par les cheminements locaux ; le routeur automobile produit un détour ou une valeur nulle inadaptée.

visits.text: If you visit between April 17 and November 8, 2026, finish at the Gärtner- und Häckermuseum, housed in a market gardener’s home dating to 1767 in the heart of the Gärtnerstadt, the gardeners’ district where crops have been grown within the city since the Middle Ages. Behind the house, the Sortengarten preserves around thirty traditional Bamberg crops, including licorice, across 400 m². The museum opens Tuesday through Sunday from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.; outside the season, stroll along Mittelstraße between the plots, about a ten-minute walk from the train station.

seo.h1_title: Nuremberg and Bamberg in 3 Days: Castle, Trials, UNESCO
seo.intro_paragraph: In 3 days, this car-free itinerary connects two cities in Franconia less than 45 minutes apart by train. Nuremberg traces the Holy Roman Empire at the Kaiserburg, then the 20th century at the Documentation Center Nazi Party Rally Grounds and in Courtroom 600, where the trials took place. Bamberg, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1993, can be explored from its episcopal town to its market gardeners’ district.
seo.seo_hook: Kaiserburg, Germanisches Nationalmuseum, Courtroom 600 and Doku-Zentrum, then Bamberg Cathedral and gardens: Nuremberg and Bamberg in 3 days, without a car.
featured_list: Nuremberg: the Kaiserburg, where each new ruler held his first assembly
Nuremberg: the Germanisches Nationalmuseum and the oldest surviving terrestrial globe
Nuremberg: the renovated Doku-Zentrum and Courtroom 600, site of the 1945–1946 trials
Bamberg: Bamberg Cathedral, Neue Residenz and 4,500 rosebushes on the episcopal hill

places_taglines.DE::kaiserburg-nuernberg: Imperial castle, a well over 50 m deep and views of Nuremberg.
places_taglines.DE::albrecht-duerer-haus: House where Albrecht Dürer lived from 1509 until his death.
places_taglines.DE::st-sebald-nuernberg: Nuremberg’s oldest parish church, home to the bronze Sebaldusgrab.
places_taglines.DE::hauptmarkt-nuernberg: Square with the Schöner Brunnen and the Männleinlaufen at noon.
places_taglines.DE::weissgerbergasse-nuernberg: Nuremberg’s largest collection of historic artisans’ houses.
places_taglines.DE::henkersteg-nuernberg: The executioner’s covered footbridge over the Pegnitz.
places_taglines.DE::st-lorenz-nuernberg: Gothic church housing Veit Stoß’s Englischer Gruß.
places_taglines.DE::germanisches-nationalmuseum: Germany’s largest museum of cultural history, founded in 1852.
places_taglines.DE::dokumentationszentrum-reichsparteita: Exhibition on the Nazi Party rallies in the unfinished Kongresshalle.
places_taglines.DE::zeppelintribuene: 360 m grandstand designed by Albert Speer, near the Dutzendteich.
places_taglines.DE::memorium-nuernberger-prozesse: Courtroom 600, where Nazi leaders were tried in 1945–1946.
places_taglines.DE::altes-rathaus-bamberg: Town hall with painted facades, built in the middle of the Regnitz.
places_taglines.DE::klein-venedig-bamberg: Former fishermen’s quarter with half-timbered houses along the Regnitz.
places_taglines.DE::schlenkerla: Historic tavern serving Rauchbier, Bamberg’s smoked beer.
places_taglines.DE::bamberger-dom: Cathedral housing the Bamberg Horseman and the tomb of Clement II.
places_taglines.DE::dioezesanmuseum-bamberg: Cathedral treasury and Henry II’s star mantle.
places_taglines.DE::alte-hofhaltung-bamberg: Former bishops’ palace with a Gothic courtyard, half-timbering and galleries.
places_taglines.DE::neue-residenz-bamberg: Baroque palace of the prince-bishops with its painted Kaisersaal.
places_taglines.DE::rosengarten-bamberg: Garden with 4,500 rosebushes overlooking the old town.
places_taglines.DE::st-michael-bamberg: Abbey church reopened in 2026, with the Himmelsgarten ceiling and terraces.
places_taglines.DE::obere-pfarre-bamberg: Bamberg’s only purely Gothic church, with a painting by Tintoretto.
places_taglines.DE::gaertnerstadt-bamberg: UNESCO-listed market gardeners’ district and its gardeners’ museum.

Courtroom 600: 21 Nazi leaders tried from November 1945 to October 1946
Bamberg Cathedral: the only papal tomb north of the Alps
St. Michael’s Church in Bamberg: reopened on April 25, 2026, after 14 years of restoration work
