itineraries.title: Fairy Tale Route in 3 Days: Hanau, Marburg, and Kassel
itineraries.subtitle: In 3 days, follow the Brothers Grimm from Hanau, their birthplace, to the water displays at Kassel’s Bergpark.
itineraries.notes: Set out on a Friday: the Märchenhaus in Alsfeld opens on Saturday morning, Kassel’s water displays run on Sundays, and most museums along the route close on Mondays. The water displays operate only from May 1 to October 3, and the Hercules monument’s viewing platform opens from April to October.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May to September, with average highs of 18 to 25 °C around Kassel, during the Bergpark’s water display season. Avoid winter: highs of 4 to 8 °C, the Hercules monument’s viewing platform closed from November to March, and Schloss Steinau closed from December 21 to the end of February. Keep a rain jacket handy, as rainfall occurs throughout the year.

visits.text: You’ll find GrimmsMärchenReich in the right wing of Schloss Philippsruhe, a Baroque palace on the banks of the Main. Opened in 2019, this interactive experience takes you through seven fairy-tale worlds and a whispering corridor, and features Jacob Grimm’s frock coat. Visit from 11 a.m., Tuesday through Sunday; the Hanau history museum occupies the rest of the palace.

At midnight, a local legend says, the two brothers swap places on Hanau’s Brüder-Grimm-Nationaldenkmal. Unveiled in 1896 on Neustädter Marktplatz, the monument by Syrius Eberle depicts Wilhelm seated and Jacob standing and rises nearly six and a half meters high. Time your visit to hear the carillon at the Neustädter Rathaus just behind it: 10 a.m., noon, 4 p.m., or 6 p.m.

Reduced to its foundations and two stone gables in March 1945, the Altstädter Rathaus, built in 1538, was faithfully reconstructed in the 1950s. It houses the Deutsches Goldschmiedehaus, whose jewelry and goldsmithing exhibitions change throughout the year, facing the figure of Justice on a fountain dating from 1607–1608. Open Tuesday through Sunday, 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.

activities.text: A newly built ruin: that is the paradox of Staatspark Wilhelmsbad. As early as 1779, Crown Prince William of Hesse-Kassel had a mock castle ruin built here, its tower concealing a small palace—a precursor to Kassel’s Löwenburg. The park is free to enter; its 1780 carousel runs only a few times a year, so come mainly for a morning stroll.

practical_info.tip: Explore the park freely; rides on the historic carousel are offered on only a few dates each year.

to_next_leg.road_type: A66 through the Kinzig Valley

visits.text: You’ll reach the Amtshaus, a half-timbered house built in 1562 at the far end of its courtyard, where the Grimm family lived from 1791 to 1796: this is the Brüder Grimm-Haus. Downstairs, the brothers’ lives and paintings by their younger brother Ludwig Emil; upstairs, ten fairy-tale rooms to see, touch, and listen to. Open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., it can be visited before the castle.

A five-sided dry moat, high retaining walls, and a keep around forty meters tall: Schloss Steinau retains the look of a fortress beneath its Renaissance reconstruction, carried out from 1528 to 1555 for the Counts of Hanau. Since 2015, a major exhibition here has traced the lives and work of the Brothers Grimm. You can visit the tower without a guide, while guided tours of the rooms are offered on weekends; the castle is closed on Mondays.

activities.text: A small town with a harmonious feel: in Steinau an der Straße, the Rathaus of 1561 and the Amtshaus of 1562 complement each other at the foot of the castle. The town’s name recalls the Via Regia, the trade route between Frankfurt and Leipzig. Save this walking tour for late afternoon, when the museums close at 5 p.m., then get back on the road to Alsfeld.

practical_info.tip: From April 20 to September 30, the Teufelshöhle, a nearby cave with mineral formations, offers guided tours lasting about 30 minutes on Friday and Saturday afternoons and on Sundays.

visits.text: Since 1516, Alsfeld’s Rathaus has stood with two half-timbered stories and three attic levels above three stone arcades, the former market hall. Around it, the Weinhaus of 1538 and the stone Hochzeitshaus, built from 1564 to 1571, form the backdrop to an old town designated a European model town for heritage preservation in 1975. Look for the ell measure attached to the left side of the Rathaus.

Excavations at the Walpurgiskirche in 1971–1972 uncovered the foundations of a small basilica with three apses, the original core of Alsfeld’s main church. Its choir was rebuilt in 1393, and its stained-glass windows by Charles Crodel date from 1963. Visit between 10:30 a.m. and 12:30 p.m. or in the afternoon Monday through Saturday; on Sundays, the church does not open until 2 p.m.

If you are passing through on a Saturday morning, Alsfeld’s Märchenhaus opens from 10:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. in its half-timbered house dating from 1628. Two floors of Grimm fairy tales, a storytelling room, and a collection of 83 dollhouses from the Erzgebirge, surrounded by several hundred dolls. On Sundays and during school vacations in Hesse, it opens only in the afternoon.

activities.text: You will reach the Leonhardsturm through the lanes of the old town, among more than 400 half-timbered houses spanning seven centuries. Standing 27 meters tall and built in 1386, it is the only surviving round tower of Alsfeld’s town walls; its nickname is “Storchennest,” the stork’s nest. Ask for a map of the route at the Tourist-Center, Rittergasse 3.

practical_info.tip: The tourist office organizes a public guided tour of the old town, including the Rathaus, on Saturdays at 11 a.m.; check the schedule for the year.

visits.text: Few churches can claim such an early start: begun in 1235, Marburg’s Elisabethkirche is considered Germany’s oldest purely Gothic church. Its two towers, about 80 meters tall, watch over the reliquary of Saint Elizabeth, made of oak clad in gilded silver and completed in 1249, and Hindenburg’s tomb, installed here in 1946. During the ongoing restoration, the rear choirs remain outside the visitor route; the nave and reliquary can be visited from 10 a.m.

Copper wings flap above the square: every hour, the rooster on the clock of Marburg’s Rathaus comes to life as the neighboring trumpeter sounds. The town hall, built from 1512 to 1527, occupies the south side of the Marktplatz, opposite Saint George’s Fountain. Stand near the fountain a few minutes before the hour for a good view of the gable dating from 1581.

“I believe there are more steps in the street than in the houses,” wrote Jacob Grimm, and the climb to the Landgrafenschloss proves him right. At the top, the 482 m² Fürstensaal ranks among Central Europe’s largest secular Gothic halls, the chapel dates from 1288, and the castle was where Luther and Zwingli debated in 1529. Open from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. except Mondays; bus 10 saves you the climb.

Marburg’s Alte Universität is a reminder that, since 1527, the city has been home to the first Protestant university to endure, founded at the initiative of Landgrave Philip. Its current wings date from 1873 to 1891 and stand beside the Universitätskirche, a former Dominican church begun in 1291. The Brothers Grimm studied here under the jurist Savigny from 1802 to 1806; look on the church for the light installation Sterntaler, station 5 on the Grimm-Dich-Pfad.

You will end the day at the Kunstmuseum Marburg, Biegenstraße 11, a museum opened in 1927 and renovated in 2018. Paintings by artists from the Willingshausen colony in the Schwalm region and works by Otto Ubbelohde, a celebrated illustrator of the Grimms’ fairy tales, share space with Kirchner and the postwar avant-garde. Open from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., closed Tuesdays; a combination ticket includes the Landgrafenschloss.

activities.text: There are no large signs for the Grimm-Dich-Pfad: its fairy tales hide on Marburg’s walls. Its 15 stations lead from the fish in The Fisherman and His Wife, at the Old Botanical Garden, to Snow White’s mirror against the castle wall and Cinderella’s red slipper in the vineyard below. Pick up the brochure at the tourist office, Wettergasse 6, and wear good shoes for the stairs.

practical_info.tip: The illuminated well “Das blaue Licht,” in the castle’s vaulted cellars, can only be seen on a guided tour booked through the Marburg tourist office.

visits.text: Locals call it the “Buttermilchturm”: according to tradition, the besieged inhabitants of Treysa coated the Totenkirche’s tower with buttermilk to suggest their supplies were still intact. Parish accounts do record milk purchases, for a white casein paint. A ruin since around 1835, the church can be viewed from the lanes, between stretches of town wall and the Hexenturm; it also hosts cultural events.

Next, in Ziegenhain, you will follow the earthen ramparts of the Wasserfestung, built from 1537 to 1546 for Landgrave Philip the Magnanimous: its 65-meter glacis could be flooded by the Schwalm. The castle, incorporated into a prison, can be viewed from outside. The red cap of the traditional Schwalm costume is said to have inspired Little Red Riding Hood; the Museum der Schwalm displays it in the afternoons during the season.

Kassel’s Grimmwelt unfolds like an alphabet book: large illuminated letters, from Ä to Z, mark a self-guided route through fairy tales and the Deutsches Wörterbuch. Opened in 2015 on the Weinberg, it tells the story of the Children’s and Household Tales, inscribed on UNESCO’s Memory of the World Register in 2005. Open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. except Mondays; the 2,000 m² roof terrace remains freely accessible.

Standing 70.5 meters tall, the Hercules monument dominates Bergpark Wilhelmshöhe, inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List in 2013. Its 8.25-meter copper statue, made from 1701 to 1717 to a design by Giovanni Francesco Guerniero, crowns an octagonal tuff structure. The panoramic platform opens Tuesday through Sunday, April through October; climb up before 2:30 p.m., when the water displays begin.

A medieval fortress built in the late 18th century: the Löwenburg, erected from 1793 to 1801 for Landgrave William IX, looks like a ruin without being one. You can visit the armor room, chapel, and prince’s crypt, but the man who commissioned it never lived here. Entry is by guided tour only, starting on the hour: book your tickets well in advance.

Schloss Wilhelmshöhe is worth a stop for its Rembrandt room alone: the Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister displays Jacob’s Blessing and Saskia alongside works by Rubens and Frans Hals. A connection to the fairy tales: Jacob Grimm was part of the delegation that brought numerous paintings back to Kassel from 1814 to 1817 after they had been taken to Paris under Napoleon. Open Tuesday through Sunday, from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.

activities.text: You will follow the water on foot: Bergpark Wilhelmshöhe’s water displays begin at 2:30 p.m. at the cascades beneath the Hercules monument, then continue to the Steinhöfer Wasserfall, the Teufelsbrücke, and the aqueduct. Around 3:45 p.m., the Große Fontäne shoots up to 50 meters high. The free display takes place from May 1 to October 3, on Wednesdays, Sundays, and public holidays in Hesse; arrive by tram, as the parking lots fill up.

practical_info.tip: Take tram 4 to Druseltal, then bus 22 or 23 toward the Hercules monument; the water travels about 2.3 km to the fountain.

seo.h1_title: Fairy Tale Route in 3 Days: Hanau, Marburg, and Kassel
seo.intro_paragraph: This 3-day road trip follows the Hessian section of the Deutsche Märchenstraße, which begins in Hanau, the birthplace of Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm. You visit their childhood home in Steinau and the half-timbered houses of Alsfeld, then spend a full day in Marburg before heading to Kassel’s UNESCO-listed Bergpark Wilhelmshöhe.
seo.seo_hook: Fairy Tale Route in 3 Days: the Grimm House in Steinau, Alsfeld’s half-timbered houses, Marburg’s Elisabethkirche, and Kassel’s Grimmwelt and Hercules monument.
featured_list: Hanau: national monument to the Brothers Grimm, unveiled in 1896
Steinau an der Straße: Renaissance castle and the Grimms’ childhood home
Alsfeld: more than 400 half-timbered houses around a town hall dating from 1516
Marburg: Elisabethkirche, Landgrafenschloss, and the 15-stop Grimm-Dich-Pfad
Schwalmstadt: Treysa’s Buttermilk Tower and Ziegenhain’s moated fortress
Kassel: Grimmwelt, the 70.5-meter Hercules monument, and free water displays

places_taglines.DE::steinau-an-der-strasse: The Grimms’ childhood home and a Renaissance castle in the Kinzig Valley.
places_taglines.DE::alsfeld: A town hall dating from 1516, lanes lined with half-timbered houses, and the House of Fairy Tales.
places_taglines.DE::marburg: The Grimms’ university town, with Elisabethkirche and the Landgraves’ Castle.
places_taglines.DE::schwalmstadt: Little Red Riding Hood country, with a moated fortress and the Buttermilk Tower.
places_taglines.DE::kassel: Grimmwelt, the Hercules monument, and water displays in a UNESCO-listed park.

Steinau an der Straße: the Amtshaus where the Grimm family lived from 1791 to 1796
Alsfeld: the Rathaus built in 1512–1516 and 83 dollhouses at the Märchenhaus

itineraries.title: The Romantic Rhine in 3 Days: From Mainz to Koblenz
itineraries.subtitle: Follow the Rhine from Mainz to Koblenz in 3 days, from the Gutenberg Bible to views of the Loreley from a boat.
itineraries.notes: KD’s scheduled cruises run from April to October, and the winter schedule does not serve Bacharach. The route follows the left bank to Sankt Goar, then the right bank to Koblenz, with a ferry crossing at Rüdesheim and another at Sankt Goar.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May–June and September, with average highs of 21 to 26 °C in Koblenz. In July–August, expect temperatures around 27 °C and more crowds on the boats and in the Drosselgasse; from October to March, most scheduled cruises stop running and the days grow shorter. Bring a jacket for the boat deck, even in summer.
specialties: Vins de Rheinhessen et du Rheingau

visits.text: Imposing outside, almost intimate inside: St. Martin’s Cathedral in Mainz strikes both notes. Archbishop Willigis began construction around 975; the building burned on the very day of its consecration in 1009, and Archbishop Bardo consecrated it again in 1036. Look for the two facing choirs and the funerary monuments of more than forty archbishops. Admission is free from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday through Saturday, and from 1 p.m. on Sunday.

Mainz’s most precious treasure can now be seen in a natural history museum. While its new building is under construction, the Gutenberg-Museum reopened in November 2024 in the left wing of the Naturhistorisches Museum under the name Gutenberg-Museum MOVED. In a walk-in vault, two copies of the 42-line Bible face each other. Time your visit for one of the hourly printing demonstrations; admission is 10 euros, with extended hours on Thursday until 8 p.m.

Head to St. Stephen’s Church in Mainz and let your eyes adjust to the blue. Marc Chagall began designing its nine stained-glass windows in 1978, at age 91: six in the east choir and three in the transept. Continue into the cloister dating from 1499, with its net vaults and pendant bosses. From March to October, the church is open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., and from noon on Sunday; in winter, it closes at 4:30 p.m.

The Kirschgarten fits into a small cobblestone square, yet packs in so much: half-timbered houses from the 15th to the 18th century, sandstone, and a fountain of the Virgin Mary in the center. Built around 1500, the Haus zum Aschaffenberg is the oldest known half-timbered house in Mainz. Continue along Augustinerstraße, a main street in the southern old town, and step into the Augustinerkirche, spared by the wars, to admire its stucco work and 18th-century organ.

activities.text: The smell of fresh bread, the voices of produce growers, crates stacked at the foot of the towers: Mainz’s Wochenmarkt fills the squares around the cathedral on Tuesday, Friday, and Saturday from 7 a.m. to 2 p.m. Come at 9 a.m. to browse without having to elbow your way through.

practical_info.tip: The Marktfrühstück takes place on Saturdays from March to November; a public holiday may shift the market day, so check the city’s calendar.

activities.text: Weather permitting, spend the end of the afternoon on Mainz’s Rhine promenade near Fischtorplatz. With lawns, wide paths, and river views, it is also one of the locations for Saturday’s Marktfrühstück. Walk from the cathedral to the riverbank in just a few minutes, then follow the water downstream.

practical_info.tip: In summer, Mainz’s urban beach brings sand and lounge chairs to the banks of the Rhine.

activities.text: “Weck, Worscht und Woi”: this is how Mainz locals sum up their national dish—a bread roll, a sausage, and wine. Mainz has been part of the Great Wine Capitals network since 2008, and wine here is often ordered as a “Schoppe,” mixed with sparkling water. Settle into a Weinstube in the old town in the evening to sample wines from Rheinhessen.

practical_info.tip: The old town’s Weinstuben fill up quickly on Friday and Saturday evenings: reserve a table or arrive early.

to_next_leg.road_type: B42 along the Rheingau

visits.text: Twelve and a half meters tall, the Germania figure of the Niederwalddenkmal holds the imperial crown above the Rhine. Inaugurated on September 28, 1883, the monument sculpted by Johannes Schilling stands 38 meters tall and faces Bingen on the opposite bank. Walk around the base, then find a bench in the shade of the Niederwald’s trees.

Crowded, noisy, yet endearing: Rüdesheim’s Drosselgasse does nothing by halves. This cobblestone lane, 144 meters long and 2 meters wide, welcomes around three million visitors a year amid wine taverns and live music. Stop by before noon, while there’s still room to breathe, and greet people with a “Gude,” just like the regulars.

Wind in your face, water lapping against the hull: on the roughly six-minute ferry crossing from Rüdesheim to Bingen, turn to look downstream. The Mäuseturm rises from its little island; the archbishops of Mainz built it between 1298 and 1371, and legend has it that Archbishop Hatto was devoured there by mice. Stay at the front of the ferry for the photo.

activities.text: Leave your car at the bottom and ride Rüdesheim’s Seilbahn up to the Niederwald: rows of vines glide beneath the gondolas all the way to the area around the monument. Rebuilt in 2005, it operates daily in 2026 from March 21 to November 1, starting at 9:30 a.m. Take one of the first rides up to find the terrace almost empty.

practical_info.tip: A chairlift also connects the Niederwald to Assmannshausen. In November 2026, the gondola lift closes from the 2nd through the 18th, then runs from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. for the Christmas market.

to_next_leg.road_type: Rüdesheim–Bingen ferry, then B9

visits.text: Few ruins tell as much of a story as Bacharach’s Wernerkapelle. Begun in the late 13th century and completed around 140 years later, this Gothic chapel fell into ruin after 1689, when the French blew up neighboring Stahleck Castle. A plaque also commemorates the anti-Jewish violence sparked by the veneration of a boy named Werner. Walk up the castle path and take time to look out over the rooftops.

The Altes Haus captures Bacharach in a single facade: 14th-century half-timbering, remodeled around 1600, in the heart of the old town. Wine made fortunes here, to the point that barrels transshipped here took the name “Bacharacher.” On Zollstraße, in the underpass beneath the railroad on the Rhine side, cast-iron markers record floods from 1882 to 1988: look up.

Follow the wall walk created in 2007 along Bacharach’s ramparts. Built starting in 1344, the town walls had sixteen towers; the French destroyed four of them in 1689. Climb to the Postenturm, one of the town’s viewpoints, to take in the rooftops and river in a single view.

activities.text: If you could take just one cruise on the Rhine, make it the trip from Bacharach to Sankt Goar. The KD boat passes Pfalzgrafenstein, a toll castle built in 1326–1327 that Victor Hugo compared to a stone ship, continues along the towers of Oberwesel, then skirts the Loreley, where the river narrows to 175 meters. Allow less than an hour downstream and almost twice as long upstream.

practical_info.tip: Park first in Sankt Goar, your overnight stop, and take a regional train to Bacharach (around 9 minutes, with one departure per hour): the boat will then bring you back close to your car. KD, which celebrates its 200th anniversary in 2026, operates from April to October; its winter schedule does not serve Bacharach. Show your train ticket at the ticket counter, as a discount is often available.

to_next_leg.road_type: B9 along the left bank

visits.text: Cold stone, dark corridors, wind on the ramparts: exploring Burg Rheinfels engages all the senses. Founded in 1245 by Count Dieter V of Katzenelnbogen, it is the largest castle ruin on the Middle Rhine; it withstood a French army of 28,000 men before being destroyed by revolutionary troops in the late 18th century. The mine tunnels can only be visited with a guide. During the season, it is open from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m., with last admission at 5 p.m.

Before dinner, make a detour to the Stiftskirche in Sankt Goar, a two-minute walk from the train station. Until the Reformation, pilgrims came here to venerate the tomb of St. Goar, and late Gothic wall paintings are still visible. Then head down to the riverbank: the Loreley rock rises directly opposite.

to_next_leg.road_type: Sankt Goar–Sankt Goarshausen ferry, then uphill

visits.text: “Ley” for rock, “loren” for listening: the Loreley is said to be the rock that listens to the echo of the rapids. On the plateau, the Kultur- und Landschaftspark Loreley, which is free to enter, links six viewpoints; a passage through a cleft leads to the Felsenspitze, around 125 meters above the Rhine. Come early in the morning to have the tip almost to yourself.

A touch theatrical, but effective: the Mythoshalle, which opened in 2025 on the Loreley plateau, stages a recreated rock with light, sound, and mist. The sorceress first appeared in 1800 in a ballad by Clemens Brentano set in Bacharach, before Heine’s 1824 poem, set to music by Silcher in 1838, established her here. In November and December, opening hours are 11 a.m. to 4 p.m.

to_next_leg.road_type: B42 along the right bank

visits.text: Never destroyed, never abandoned: Marksburg is the only hilltop castle on the Middle Rhine to have survived intact. The Deutsche Burgenvereinigung bought it in 1900 for 1,000 gold marks and established its headquarters there. Visits are by guided tour only and last about 50 minutes, taking you from the medieval kitchen to the armory. Park below the castle and allow for 120 steps up to the entrance.

Lovage, butterbur, henbane: Marksburg’s small medieval herb garden smells of dried herbs and old apothecaries. It is tucked away within the walls of the castle, which is perched on a cone of slate above Braubach. Keep your camera ready: from the walls, the view sweeps down over Braubach’s rooftops and the Rhine.

to_next_leg.road_type: B42 via Lahnstein

visits.text: The Deutsches Eck juts out like a ship’s bow where the Moselle meets the Rhine. William I sits astride his horse here: a 14-meter equestrian statue atop a monument more than 37 meters tall, inaugurated in 1897. The original was dismantled after World War II; the current replica was placed on the pedestal in 1993. Climb the monument at sunset, when both rivers catch the light.

In 842, the Basilika St. Kastor hosted a decisive meeting between the sons of Louis the Pious; the following year, the Treaty of Verdun divided the Frankish Empire. Consecrated in 836, the oldest church in Koblenz now has a Romanesque appearance dating from the mid-12th century. It stands close to the lower gondola lift station; in winter, it is open from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.

You come up for the view and stay for the ramparts: Festung Ehrenbreitstein deserves at least two hours. Perched 118 meters above the Rhine, this Prussian fortress took its present form between 1817 and 1828; the Koblenz tourist office describes it as Europe’s largest historic fortress after Gibraltar. The Landesmuseum occupies four buildings, and the Rhein-Mosel-Blick viewing platform overlooks the confluence. From March 29 to November 1, 2026, it is open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

Onion-domed bell towers rise above the rooftops: the Liebfrauenkirche marks the heart of Koblenz’s old town. Nearby, the Vier Türme display their ornate corner oriel windows, while the Romanesque Florinskirche watches over the Florinsmarkt. Take the Kunstgässchen, the alley linking the church to Münzplatz, one of the city’s oldest squares.

An apparently well-behaved little bronze figure, the Schängel on the Schängelbrunnen spits a jet of water well beyond the basin every few minutes. Created by Carl Burger and inaugurated in 1941 in Koblenz’s city hall square, the fountain takes its name from a local nickname derived from the French “Jean,” which originated under French rule in the 19th century. Keep your distance when taking photos.

activities.text: Cross the Rhine by gondola lift: Koblenz’s Seilbahn travels 890 meters and climbs 112 meters to the fortress. Opened in 2010 for the 2011 Bundesgartenschau, it can carry 7,600 passengers per hour in each direction in its 18 cabins. As you ascend, look for the Deutsches Eck below, at the tip of the confluence.

practical_info.tip: A combined gondola lift and fortress ticket is available. The gondola lift takes its annual break from November 2 to 18, 2026, and resumes service on November 19.

activities.text: If the evening is mild, follow Koblenz’s Rhine promenade upstream from the Deutsches Eck to the Kurfürstliches Schloss. The former residence of the prince-electors of Trier stretches its classical facade toward the river, surrounded by extensive gardens. Sit on a riverside bench: the fortress you visited that afternoon stands silhouetted across the water.

practical_info.tip: The Koblenz tourist office, open daily from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., provides information on guided tours of the old town.

seo.h1_title: The Romantic Rhine in 3 Days: From Mainz to Koblenz
seo.intro_paragraph: In 3 days, this road trip follows the Romantic Rhine from Mainz to Koblenz through the Upper Middle Rhine Valley, designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2002. You see the Gutenberg Bibles, ascend to the Germania monument in the Niederwald, cruise from Bacharach to Sankt Goar beneath the Loreley, then visit Marksburg and Ehrenbreitstein Fortress.
seo.seo_hook: Gutenberg Bibles, a cruise past the Loreley, Rheinfels, Marksburg, and Ehrenbreitstein: the Romantic Rhine in 3 days from Mainz to Koblenz.
featured_list: Mainz: a thousand-year-old cathedral and Gutenberg Bibles
Rüdesheim: a gondola lift above the vineyards to the Niederwalddenkmal
Bacharach: ramparts dating from 1344 and a cruise to Sankt Goar
Sankt Goar: Burg Rheinfels, founded in 1245
Loreley: viewpoint approximately 125 meters above the Rhine
Koblenz: Deutsches Eck, 890-meter gondola lift, and Ehrenbreitstein

itineraries.title: Nahe and Hunsrück in 4 Days: From Bad Kreuznach to Simmern
itineraries.subtitle: Over 4 days, follow the Nahe from Bad Kreuznach to Idar-Oberstein, then head up into the Hunsrück to Simmern.
itineraries.notes: Start on a Wednesday or Thursday: Bad Kreuznach’s museums are closed on Mondays, the Felsenkirche is closed to visitors on Mondays outside school vacations, and the Hunsrück-Museum in Simmern is closed on both Mondays and Tuesdays. To return your car, Bad Kreuznach train station is about 45 minutes from Simmern, and Frankfurt-Hahn Airport is about 20 minutes away.
itineraries.climate: Aim for May through September: in Bad Kreuznach, sheltered from rain by the Hunsrück, average monthly temperatures range from 13.5 °C in May to 18.4 °C in July (DWD records, 1961–1990). Simmern sits at an elevation of 400 m, compared with 104 m for Bad Kreuznach: bring a jacket for Geierlay, and avoid afternoons on the Rotenfels during heat waves (39.3 °C was recorded in Bad Kreuznach on June 30, 2019). Avoid mid-November through mid-March, when the Felsenkirche, the Steinkaulenberg mines, and the Freilichtmuseum are closed to visitors.

visits.text: Built without permission, the Brückenhäuser nevertheless became the symbol of Bad Kreuznach. Between 1480 and 1600, a shortage of land led residents to build these half-timbered houses on the piers of the Alte Nahebrücke, a stone bridge erected around 1300; the bridge’s former gunpowder magazines serve as their cellars. Look for the cannonball embedded in one facade, a reminder of the sieges during the Thirty Years’ War. For a photo, head to the Geißenbrücke near the Pauluskirche.

In 1507, a certain Magister Faust became head of Kreuznach’s Latin school, then fled shortly afterward amid accusations. The Neustadt, home to the city’s oldest houses, preserves his name in Magister-Faust-Gasse and on the “Fausthaus,” although an inscription in its cellar dates the house to thirty years after his stay. Lose yourself in the winding lanes around the Eiermarkt; on Tuesdays and Fridays, from 7 a.m. to 1 p.m., the market on the Kornmarkt rounds out the walk.

Gladiators grappling with wild beasts, a sea god surrounded by ships and merchants: the mosaics at the Römerhalle teem with movement. They come from a third-century peristyle villa whose foundations are visible at ground level right beside the museum: more than 5,000 m² of interior space and over fifty ground-floor rooms, the equivalent of a small palace. Start with the Oceanus mosaic, then walk around the walls outside. On Tuesdays, the museum is open only from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m., and it is closed in February.

You come to the Schlosspark-Museum for the sculptures and leave talking about the hunting room. Built in 1776 by Andreas von Recum, the house gained a wood-paneled room designed by a decorator who worked for Ludwig II of Bavaria while it belonged to the Puricelli family of industrialists. The galleries tell the story of the nineteenth-century spa town and the Cauer dynasty of sculptors, beginning with Emil Cauer the Elder (1800–1867), with glasswork by Ida Paulin as a bonus. Allow 45 minutes; the museum is closed on Mondays.

If you’re traveling with children, set aside 1 hour for the Museum für PuppentheaterKultur, nicknamed PuK. More than 2,500 figures trace the history of puppet theater, from nineteenth-century traveling theaters to permanent stages and television stars. The museum is on Hüffelsheimer Straße, the same street as the Römerhalle, so visit the two in succession. They also share the same opening schedule: Tuesday through Sunday, mornings only on Tuesdays, and closed in February.

Climb from the Neustadt to the Kauzenburg on the Kauzenberg. The counts of Sponheim built it between 1206 and 1230, despite a ban imposed by King Philip of Swabia, before Boufflers’s French troops blew it up in 1688. In 1970–1971, architect Gottfried Böhm built a structure on its ruins that now houses restaurants.

Bad Kreuznach’s Kurpark occupies the tip of an island between the Nahe and a millrace. Laid out after 1830 around the Elisabethquelle saline spring, it has 145 large trees, including a gnarled plane tree planted in 1840 and a 150-year-old copper beech. Follow the embankment lined with century-old horse chestnut trees to the Kurhaus, built in 1912–1913. Avoid the riverbanks after heavy winter rains: the park is one of the first places in the city where the Nahe overflows.

activities.text: A touch of sea air in the heart of the Nahe Valley: in the Salinental, brine trickles down graduation towers made of blackthorn branches, standing 9 meters high and stretching for 1.1 km. The tourist office describes the site as Europe’s largest open-air inhalation facility; salt was extracted from this brine for 270 years, and a waterwheel powered by the Nahe still pumps it to the top of the towers. Breathe deeply as you follow the path. Free admission year-round.

practical_info.tip: Brine flows over the graduation towers from April to early November. The site borders the B48 between Bad Kreuznach and Bad Münster am Stein (Karlshalle and Theodorshalle).

activities.text: Get a taste of the Nahe in one stop at the Nahe-Vinothek, housed in the Dienheimer Hof, a former noble residence in the old town. It offers 150 wines from 50 regional winemakers at winery prices. With around 800 hectares of vineyards, Bad Kreuznach ranks among the largest winegrowing municipalities in the Naheland, with Riesling the dominant grape. Ask to compare a wine grown on porphyry with one grown on clay soil.

practical_info.tip: Mannheimer Straße 6. Call to check opening hours (0671 92005645) before stopping by.

to_next_leg.road_type: B48 through the Salinental

visits.text: The Brunnenhalle in Bad Münster am Stein’s Kurmittelhaus, built in 1911, displays in glass cylinders the three springs collectively known as the Rheingrafenquelle. A small exhibition tells the story of salt and of brine and radon baths. A graduation tower still operates in the Kurpark: pause at its base before heading to the ferry.

More than its walls, largely rebuilt in the 19th century, it is Ebernburg’s history that leaves an impression. Franz von Sickingen offered Luther asylum here in 1521; Luther declined, but Bucer and Oecolampadius came, and Ulrich von Hutten nicknamed it the “inn of justice.” A small exhibition traces the history of the castle, which is open year-round.

activities.text: A sheer 200-meter wall of red rhyolite: admire the Rotenfels from the banks of the Nahe in Bad Münster am Stein. To protect peregrine falcons, climbing is normally prohibited east of the Bastei from January 1 to June 30, and west of it year-round. Parts of the rock formation and the hiking trails are currently closed following a fire: do not plan on walking along the ridge.

practical_info.tip: The marked “Intro” loop trails around Rotenfels, Rheingrafenstein, and Ebernburg range from 3 to 4.5 km; walk the Rotenfels in the morning, before the heat.

activities.text: If the ferryman is at his post, board the Nahefähre in the Huttental: pulled by hand along a cable, it is the only ferry of its kind in Rhineland-Palatinate. On the opposite bank, a trail followed by steps cut into the rock leads to the ruins of Rheingrafenstein, perched on a 135-meter spur. Expect to pay €1.50 for the crossing.

practical_info.tip: The ferry operates from April 1 to October 31: Wednesday and Thursday from noon to 4 p.m., Friday through Sunday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Without the ferry, the walking detour via the campground and the bridge over the Alsenz takes 45 to 60 minutes.

visits.text: Allow 2 hours for the Rheinland-Pfälzisches Freilichtmuseum, spread across 35 hectares in the Nachtigallental. Nearly 40 buildings dismantled throughout the state form four groups here: Hunsrück-Nahe, Middle Rhine-Westerwald, Moselle-Eifel, and Rhenish Hesse-Palatinate. Chickens roam freely, so dogs must be leashed. Admission is €9; open Tuesday through Sunday, from mid-March to early November.

activities.text: A knee-deep mud basin starts off the Barfußpfad in Bad Sobernheim, which opened in 1992 and ranks among Germany’s oldest barefoot trails. The roughly 3.5 km loop crosses the Nahe twice, once over a footbridge and once in a boat you pull across yourself. Bring a towel: lockers and foot-washing facilities are available on-site.

practical_info.tip: Generally open from May 1 to October 3, a few kilometers east of the Freilichtmuseum, at Staudernheimer Straße 90.

to_next_leg.road_type: B41 through the Nahe Valley

visits.text: Even if jewelry is not your passion, the Deutsches Edelsteinmuseum in Idar is worth a visit. Across three floors and 800 m², more than 10,000 pieces span 6,000 years of gem cutting and engraving, from local agates to lapis lazuli and tourmaline. One date to remember: in 1827, emigrants from the region discovered immense agate deposits in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, with shipments reaching Idar and Oberstein as early as 1834. Open daily except from mid-January to mid-February; admission €9.50.

Lying on their stomachs on tilting “Kippstühle,” the gem cutters at the Historische Weiherschleife spent their days bent over the grinding wheel. This mill is the last on the Idarbach still powered by a waterwheel; it operated, with interruptions, until 1945. A gem-cutting demonstration conveys the physical demands of the trade better than any display case. Allow 1 hour, including the gemstone exhibition, plus a pedal boat ride on the Kallwiesweiher pond if the weather permits. Call before visiting (06781 901918), Tiefensteiner Straße 87.

A church in the cliff, with no road leading up to it: Idar-Oberstein’s Felsenkirche, built between 1482 and 1484 in a rocky recess, can only be reached by stairs or a long trail, followed by a tunnel with around 40 steps. Legend has it that a knight had it hollowed out to atone for murdering his brother by throwing him from a castle window. Inside, a Gothic winged altarpiece depicts the Passion. Guided tours only, Tuesday through Sunday at 1:30 p.m. and 3 p.m., from mid-March to mid-November; €5.

The Deutsches Mineralienmuseum occupies a Wilhelmine-era house on Oberstein’s Hauptstraße, at the foot of the Felsenkirche, with 24 rooms across four floors. Its crystal room, described by the city as unique in Germany, is worth the stop on its own. On your way out, look at the B41: since the 1980s, the Nahe has flowed beneath it in a concrete channel nearly 2 kilometers long. Open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. in season; admission €8.

If your legs are up to it, climb from the Felsenkirche to the two ruins crowning the cliff. Schloss Oberstein, built in 1320, is recorded in 1330 as “the house above the house of the rock,” referring to the older, neighboring Burg Bosselstein. Its rooms, restored since 1981, host receptions, but the view down over Oberstein and the Nahe Valley is the reward for the climb. The trail is steep and includes flights of steps: wear sturdy shoes.

activities.text: Put on a helmet and descend into the Edelsteinminen Steinkaulenberg, described by the city as Europe’s only gemstone mine gallery open to visitors. The 400-meter route follows veins of agate, amethyst, rock crystal, and jasper. Commercial mining ceased in 1875, undercut by larger, cheaper agates from Brazil. After the tour, children can search for stones in the prospecting area for an additional fee.

practical_info.tip: Open daily from March 15 to November 15, from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., with the last tour at 4 p.m.; €9 per adult, €12 for the prospecting area. An audio guide is available in French.

activities.text: In Idar-Oberstein, Spießbraten is not described as “grilled”: the word is “braten,” and “schwenken” or “grillen” are considered inappropriate. The Idar version, the most common, marinates overnight in raw onion, salt, and pepper before cooking over a beechwood fire; the Oberstein version is a rolled roast cooked on a spit. The recipe is said to come from the gauchos’ churrasco, brought back along with agates from Argentina and Brazil. Order it for dinner with a beer.

practical_info.tip: The major Spießbraten festival, held in late June until 2019, no longer takes place: look for the dish on menus at restaurants around town.

visits.text: Herrstein looks like a movie set: Edgar Reitz filmed “Home from Home: Chronicle of a Vision” here. Granted town status in 1428, it owes its exposed half-timbering to a restoration in the 1970s that removed the plaster and slate cladding. Climb to the Uhrturm, then follow the rampart walk to the tower where Schinderhannes spent a night in 1798.

Step inside Herrstein’s church, the former castle chapel built in a defensive position: a Gothic chancel, a Baroque nave, and a Stumm organ from 1772. The Stumm family, from Rhaunen-Sulzbach, built more than 370 organs over seven generations. On Saturdays at 2:30 p.m., from May through October, a guided tour lasting about 1 hour 30 minutes starts at the Uhrturm.

to_next_leg.road_type: Partly along the Hunsrückhöhenstraße (B327)

visits.text: Three hundred sixty meters of Douglas fir planks, nearly 100 meters above the ground: the Hängeseilbrücke Geierlay, inaugurated on October 3, 2015, and modeled on Nepalese footbridges, connects Mörsdorf to Sosberg. It was Germany’s longest until 2017. Allow for a 1.8 km walk from the Besucherzentrum, and leave your stroller in the car: strollers are prohibited.

activities.text: Walk the longer Geierlayschleife loop, about 5.5 km: after crossing the Geierlay, the trail joins the Saar-Hunsrück-Steig and passes beneath the footbridge before climbing back toward Mörsdorf. From below, you can appreciate its full scale. Short on time? The shorter 3.6 km loop cuts through the meadows.

practical_info.tip: Free to cross, day and night, year-round. Paid parking at the Besucherzentrum in Mörsdorf, with a bistro and tourist information; dogs allowed on a leash.

visits.text: Simmern’s Neues Schloss, built from 1708 to 1713 on the site of the ducal castle destroyed in 1689, houses the Hunsrück-Museum. Its exhibits trace the town’s history, from the dukes of Palatinate-Simmern to the outlaw Schinderhannes. Visit Wednesday through Sunday: the museum is closed on Mondays and Tuesdays, and on weekends it opens only from 2 p.m. to 5 p.m.

Dim light, carved stone, and silence: inside the Stephanskirche, built from 1486 to 1510, St. Anne’s Chapel holds a row of tombs of the dukes of Simmern, with epitaphs by Johann von Trarbach. Beneath the bell tower, a crypt holds the coffins of the last ducal couple, who died in 1674 and 1688. If the door is closed, ask at the castle’s Tourist-Information.

Reputed to be escape-proof, the Schinderhannesturm nevertheless let two prisoners slip away: “Schwarzer Peter” in November 1798, then Schinderhannes himself on the night of August 19–20, 1799. His hat, his pistol, and a replica of the blade that beheaded him in Mainz in 1803 are on display, with free admission. The full tower can only be visited with a guide.

Less conspicuous than the Stephanskirche, the Baroque Sankt Josef church (1749–1752) rewards a look upward: its ceiling frescoes, painted from 1752 to 1756 by Francesco Bernardini, court painter in Mannheim, depict the Adoration of the Christ Child. The organ, delivered by the Stumm family in 1753, complements the one in the Stephanskirche, which dates to 1776.

If you have an hour left, drive 9 km to Ravengiersburg: the Romanesque facade of the “Hunsrückdom,” flanked by two towers about 40 meters tall, dominates the village. The monastery was founded in 1074 for twelve canons. Beneath the dwarf gallery between the towers, look for Christ enthroned within a mandorla, carved in the late 12th or early 13th century.

seo.h1_title: Nahe and Hunsrück in 4 Days: From Bad Kreuznach to Simmern
seo.intro_paragraph: In 4 days, this road trip follows the Nahe upstream from Bad Kreuznach’s bridge houses to the gemstone workshops of Idar-Oberstein, then heads into the Hunsrück uplands. Along the way, you pass the Rotenfels cliff, the open-air museum in Bad Sobernheim, the town of Herrstein, and the Geierlay footbridge before finishing in Simmern.
seo.seo_hook: Bad Kreuznach’s Brückenhäuser, the Rotenfels cliff, Idar-Oberstein’s Felsenkirche, and the Geierlay footbridge: 4 days exploring the Nahe and Hunsrück.
featured_list: Bad Kreuznach: half-timbered houses built starting in 1480 on the piers of a bridge dating to 1300
Rotenfels: a rhyolite rock face about 200 meters high, Bastei viewpoint
Idar-Oberstein: Felsenkirche dating to 1482–1484 and an agate mine with 400 meters open to visitors
Mörsdorf: Geierlay, a 360-meter footbridge nearly 100 meters above the ground
Simmern: the tower from which Schinderhannes escaped on the night of August 19–20, 1799

places_taglines.DE::bad-kreuznach: Houses on a bridge, Roman mosaics, and brine walls in the Salinental.
places_taglines.DE::rotenfels: A 200-meter red cliff, a hand-pulled ferry, and hilltop ruins.
places_taglines.DE::bad-sobernheim: Nearly forty reassembled rural houses and a barefoot trail.
places_taglines.DE::idar-oberstein: A church in the cliff, an agate mine, and gemstone museums.
places_taglines.DE::herrstein: A town of half-timbered houses, a clock tower, and Schinderhannes’s dungeon.
places_taglines.DE::moersdorf: Gateway village to Geierlay, a 360-meter footbridge.
places_taglines.DE::simmern: A castle housing the Hunsrück Museum, ducal tombs, and the Schinderhannes Tower.

Salinental: 1.1 km of brine graduation towers standing 9 meters high
Rotenfels: a rhyolite cliff rising about 200 meters above the Nahe
Idar-Oberstein: the Felsenkirche, built into the cliff between 1482 and 1484
Steinkaulenberg: a 400-meter underground route through an agate mine
Geierlay: a 360-meter footbridge nearly 100 meters above the ground

itineraries.title: Palatinate Wine Route in 3 Days, from Worms to Schweigen
itineraries.subtitle: In 3 days, follow the Palatinate Wine Route from the cathedrals of Worms and Speyer to the Weintor in Schweigen.
itineraries.notes: The route runs one way from Worms to the French border: plan on a one-way car rental or a return trip north. Ideally, start on a Friday, since Heiliger Sand is closed on Saturdays and Villa Ludwigshöhe opens Wednesday through Sunday.
itineraries.climate: Aim for May–June or September–October: average highs hover around 19 to 22 °C in May–June, 20 °C in September, and 14 °C in October, during the grape harvest season. July and August reach around 24 °C, with very busy wine festival weekends; avoid Bad Dürkheim during September’s Wurstmarkt if you book late. In winter, the Rietburgbahn does not operate, and several sites reduce their hours.

visits.text: Less famous than Speyer Cathedral, St. Peter’s Cathedral in Worms has more flair: Balthasar Neumann’s Baroque high altar, with gilded wood and colored marble, blazes in a Romanesque nave consecrated in 1181. The Song of the Nibelungs places the quarrel between Kriemhild and Brünhild here, before a north portal destroyed in 1689. Admission is free Monday through Saturday until 5:45 p.m.; head down to the crypt, where relatives of Emperor Conrad II are buried.

A deep silence hangs over the courtyard of the Worms synagogue. Destroyed during the pogrom of 1938, it reopened in 1961, modeled on the columned hall of 1174–1175 that inspired those in Regensburg, Vienna, Prague, and Kraków. Its Frauenschul, an annex reserved for women built in 1212–1213, is the earliest known in Europe. Admission is free daily; men must cover their heads—a cap is sufficient.

You’ll better understand what UNESCO inscribed in 2021 with a visit to the Jüdisches Museum in the Raschi-Haus on Hintere Judengasse. The building rests on medieval walls from the former community house, and the exhibition traces Jewish life in SchUM, the Hebrew acronym for Speyer, Worms, and Mainz, from the Middle Ages to the present. Open Tuesday through Sunday, 10 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., with admission of €2.50; get the audio guide.

More than 2,000 gravestones still stand at Heiliger Sand, in use as early as the 11th century and described by the city as Europe’s oldest surviving Jewish cemetery. It shares World Heritage status with the synagogue, just beyond Willy-Brandt-Ring. The cemetery welcomes visitors Sunday through Friday, never on Saturdays or Jewish holidays; men must cover their heads.

A rebellious monk turned into a 3.5 m statue: on the Lutherdenkmal, unveiled in 1868, Luther towers over his forerunners Peter Waldo, Wycliffe, Jan Hus, and Savonarola. The ensemble rivals Geneva’s for the title of largest Reformation monument. Then head to the Heylshof garden, which marks the site of the Diet of 1521, where Luther refused to recant. The garden is free to enter, even when the museum is closed.

Speyer’s Kaiserdom makes an imposing impression with its 134 m length: it is the largest Romanesque church still standing, commissioned by Conrad II, consecrated in 1061, and inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1981. Eight emperors and kings lie in the crypt dating from 1041 and the adjacent burial vault. In front of the entrance, each new bishop would fill the Domnapf, a large stone basin, with wine for the townspeople. There is an admission charge for the crypt; the Kaisersaal and tower can be visited from April through October.

The air grows cooler with every step at the Judenhof: a long staircase passes through a Romanesque portal and descends to the pool of the mikveh, built around 1120 and described as Europe’s oldest surviving monumental ritual bath. Above ground, the walls of the 1104 synagogue and the 13th-century Frauenschul remain. The €5 ticket includes the SchPIRA Museum, which opened in 2010; from April through October, admission is daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Walk up Maximilianstraße, a former triumphal route about 700 m long, to the Altpörtel, a 55 m city gate first mentioned in 1176. Its gallery, some 30 m above ground, is reached by 154 steps and overlooks the entire old town. Visits run in time slots, with fifteen people at a time: from April through October, aim for Wednesday or Friday afternoon, or Saturday morning.

In 1529, at the Diet of Speyer, Lutheran princes issued a solemn protest in defense of their faith. The Gedächtniskirche der Protestation, built from 1893 to 1904, commemorates the event with a 100 m tower, the tallest in the Palatinate. In the ground-floor hall, a bronze Luther tramples the papal bull excommunicating him. Allow 20 minutes; open Tuesday through Sunday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.

At the Technik Museum Speyer, you can climb onto the left wing of a Lufthansa Boeing 747, some 20 m above the ground. Farther along, the Buran OK-GLI, a Soviet prototype with four jet engines, made 25 test flights before traveling up the Rhine on a pontoon in 2008. Add the U9 submarine and the 5,000 m² space exhibition, covering nearly three-quarters of a soccer field. Open daily from 9 a.m., admission €25: save it for the following morning.

Our favorite ruin along the Weinstraße: Kloster Limburg, a family monastery of the Salian dynasty founded beginning in 1025, overlooks the Isenach Valley above Bad Dürkheim. Count Emich IX of Leiningen-Hardenburg burned it down on August 30, 1504, and its nave has remained open to the sky. Admission is free outside events; walk up via Grethen or park on the Seebach side.

Salt tingles on your lips along the Gradierbau: brine trickles over some 250,000 bundles of thorny brushwood, filling the air with spray as if you were by the sea. Built in 1847 and measuring 333 m long—more than three soccer fields end to end—it was rebuilt in 2010 after an arson attack in 2007. Climb to the platform at the top, where the air is saltier; admission is €2.50, and it is open until 8 p.m. from April through October.

activities.text: The Dürkheimer Riesenfass is a barrel you can have lunch inside: 13.5 m in diameter, with a capacity of some 1.7 million liters, it was assembled in 1934 by cooper Fritz Keller using nearly 200 fir trees from the Black Forest. It seats close to 430 diners on two levels. Reserve on weekends; in September, the Wurstmarkt, which attracts more than 600,000 visitors, takes place right outside on the Brühlwiesen.

practical_info.tip: During the Wurstmarkt, on the second and third weekends of September, accommodations in Bad Dürkheim are often fully booked.

to_next_leg.road_type: Wine route through the vineyards

visits.text: Every Whit Tuesday, a billy goat delivered by the neighboring municipality of Lambrecht is auctioned outside Deidesheim’s Historisches Rathaus as symbolic payment for historic grazing rights. The setting fits the occasion: an exterior staircase from 1724 and the Museum für Weinkultur, established inside in 1986. Continue to St. Ulrich’s Church, built from 1444 to 1473. The museum opens only a few afternoons a week during the season: check before you come.

activities.text: Here you’ll raise a glass in the first place in the Palatinate where estates began producing quality wines in the early 19th century. Reichsrat von Buhl and Bassermann-Jordan, established in 1849 when the Jordan estate was divided, are based in Deidesheim, and many winemakers open their cellars for tastings. Book on weekdays and walk back: the small town is easy to explore without a car.

practical_info.tip: Deidesheim’s Weinkerwe brings the old town to life on the second and third weekends of August: book early.

activities.text: Saumagen means “sow’s stomach”: hardly diplomatic, yet Helmut Kohl served this Palatinate specialty to Margaret Thatcher, Mikhail Gorbachev, and Boris Yeltsin when he hosted them in Deidesheim between 1989 and 1997. Order it for dinner at a Weinstube in the old town, with a glass of local wine; reserve a table on weekends.

practical_info.tip: You’re staying in Deidesheim tonight, so there’s no need to drive after dinner.

to_next_leg.road_type: Wine route through the vineyards

map_keywords: Collegiate Church Neustadt an der Weinstraße

visits.text: Neustadt’s Stiftskirche conceals a wall right down the middle: since 1708, a partition has separated the Catholic choir from the Protestant nave, one of the few such partitions still standing in Germany. Begun in 1356, the church borders the medieval Marktplatz, and its Kaiserglocke is reputed to be the world’s largest cast-steel bell. The Protestant section opens mainly for services, so take a walk around the square too.

In the Palatinate, you may be offered a hunting license for the Elwetritsche, an imaginary bird said to hide in the vineyards. Neustadt, its unofficial capital, dedicated Gernot Rumpf’s Elwetritschebrunnen to it in 1978 on Marstallplatz: 21 bronze creatures, including a bird with a fox’s head representing the mayor. Allow 15 minutes and look for the little mouse, the sculptor’s signature, near the lantern.

In our view, no castle on the Weinstraße carries as much historical weight as Hambacher Schloss: on May 27, 1832, 20,000 to 30,000 people climbed up here to demand unity, freedom, and popular sovereignty, many beneath black, red, and gold flags. The “Deutschlands Wiedergeburt” flag carried that day is displayed in the museum and may not be photographed. Open daily, €6.50; allow 90 minutes for the exhibition, then visit the terrace overlooking the Rhine Plain.

to_next_leg.road_type: Wine route at the foot of the Pfälzerwald

visits.text: If you dream of Italy without leaving the Palatinate, Villa Ludwigshöhe will give you that illusion: Ludwig I of Bavaria wanted it built in the region’s mildest climate and had it constructed between 1846 and 1852 to designs by Friedrich von Gärtner. Restored from 2019 to 2025, it features parquet floors made of fine woods and Pompeian-style murals. Open Wednesday through Sunday, €6; French audio guide available for €1.

activities.text: Take the two-seat chairlift from the villa up to Rietburg: an eight-minute ride with an elevation gain of about 220 m brings you to the ruins of a castle built between 1200 and 1204 and destroyed during the Thirty Years’ War. From the top, the view stretches across the vineyards and the Rhine Plain to the Odenwald and, on clear days, the Black Forest; a fallow deer enclosure also awaits you at the summit. A round-trip ride on the Rietburgbahn costs €8.50.

practical_info.tip: The Rietburgbahn runs from early March to early November; from May through October, hours are 10:00 a.m. to 5:30 p.m. on weekdays and 9:30 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. on weekends.

to_next_leg.road_type: Wine route via Bad Bergzabern

visits.text: Monumental though it is, cars no longer pass through it: the Deutsches Weintor, a gateway clad in pink sandstone and built in 1936 to promote Palatinate wines, admits only pedestrians and cyclists. On the side facing Wissembourg, the imperial eagle once held a swastika, which was removed in 1945. Beneath the arch, graffiti from March 1945 salutes Mineral Wells, Texas. A staircase on the east side leads to the gallery.

activities.text: If you take just one walk through the vineyards, choose the Erster Deutscher Weinlehrpfad, opened in 1969 and starting at the Alte Kelter near the Weintor. Its 26 stations, from the statue of Saint Urban to the carved grape thief, lead up the Sonnenberg to a hut with views stretching across the Rhine Plain to the Black Forest. The trail continues into France without border checks if you feel like going farther.

practical_info.tip: Local winemakers staff the Sonnenberg hut only on Sundays and public holidays, through the end of October.

activities.text: Finish the Wine Route with a glass in hand: book a tasting with a winemaker in Schweigen-Rechtenbach, some of whom also tend vineyards on the French side, or sit down for a meal at the Weintor restaurant, run by the Deutsches Weintor cooperative. Staying overnight in the village means you won’t have to drive after the tasting.

practical_info.tip: Park once near the Weintor: the trail, restaurant, and wine cellars are all within walking distance.

seo.h1_title: Palatinate Wine Route in 3 Days, from Worms to Schweigen
seo.intro_paragraph: This 3-day itinerary starts at the imperial cathedrals of Worms and Speyer, then follows the Deutsche Weinstraße from Bad Dürkheim to the Deutsches Weintor in Schweigen. Along the way, you visit Jewish sites inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2021, the Technik Museum, wine villages, Hambacher Schloss, and the summer villa of Ludwig I of Bavaria.
seo.seo_hook: Palatinate Wine Route in 3 Days: Worms and Speyer cathedrals, Hambacher Schloss, Bad Dürkheim’s giant wine barrel, and Schweigen’s Weintor.
featured_list: Worms: synagogue and Heiliger Sand cemetery, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2021
Speyer: 134 m Romanesque cathedral and mikveh built around 1120
Speyer: Boeing 747 wing and Buran space shuttle at the Technik Museum
Bad Dürkheim: giant wine barrel from 1934 and 333 m-long graduation tower
Deidesheim: billy goat auction on Whit Tuesday
Neustadt: Hambacher Schloss and flag from the 1832 festival
Edenkoben: Ludwig I’s villa and the Rietburg chairlift
Schweigen: Deutsches Weintor from 1936 and wine trail from 1969

places_taglines.DE::speyer: Imperial cathedral, medieval mikveh, and the Technik Museum’s Boeing 747.
places_taglines.DE::bad-durkheim: Giant wine barrel, 333 m graduation tower, and ruins of the Salian monastery.
places_taglines.DE::deidesheim: Wine town known for its great estates and billy goat auction.
places_taglines.DE::neustadt-an-der-weinstrasse: Hambacher Schloss of 1832 fame, shared church, and Elwetritschen fountain.
places_taglines.DE::edenkoben: Ludwig I’s summer villa and chairlift up to Rietburg.
places_taglines.DE::schweigen-rechtenbach: Monumental gateway to the Wine Route, facing Wissembourg.

highlights: Worms: synagogue reopened in 1961 and more than 2,000 gravestones at Heiliger Sand
Speyer: imperial crypt dating to 1041 and mikveh built around 1120
Technik Museum: Boeing 747 wing about 20 meters above the ground
Hambacher Schloss: original flag from the 1832 festival
Rietburgbahn: approximately 220 m of elevation gain by chairlift above the vineyards
Schweigen: Weinlehrpfad opened in 1969 at the foot of the Weintor

itineraries.title: Cologne, Bonn, and Aachen in 3 Days: Cathedrals and Treasures
itineraries.subtitle: In 3 days, connect Beethoven’s birthplace in Bonn with the cathedrals and treasures of Cologne and Aachen.
itineraries.notes: Ideally, start on a Wednesday: the Beethoven-Haus is closed on Tuesdays, most museums on Mondays, and Aachen Cathedral only opens to tourists at 1 p.m. on weekends. Since July 1, 2026, admission to Cologne Cathedral costs €12 and must be booked online.
itineraries.climate: Aim for May through September: in Cologne, average highs range from 20 to 25 °C, ideal for combining museums with time along the Rhine. Avoid December through February if you want to visit Brühl Palace, which is closed during those months, as well as Carnival days, when Cologne Cathedral’s tower and treasury or the Beethoven-Haus close. In winter, highs top out at around 6 to 7 °C.

visits.text: Bonn’s most engaging history lesson is free: you’ll find it at the Haus der Geschichte on the Museumsmeile. Around 4,000 objects tell Germany’s story since 1945, from a section of the Bundestag’s plenary chamber to a homemade escape airplane. Arrive as early as 9 a.m. on weekdays or 10 a.m. on weekends; closed Mondays.

Set aside a good hour for the Beethoven-Haus at 20 Bonngasse: Ludwig van Beethoven was born here in December 1770, and it is his family’s only surviving home. Twelve rooms hold more than a hundred original items, including his last fortepiano, made by Conrad Graf. Closed Tuesdays; expect to pay €15 for admission, a little more during temporary exhibitions.

Completed in 1248, the very year Cologne laid the foundation stone of its cathedral, Bonn Minster rises above the tombs of the martyrs Cassius and Florentius, whose two giant granite heads stand watch outside the apse. Restored from 2017 to 2021, it has regained its Romanesque cloister, open from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday through Saturday.

Bonn’s Altes Rathaus, built in 1737–1738 in the Rococo style, served as a stage for the young Federal Republic. From its gilded staircase, Charles de Gaulle in 1962, John F. Kennedy in 1963, and Mikhail Gorbachev in 1989 greeted the crowds in the Marktplatz. For a photo, step back to the middle of the square.

to_next_leg.road_type: A555 toward Cologne

visits.text: An archbishop-elector’s residence, then a republic’s ceremonial reception venue: Augustusburg Palace welcomed the federal president’s state guests until 1994. Begun in 1725 for Clemens August and inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1984, it can be visited on a guided tour, including Balthasar Neumann’s grand staircase. Admission is €15; closed Mondays and from December through February.

activities.text: Crunching gravel, fountains, and ornamental flower beds: Brühl’s Schlosspark, a French formal garden designed by Dominique Girard, takes 30 minutes to explore. Open year-round, it has longer opening hours than the palace. Save this walk for the end, once your guided tour is over.

practical_info.tip: With an extra hour, walk to Falkenlust hunting lodge, about 30 minutes from the palace (separate admission, €8).

visits.text: Walk across the Hohenzollernbrücke toward the end of the day, with the cathedral behind you and the Rhine beneath your feet. More than 1,200 trains cross it each day, and hundreds of thousands of love locks have been attached to it since 2008. Its 409 meters take about ten minutes to cross, including photo stops.

The KölnTriangle offers something the cathedral tower cannot: a view of the cathedral itself. An elevator takes you to the 28th floor, then a few steps lead to the viewing platform, more than 100 meters up, with the cathedral at eye level beyond the Hohenzollernbrücke. Admission is €5, open until 8 p.m.; closed during thunderstorms.

activities.text: “Köbes”: in the Brauhäuser of Cologne’s Old Town, this is the server who replaces your 0.2-liter Stange of Kölsch without waiting to be asked. This beer, protected in the European Union since 1997, must be brewed less than 50 km from the city. To stop the rounds, place your coaster on your empty glass.

practical_info.tip: The Köbes marks each glass with a tally on your coaster: that is where you can read your tab.

visits.text: A shower of colored squares falls across the south transept of Cologne Cathedral: Gerhard Richter’s stained-glass window, installed in 2007, combines 11,500 pieces of glass randomly arranged by computer. The cathedral around it took more than six centuries to complete, from 1248 to 1880, including its 157-meter spires. Leave time for the Shrine of the Three Kings, made between 1190 and 1225 by Nicholas of Verdun. Since July 1, 2026, admission has cost €12: book your time slot online, between 10 a.m. and 5:30 p.m. on weekdays.

The Domschatzkammer occupies medieval vaulted cellars beneath the cathedral’s sacristy, housing reliquaries, liturgical vessels, and textiles from the 4th to the 20th century. Displays include the archbishops’ insignia, Frankish tombs from the early Middle Ages, and the Heiltumskammer, which holds the cathedral’s most precious relics. Get the combined ticket with the tower for €12 instead of €8 each, online or at the Kurienhaus ticket counter, Roncalliplatz 2.

For anyone who loves 20th-century art, the Museum Ludwig, next to the cathedral, makes a stop in Cologne worthwhile all on its own. Founded in 1976 with a donation from Peter and Irene Ludwig, it brings together around 900 works by Picasso, one of Europe’s largest collections, Pop Art by Warhol and Lichtenstein, and the most comprehensive collection of Russian avant-garde art outside Russia. Closed Mondays; on the first Thursday of the month, it stays open until 10 p.m., and a free guided tour starts on Tuesdays at 2 p.m.

Head below Groß St. Martin before looking up at its crossing tower: the excavation area reveals the foundations of Roman warehouses on which the church was built, on the site of a former island in the Rhine. The current Romanesque basilica dates from 1150 to 1250; it was devastated by bombing in 1942 and 1945, and its interior was not restored until 1985. Admission is free, but the church is closed on Mondays and remains a place of prayer: avoid service times.

Gothic in its facade, Roman underground: Cologne’s Rathaus, Germany’s oldest city hall with some 900 years of documented history, stands on the site of the ancient praetorium. Its tower dates from 1407–1414, its Renaissance loggia from 1569–1573. Afterward, walk through the nearby Alter Markt and listen: the tower’s carillon plays four times a day.

Follow the Rhine south to the Rheinauhafen peninsula: the Schokoladenmuseum, opened there in 1993 by chocolatier Hans Imhoff, welcomes around 700,000 visitors a year, more than any other museum in the city. A tropical greenhouse measuring 10 meters on each side and planted with cacao trees, a glass-walled factory, and a chocolate fountain around 3 meters tall: touristy, but well done. Open daily from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.; book online to go straight into the exhibition.

activities.text: If your calves are up to it, climb the 533 steps of Cologne Cathedral’s south tower: a spiral staircase takes you up to 75 meters, followed by a metal staircase to the platform at around 100 meters. Along the way, you pass through the chamber where eight of the cathedral’s twelve bells hang. Allow 30 to 45 minutes; there is no elevator or bag storage, and only small backpacks are allowed.

practical_info.tip: Tower access is from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. from March through October and from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. from November through February, with last admission 30 minutes before closing. On Sundays and public holidays, the bell chamber does not open until 2 p.m.

to_next_leg.road_type: A4 then A544

visits.text: The Centre Charlemagne, on the Katschhof between the cathedral and city hall, tells Aachen’s story through three eras: the Carolingian Empire, the coronation city, and then the Baroque spa town. It is also the first stop on the Route Charlemagne, the thread linking the city’s major sights. Start your day here when it opens at 10 a.m. to get your bearings before visiting the cathedral; the museum is closed on Mondays.

The highlight of the trip awaits beneath the octagon of Aachen Cathedral, Charlemagne’s palatine chapel, consecrated in 805, where the emperor has rested since 814. More than thirty kings were crowned here between 936 and 1531, and in 1978 the building became the first German monument inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. Charlemagne’s throne and the Gothic choir can only be seen on the paid guided tour, which costs €8.50 and lasts about 45 minutes. Outside guided tours, tourists may enter from 11 a.m. on weekdays and 1 p.m. on weekends.

Around 985, goldsmiths covered the Cross of Lothair, the centerpiece of Aachen’s Domschatzkammer, with precious stones and pearls. Around it are some 130 objects on three levels, including the silver-gilt reliquary bust of Charlemagne and the Proserpina Sarcophagus, a 3rd-century marble piece believed to have served as the emperor’s first tomb. Tickets are sold only at the Dominformation, directly opposite; on Mondays, the treasury closes as early as 2 p.m.

Make your way to the coronation hall in Aachen’s Rathaus, built starting in 1330 on the walls of the great hall of Charlemagne’s palace. Coronation banquets were held here from 936 to 1531; today, Alfred Rethel’s frescoes depicting the emperor’s life surround replicas of the Imperial Regalia made around 1915. Outside, look up: the facade facing the Markt features a row of 50 statues of kings. Open daily from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., except during certain events.

“Aachen’s most beautiful living room”: that is how the Couven Museum describes itself, and the phrase fits. In this house on the Hühnermarkt, where the Eagle Pharmacy opened in 1662 before Jakob Couven remodeled it in 1786, the rooms range from Rococo to Biedermeier, including a historic kitchen and a music room. Two rooms display around 6,000 tin-glazed earthenware tiles. Admission is €10; open from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. on Tuesdays and Wednesdays, and from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Thursday through Sunday.

A smell of rotten eggs drifts beneath the Elisenbrunnen’s colonnade: sulfur-rich water from the Kaiserquelle gushes from two lion mouths at 52 °C. Inaugurated in 1827 to plans revised by Karl Friedrich Schinkel, the pavilion bears marble plaques naming some famous drinkers of the waters, from Peter the Great to Casanova and Handel. Try a sip, more out of curiosity than pleasure; the tourist office is on the same square.

activities.text: Around 1806, Napoleon’s Continental Blockade deprived Aachen of cane sugar and honey: bakers switched to beet syrup, and Printen took on their modern form, hard and spicy. This fat-free gingerbread, flavored with anise, cloves, or cardamom, has protected geographical indication status. Try some in a shop or café on Münsterplatz, just steps from the cathedral.

practical_info.tip: Weichprinten, the soft version, appeared later: choose them if you prefer a less hard texture.

activities.text: If you still have energy, end the day at the Carolus Thermen, northeast of the center, in the thermal waters that made Aachen a spa town. Indoor and outdoor pools, around fifteen saunas, and a garden with a pond: expect to pay €18 on weekdays and €20 on weekends for 3 hours 30 minutes of thermal bathing, without sauna access. Open daily from 9 a.m. to 11 p.m., with last admission at 9:30 p.m.

practical_info.tip: Prices checked in June 2025. Parking costs €6 per car, with a height limit of 1.95 m; reduced hours on December 24, 25, and 31 and January 1.

seo.h1_title: Cologne, Bonn, and Aachen in 3 Days: Cathedrals and Treasures
seo.intro_paragraph: This 3-day itinerary starts in Bonn, stops at Augustusburg Palace in Brühl, then devotes an evening and a full day to Cologne, taking in Cologne Cathedral, Museum Ludwig, and the Schokoladenmuseum. It ends in Aachen, where Charlemagne’s Palatine Chapel, its treasury, and the Coronation Hall fill the final day.
seo.seo_hook: Beethoven-Haus in Bonn, Brühl Palace, Cologne Cathedral and Museum Ludwig in Cologne, and Charlemagne’s throne in Aachen: 3 days of museums and treasures.
featured_list: Bonn: the Haus der Geschichte tells the story of Germany since 1945 through around 4,000 objects
Brühl: Balthasar Neumann’s grand staircase at Augustusburg Palace
Cologne: Gerhard Richter’s stained-glass window, with 11,500 pieces of glass, in the south transept of Cologne Cathedral
Cologne: the Schokoladenmuseum and its tropical greenhouse measuring 10 meters on each side
Aachen: more than thirty kings crowned at Aachen Cathedral between 936 and 1531

places_taglines.DE::bonn: Beethoven’s birthplace, Romanesque Bonn Minster, and a museum of West Germany.
places_taglines.DE::bruhl: UNESCO-listed Rococo Augustusburg Palace and Balthasar Neumann’s staircase.
places_taglines.DE::koln: Gothic Cologne Cathedral, Museum Ludwig, Kölsch, and views from the KölnTriangle.
places_taglines.DE::aachen: Charlemagne’s Palatine Chapel, Aachen Cathedral’s treasury, and the Coronation Hall.

Brühl: Augustusburg Palace, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1984
Cologne: 533 steps to the viewing platform of the cathedral’s south tower
Cologne: around 900 works by Picasso at Museum Ludwig
Aachen: Charlemagne’s Palatine Chapel, consecrated in 805
