itineraries.title: Saale-Unstrut in 3 Days: Naumburg, Vineyards, and Nebra
itineraries.subtitle: In 3 days, connect Naumburg Cathedral with the vineyards of Freyburg, the Goseck circle, and the Nebra Sky Disc.
itineraries.notes: Several sites are open only from April through October, and most museums close on Mondays: start on a Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, or Friday to see everything. The original Sky Disc is displayed at the Landesmuseum für Vorgeschichte in Halle, outside this itinerary.
itineraries.climate: Aim for May through September: in Naumburg, average highs rise from around 19 °C in May to 25 or 26 °C in July and August. September is the month of Freyburg’s Winzerfest. Avoid December through February: lows hover around 0 °C, and several seasonal towers, gates, and museums (Wenzelsturm, Marientor, Max Klinger House) are closed.

visits.text: Nothing quite prepares you for Uta’s gaze. In the west choir of Naumburg Cathedral, twelve life-size donor statues surround visitors: eight men and four women carved in the mid-13th century by the workshop of the Naumburg Master. Uta is paired with Margrave Ekkehard II. The Cranach-Triegel altarpiece, criticized for obscuring these two statues, has been on a two-year loan to Rome since fall 2025. Admission is €9.50, including an audio guide; on Sundays, worship services occupy the morning, and visits resume at noon.

A 45 kg missal and a 14th-century Pietà: the Domschatzgewölbe displays the treasury of the cathedral, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2018, across 285 m². In the Elisabethkapelle, three stained-glass windows by Neo Rauch, installed in 2007, contrast with the medieval stonework. Finish in the Domgarten, nearly a hectare of regional plants that served as models for some 200 foliage carvings in the west choir: compare a living leaf with its stone copy.

Naumburg’s Markt centers on a Renaissance town hall built between 1517 and 1528. On the square, the Hohe Lilie, whose street-facing tower dates to around 1250, houses the Stadtmuseum: visitors can trace 750 years of occupation, from a private well to traces of the fire of 1517. Admission is €5.50, free for visitors under 18, Tuesday through Sunday from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.; the ticket also includes same-day admission to the exhibitions at the Galerie im Schlösschen.

The rumble of bass notes makes the nave of Stadtkirche St. Wenzel vibrate as the Hildebrandt organ comes to life. Built between 1743 and 1746, the instrument was inspected on September 27, 1746, by Johann Sebastian Bach and Gottfried Silbermann; it has three manuals and more than fifty stops. From May through October, a 30-minute concert takes place at noon on Wednesdays, Saturdays, Sundays, and public holidays (€6.50): take your seat a few minutes early.

You’ll climb 202 steps to reach the Wenzelsturm platform, 53 m above Naumburg’s rooftops. Until 1892, a tower watchman lived here at a height of 45 m, keeping watch for enemies and fires; the bell tower houses Saxony-Anhalt’s only fully preserved medieval peal of three bells, the largest weighing 2,309 kg. You can climb the tower from April 1 through October 31, Tuesday through Sunday from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., for €3.

The philosopher of “God is dead” grew up a few streets from a cathedral, at the Nietzsche-Haus at Weingarten 18. His mother, Franziska, rented an upstairs apartment there in 1858, bought the house in 1878, and lived there until her death in 1897. The museum, which opened in 1994 and has been supported by a neighboring documentation center since 2010, traces the philosopher’s life and work. Come in the afternoon: on weekdays, the house opens at 2 p.m., except on Mondays.

If you pass through just one gate, make it the Marientor, the only one of Naumburg’s seven gates still standing. Its tower dates to the second half of the 14th century, and its barbican, added around 1456, formed a courtyard designed to trap attackers. From April through October, Tuesday through Sunday from 11 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., admission costs €1, paid in coins at the ticket machine; in summer, the courtyard hosts theater performances and concerts.

activities.text: Hop aboard the Naumburger Straßenbahn, in service since 1892: line 4 connects the Hauptbahnhof with the Salztor every 30 minutes using streetcars built in Gotha. It is Germany’s smallest streetcar network with daily service. Expect to pay a little over €2 per ride, or board with the Deutschlandticket, which is accepted on board: a convenient way to reach the station after your visit.

practical_info.tip: The historic streetcar depot at Heinrich-von-Stephan-Platz 5 offers a 1-hour tour on Saturdays at 2:15 p.m. from March through October for €3 (tourist office’s 2025 program).

visits.text: Kloster Pforta traded prayer for study: Cistercian monks settled here in 1137, and a state school has occupied the site since 1543. Klopstock, Fichte, and Nietzsche were students here. The Gothic church, reconsecrated in 1268, has an exceptionally long nave. Open daily from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. from April through October; the audio guide is recommended.

Step into another century at the Romanisches Haus in Bad Kösen, built between 1150 and 1175 and considered one of the oldest surviving residential buildings in central Germany. In the former sheep barn next door, more than 270 dolls recall Käthe Kruse’s work here from 1912 to 1950. Tuesday through Sunday, 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., €5.50, free for visitors under 18.

Breathing Baltic Sea air in the Saale Valley: that is the promise of Bad Kösen’s Gradierwerk, a graduation tower more than 300 m long and nearly 20 m high that has been in operation since 1779. Brine trickles over bundles of blackthorn branches while the Saale turns a waterwheel. Walk alongside it and breathe deeply.

activities.text: Tasting wine at the foot of a Cistercian abbey remains the finest way to round off a visit to Schulpforte. The Vinothek at Landesweingut Kloster Pforta opens daily from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. The monks were already growing grapes here on a large scale: ask for a Müller-Thurgau.

practical_info.tip: If you are driving, limit yourself to one tasting and take a bottle for the evening in Freyburg.

activities.text: “An der Saale hellem Strande”: Franz Kugler composed this song in 1826 during a stop at Rudelsburg, a ruined castle mentioned as early as 1171, perched some 85 m above the river. The path from Bad Kösen passes four monuments to student fraternities. On the neighboring hill, Burg Saaleck sheltered Walther Rathenau’s assassins in 1922. Sturdy shoes are recommended.

practical_info.tip: The Burggaststätte at Rudelsburg serves lunch: check its hours before heading up.

visits.text: New oak posts, but a layout some 7,000 years old: the Sonnenobservatorium Goseck, an enclosure about 70 m in diameter, dates to around 4900 B.C. It opened to the public on December 21, 2005, the winter solstice, and its gates align with sunrise and sunset on that day. Free access year-round.

Goseck Castle deserves as much attention as the circle. Schloss Goseck grew out of a Benedictine monastery founded in 1041; the crypt, choir, and transept survive from the church consecrated in 1053, incorporated into the Renaissance castle of 1609–1635. Its information center opens daily from April through October, 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. (€2, €5 including the Schlosskirche).

The sandstone warms in the sun among the vines, with Noah depicted as the first winegrower: the Steinernes Bilderbuch in Großjena features twelve scenes carved in 1722. Court jeweler Johann Christian Steinauer dedicated them to Duke Christian of Saxe-Weissenfels to mark his ten years of rule. The Naumburg–Freyburg trail passes close by: come on foot if possible.

Next, head up to the Max-Klinger-Haus, near the Blütengrund where the Unstrut joins the Saale. The painter and sculptor bought this vineyard and its small Baroque house in 1903 and died here on July 4, 1920; his grave lies on a small plateau above the house. Tuesday through Sunday, 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., from April to early November, €5.50.

Schloss Neuenburg has watched over Freyburg since the 1090s, when Louis the Jumper had it built; it was once five times the size of the Wartburg. Its double chapel dates to around 1180, and the Dicker Wilhelm keep, begun in 1150, has served as a lookout since 1991. Allow 30 minutes to walk from the center; the museum opens at 10 a.m., except on Mondays.

activities.text: A lawsuit lost to a champagne house gave the brand its name: sued in 1894 over its “Monopol” name, Rotkäppchen Sektkellerei, founded in 1856, adopted the name of its red bottle cap, registered in 1895. Its Domkeller, built in 1896, houses Germany’s largest wooden blending cask. Guided tours Wednesday through Sunday: €20 online, €25 at the ticket counter.

practical_info.tip: The Erlebniswelt, which opened in May 2023, has more than 50 stations across 1,400 m²: allow 90 to 180 minutes, depending on the option you choose.

activities.text: “Tuscany of the East”: that is the region’s nickname, and Freyburg’s Herzoglicher Weinberg shows why. Its six-sided Rococo vineyard house, built around 1774, overlooks the terraces; the Schweigenberg has some 90 vineyard cottages from the 18th century. Stroll here on the evening you arrive, then taste a wine from the Winzervereinigung Freyburg, which brings together more than 300 winegrowers.

practical_info.tip: Freyburg’s Winzerfest takes place on the second weekend in September (September 11–13 in 2026): a wristband is required to enter the town center during the festival.

to_next_leg.road_type: Along the Unstrut Valley

visits.text: Two rulers died here: Henry I in 936, then Otto the Great in 973. At Kloster Memleben, Otto II and Theophanu founded an abbey no later than 979 whose church measured about 82 m in length; ruins and a Romanesque crypt, the only intact chamber, survive. Open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. during the season, March 14 to November 8 in 2026.

The silence of the ruins extends into the medieval garden at Memleben Monastery, which is open to visitors along with the exhibitions. The site also appeals to wine lovers: the wines of Memleben Abbey, mentioned in 998, are the first documented wines of Saale-Unstrut. Stop by the monastery shop before heading up toward Wangen and the Arche.

to_next_leg.road_type: Road to Arche Nebra, then Mittelberg footpath
to_next_leg.justification: La route rejoint le secteur de l’Arche Nebra, mais la montée au site de découverte du Mittelberg se fait à pied : accès interdit aux voitures particulières. La portion piétonne est estimée depuis le secteur du centre d’accueil.

visits.text: Arche Nebra, a 60 m building resembling a solar boat, tells the story of the Sky Disc: approximately 32 cm across and weighing 2 kg, it was unearthed by looters in 1999 and seized in 2002 during a sting operation at a hotel in Basel. Its 42-seat planetarium screens two 25-minute shows per hour. Admission is €8.50; the original is on display in Halle.

activities.text: If you’re traveling with children, set aside half an hour for Outer Space, Arche Nebra’s UFO, which opened on July 9, 2025. You can explore both its interior and its roof, with a command center, interactive stations, and a panoramic rooftop walkway. Admission is free, as is access to the outdoor area at Mittelberg.

practical_info.tip: According to Arche Nebra, 90% of Outer Space is accessible without barriers.

activities.text: You’ll finish at Mittelberg, about 3 km from Arche Nebra, where the disc lay for some 3,600 years. At the foot of the 30 m tower, which tilts at 10°, the Himmelsauge, a 3 m polished steel disc, marks the discovery site; on clear days, the view extends to the Kyffhäuser. Access is free, but there are no restrooms, so plan accordingly.

practical_info.tip: From April through October, Arche Nebra is open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., and the last planetarium show starts 45 minutes before closing. Visit before heading up to Mittelberg, which is freely accessible in the evening. The RB 77 line also connects Wangen (Unstrut) with Naumburg.

seo.h1_title: Saale-Unstrut in 3 Days: Naumburg, Vineyards, and Nebra
seo.intro_paragraph: This 3-day itinerary through Saale-Unstrut begins in Naumburg, whose cathedral has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2018, then follows the Saale to Bad Kösen and Schulpforte before continuing to Goseck, Großjena, and the vineyards of Freyburg. The final day follows the Unstrut upstream to the ruins of Memleben and Mittelberg, where the Nebra Sky Disc was discovered.
seo.seo_hook: Naumburg’s donor statues, Pforta Abbey, Goseck’s solar circle, Freyburg’s vineyards, and the Nebra Sky Disc: Saale-Unstrut in 3 days.
featured_list: Naumburg: twelve 13th-century donor statues in the cathedral’s west choir
Bad Kösen: Pforta Abbey, founded in 1137, and a graduation tower in operation since 1779
Goseck: a solar enclosure approximately 7,000 years old, aligned with the winter solstice
Großjena: twelve biblical and winegrowing reliefs carved into the rock in 1722
Freyburg: Neuenburg Castle and the Rotkäppchen cellars, founded in 1856
Mittelberg: a 30 m tower at the discovery site of the Nebra Sky Disc

places_taglines.DE::naumburg: UNESCO-listed cathedral, an organ examined by Bach, and the last medieval gate.
places_taglines.DE::bad-koesen: Pforta Abbey, 18th-century saltworks, and the ruins of Rudelsburg Castle.
places_taglines.DE::goseck: Reconstructed Neolithic solar circle and a castle converted from a monastery.
places_taglines.DE::grossjena: Baroque reliefs from 1722 and painter Max Klinger’s vineyard.
places_taglines.DE::freyburg: Neuenburg Castle, Rotkäppchen cellars, and terraced hillsides.
places_taglines.DE::memleben: Ruins of the Ottonian abbey and an intact Romanesque crypt.
places_taglines.DE::mittelberg-nebra: The hill where the Sky Disc lay, above Arche Nebra.

highlights: Naumburg Cathedral: Uta and the donor statues, in a cathedral inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2018
Wenzelsturm: 202 steps to a platform at 53 m
Kloster Pforta: a Cistercian abbey that became a state school in 1543
Sonnenobservatorium Goseck: opened to the public on the winter solstice in 2005
Rotkäppchen: Germany’s largest wooden blending cask
Arche Nebra: a planetarium and the history of the Sky Disc

itineraries.title: Saarland in 3 Days: Saarbrücken, the Saarschleife, and Homburg
itineraries.subtitle: In 3 days, travel from Saarbrücken to Homburg via the Völklinger Hütte, Saarlouis, and the Saar Loop.
itineraries.notes: Ideally, start on a Friday: the Ludwigskirche’s interior is open only Friday through Sunday, and Saarbrücken’s museums are closed to visitors on Mondays. In December and January, Homburg’s Schlossberghöhlen and Römermuseum remain closed for the season.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May through September, with average highs of 19 to 24 °C in Saarbrücken. Avoid December and January: highs hover around 4 to 5 °C, these months are among the rainiest, and Homburg’s caves and Roman museum are closed. Rain is possible in every season; keep a lightweight raincoat handy, even in summer.

visits.text: Baroque wings, glass and steel at the center: the Saarbrücker Schloss embraces its dual character. Friedrich Joachim Stengel built it between 1738 and 1748; after structural stability problems, Gottfried Böhm renovated the interior and designed the modern central section, inaugurated in 1989. Admission is free, and a free guided tour starts at 3 p.m. on both Saturday and Sunday: keep it in mind if you arrive on the weekend.

Fourteen meters beneath Schlossplatz, the castle fortifications have been accessible through the Historisches Museum Saar since 2007. You walk past the remains of the medieval castle, Renaissance casemates, and an 18th-century dungeon before reaching the galleries devoted to Saarland from 1870 to the end of the 20th century, including the Nazi period. Get the combined ticket for the Schlossplatz museums for €8; on Thursdays, admission is free after 5 p.m.

Nothing on Schlossplatz shines quite as brightly as the treasure of the Celtic princess of Reinheim, displayed at the Museum für Vor- und Frühgeschichte. Dating to around 370 BCE, it brings together gold jewelry, amber, and bronze; the museum also displays gladiator murals from a Roman villa in Mechern. Allow 40 minutes, and aim for Thursday after 3 p.m. if you can: admission is free then.

Step inside the Schlosskirche on Schlossplatz: its museum of sacred art is free. A chapel stood here as early as 1261; the current church dates to the late 15th century, and Stengel topped it with a Baroque onion dome in 1743. Inside, look for the tombs of the counts and princes of Saarbrücken, dating from 1700 to 1768, then head up toward Ludwigsplatz, a few minutes away on foot.

Rows of palace facades and statues perched on the balustrade: Ludwigsplatz provides the setting for the Ludwigskirche, Stengel’s masterpiece. Consecrated in 1775 and reduced to its outer walls by the bombing of October 1944, the church was rebuilt in stages; only 13 of the balustrade’s 28 figures survive. The interior is open free of charge Friday through Sunday, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.; on Sundays, the 11 a.m. service takes priority.

In 1938, about 61 facades around St. Johanner Markt were remodeled in two months to create a uniform Baroque backdrop for Hitler’s visit. Reach the square via the Alte Brücke, built from 1546 to 1548 on the orders of Charles V and reserved for pedestrians since 1964. Look for the Baroque fountain dating to 1759–1760, then slip into Fröschengasse: bars, bistros, and restaurants line the street, so save them for dinner.

If you enjoyed the Protestant Baroque of the Ludwigskirche, the Basilika St. Johann reveals Stengel’s Catholic side. He built it from 1754 to 1758, the tower followed in 1763, and restoration work from 1972 to 1975 returned it to its original Baroque appearance. Then continue to the Gothic Revival Rathaus St. Johann, whose tower rises to 54 m: its carillon rings daily at 3:15 p.m.

A little blue horse alone makes the Saarlandmuseum’s Moderne Galerie worth a visit. Franz Marc painted Blaues Pferdchen in 1912 for Walterchen, the son of his friend August Macke, and the dedication is still visible in the upper-right corner of the canvas. Nearby are works by Liebermann, Corinth, Kirchner, and Pechstein; in the sculpture garden, Maillol’s armless Venus. Open Tuesday through Sunday, until 8 p.m. on Wednesdays; free for visitors under 18.

activities.text: Finish the afternoon on the Staden, the leafy promenade that follows the Saar through the city. Lawns, playgrounds, and beer gardens line the route beside the meadows, and the pace finally changes after three museums and two Baroque churches. Set aside just under 1 hour to enjoy the promenade, sitting or strolling, then head back to St. Johanner Markt for dinner.

practical_info.tip: Beer garden hours depend on the weather; if it’s raining, check before heading out.

to_next_leg.road_type: A620 along the Saar River

visits.text: Rust, girders, and steel stairways as far as the eye can see: exploring the Völklinger Hütte feels like walking through an industrial city frozen in 1986, when pig iron production stopped. Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1994, it offers a climb to the panoramic platform atop the blast furnaces. Wear sturdy shoes: more than 5,000 m of walkways await.

The Gebläsehalle at the Völklinger Hütte houses the giant blowers that supplied compressed air to the hot-blast stoves and blast furnaces. Built between 1905 and 1914 according to UNESCO, these machines now provide a backdrop for major exhibitions. Check the program before visiting: the site hosts up to three exhibitions a year.

If you’re traveling with children, set aside 45 minutes for Ferrodrom, the Völklinger Hütte’s science center. More than 100 interactive stations explain iron, steel, and the four elements, from fire to air. Visit after the blast furnaces: hands-on activities help restore attention when the machines start to look alike.

activities.text: A coking plant turned wild garden: Paradies at the Völklinger Hütte has an almost ironic name. Plants and animals have reclaimed these former industrial grounds, between Mosko’s street-art leopard and Ottmar Hörl’s 10 m King Kong. Save it for last: after the industrial halls, this green retreat gives your eyes a rest.

practical_info.tip: The site opens daily at 10 a.m.; adult admission is €17 in 2026, with free admission for visitors age 18 and under and students under 27.

to_next_leg.road_type: A620 along the Saar River

visits.text: Saarlouis is nicknamed “the royal hexagon”: at its center, the Großer Markt, a parade ground designed by Vauban, forms a square measuring about 135 m on each side. The Kommandantur, built in 1680–1683 and reconstructed to match the original in the 1970s, housed the governor. Park around the square, which offers more than 300 parking spaces.

A Gothic Revival bell tower in front, exposed concrete behind: St. Ludwig is a puzzling sight even from the Großer Markt. In 1970, Gottfried Böhm, who also redesigned Saarbrücken Castle, replaced the nave with a Brutalist structure whose folded ceiling evokes a tent. The porch facing the square is always open: a few minutes are enough to appreciate the effect.

Sit down for a meal in the Kasematten on either side of the Deutsches Tor: the Prussians built these casemates between 1824 and 1829 to shelter soldiers and horses during bombardments. Those along the east side of Deutsche Straße now house numerous restaurants. Have lunch there, then look up at the gilded Prussian crown adorning the gate.

The Vauban-Insel, a former ravelin in the fortifications, holds monuments to Marshal Ney and the soldier Lacroix. Ney, “the bravest of the brave,” was born in Saarlouis on January 10, 1769, the son of a cooper; his birthplace stands on Bierstraße, in the heart of the Altstadt. Finish by exploring these narrow lanes before driving to Mettlach.

Two kilometers as the crow flies, nearly ten along the river: from the Cloef viewpoint, the Saarschleife reveals the full detour the Saar River takes between Besseringen and Mettlach. The overlook stands about 180 m above the water. Head up when you arrive from Saarlouis, then return the following morning for the Baumwipfelpfad, which starts right beside the Cloef-Atrium.

The most intriguing detail at Villeroy & Boch The Experience involves the Titanic: its ceramic bathroom fixtures rank among the company’s landmark projects. More than 2,000 m² of exhibition space fill the Baroque abbey built between 1727 and 1780, which Jean François Boch purchased in 1809. Open Monday through Saturday, 10 a.m.–6 p.m.; booking tickets online is recommended.

If you visit just one medieval monument in Saarland, choose Mettlach’s Alter Turm, built around 990–994 as a funerary chapel for Saint Lutwinus. This Ottonian octagon, inspired by Aachen Cathedral, is the oldest medieval building still standing in the state. Admire it from the Abteipark, an English landscape garden with more than 30 tree species.

activities.text: Follow the gentle incline of the Baumwipfelpfad Saarschleife, which opened above the Cloef in 2016. The 1,250 m trail runs up to 23 m above the ground among beech, oak, and Douglas fir trees, then spirals up a 42 m tower. Arrive when it opens at 9:30 a.m. so you can drive to Homburg in the late morning.

practical_info.tip: The route is accessible to wheelchairs and strollers, with a maximum grade of 6%; last entry is 1 hour before closing. Dogs are not allowed except service dogs.

visits.text: A helmet on your head, sand underfoot, and temperatures of 10–14 °C: bring a sweater to visit Homburg’s Schlossberghöhlen. Excavated to extract quartz-rich sand, they are described as Europe’s largest caves in variegated sandstone. Guided tours last 40 to 50 minutes and cover about 800 m; cash only.

Hohenburg crowns the Schlossberg, just above the caves: the seat of the counts of Homburg in the 12th century, it gave the town its name. Vauban transformed it into a fortress for Louis XIV; his fortifications were dismantled in 1714. Walk up after visiting the caves: you can freely explore the walls, moat, and surviving fortifications.

Head back down to the Marktplatz, the heart of an Altstadt whose layout dates to Vauban’s work. Emperor Louis the Bavarian granted the town its charter in 1330, and St. Michael, a Romanesque Revival church built in red sandstone (1836–1841), stands at the foot of the Schlossberg. The pedestrian streets and fountains date from the renovation launched in 1978: perfect for a coffee break.

The Römermuseum Schwarzenacker deserves much more than a quick detour: the small Roman town destroyed by the Alemanni in 275 comes back to life here. Explore the eye doctor’s house, the house with the five-column cellar, and the reconstructed Temple of Mercury, followed by the Baroque Edelhaus and its garden. Buy a combination ticket for the museum and the caves; both welcome visitors from March through October.

seo.h1_title: Saarland in 3 Days: Saarbrücken, the Saarschleife, and Homburg
seo.intro_paragraph: This 3-day itinerary devotes a full day to Saarbrücken, its museums around Schlossplatz, and Stengel’s Baroque architecture. It then follows the Saar River via the Völklinger Hütte, Saarlouis, and the Saarschleife, before ending in Homburg with its sandstone caves and Roman town.
seo.seo_hook: Saarbrücken’s Ludwigskirche, Völklingen’s blast furnaces, the Saarschleife, and Homburg’s caves: Saarland in 3 days, from Baroque to steel.
featured_list: Saarbrücken: the Ludwigskirche, consecrated in 1775, on a royal square designed by Stengel
Völklingen: an ironworks producing pig iron, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1994
Saarlouis: Vauban’s parade ground, a square measuring approximately 135 m on each side
Mettlach: nearly 10 km of river over a straight-line distance of 2 km
Homburg: caves carved into sandstone and the Roman vicus of Schwarzenacker

places_taglines.DE::saarlouis: Vauban’s fortified town, built in 1680 around a parade ground.
places_taglines.DE::mettlach: The Saar River forms its great loop below the Cloef viewpoint.

itineraries.title: The Ore Mountains in 3 Days: Mines, Toys, and Fichtelberg
itineraries.subtitle: In 3 days, travel from Freiberg’s silver mine to the summit of Fichtelberg via Seiffen and Annaberg.
itineraries.notes: Start on a Wednesday or Thursday: the Freiberg mine only welcomes visitors Wednesday through Saturday, Marienberg’s museums are closed on Mondays, and the Adam Ries Museum is closed on Sundays and Mondays. The Fichtelberg cable car shuts down for maintenance in early November and in April.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May through September, with average highs of around 19 to 25 °C in the foothills around Freiberg, but 11 to 17 °C at the summit of Fichtelberg. Bring a warm jacket and prepare for rain even in summer: the summit receives more than 100 mm of precipitation each month from June through September. In winter, snow covers the ground there for more than 160 days a year: come equipped for mountain roads.
specialties: Jouets en bois et art populaire

visits.text: By around 1225, the Goldene Pforte already adorned the Romanesque basilica that preceded Freiberg Cathedral, and this sculpted portal has been preserved. Inside, the Tulpenkanzel, a tulip-shaped pulpit dating to around 1505, and Gottfried Silbermann’s great organ, completed in 1714 with 2,574 pipes, vie for attention. In the choir, 38 members of the House of Wettin were buried between 1541 and 1696. Choose a guided tour with organ music: Sundays at 11:30 a.m., or Wednesdays at 2 p.m. from May through October.

Even if geology is not your passion, terra mineralia at Schloss Freudenstein is well worth 2 hours of your time. More than 3,500 minerals, gemstones, and meteorites from five continents fill 1,500 m² across three levels, an area equivalent to nearly six tennis courts. They come from the collection of Erika Pohl-Ströher, a member of the family that founded Wella. Save the treasure chamber, beneath a historic vault, for last. The exhibition is closed on Mondays; arrive at least 1 hour before closing.

Next, head to the Obermarkt, Freiberg’s civic heart. The Rathaus, begun in 1410, sounds a Meissen porcelain carillon, while a stone in the pavement marks the spot where Kunz von Kauffungen was executed in 1455. In the center, a statue of the city’s founder towers over a fountain where four lions bearing the arms of Meissen spout water. Return in December if you can: the Christmas market takes over the square then.

If your descent underground has made you want to understand the city, set aside 45 minutes for the Stadt- und Bergbaumuseum at Am Dom 1 on the Untermarkt. The museum is reopening in stages: since March 27, 2026, its second floor has explored mining-inspired art, Freiberg in the 17th and 18th centuries, and the Knappschaft, the miners’ guild. The “Licht im Schacht” exhibition runs there through February 2, 2027. The museum is open Wednesday through Monday, and admission is free for visitors age 16 and under.

activities.text: Ten degrees year-round, with a hard hat firmly on your head: at Silberbergwerk Freiberg, the Reiche Zeche mine cage takes you 150 meters underground. It all began in 1168 with the discovery of silver near Christiansdorf. Led by volunteers, the GrubenTour traces mining activity from the Middle Ages to the present in a mine where students and researchers from the TU Bergakademie, founded in 1765, still work.

practical_info.tip: Reservations are required by phone or email (contact details at silberbergwerk-freiberg.de); arrive 10 minutes before departure at the main entrance to the shaft building. Hard hats and protective clothing are provided.

visits.text: A simple wooden ring, yet a whole herd within it: at the Erzgebirgisches Freilichtmuseum, the woodturner shapes a ring, each slice of which will become an animal. Its Drehwerk, dating from 1758–1760, retains a 5.20 m waterwheel, operated only on special occasions.

Across three floors, the Erzgebirgisches Spielzeugmuseum explores the toys and Christmas traditions of the Ore Mountains through some 5,000 objects. Opened in 1920 and reopened in 1953, it invites hands-on discovery: the sign “Use me!” marks items you can handle. It is open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. at Hauptstraße 73.

You will see a figurine take shape piece by piece at the Seiffener Volkskunst demonstration workshop at Bahnhofstraße 12. Here, craftspeople assemble figures from numerous components in several stages, following traditional or modern designs. Open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.; plan to visit in the late morning, after the museums.

In 1779, Seiffen consecrated the Bergkirche, an octagonal church designed by Christian Gotthelf Reuther after Dresden’s Frauenkirche. Since then, the village’s craftspeople have reproduced it millions of times in miniature: you may already have seen it on a shelf. It is open to visitors Monday through Saturday, from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m.

activities.text: The ground suddenly opens up near the Bergkirche: the Seiffen Pinge consists of two collapse craters, the Geyerin and the Neuglücker Stockwerkspinge, reaching depths of up to 34 m. They are scars left by tin mining, which officially ended in 1855. Follow the marked Bergbausteig trail to enjoy the viewpoints.

practical_info.tip: An outdoor stage has occupied one of the craters since 1934; ask for the event schedule at the Seiffen tourist office, Hauptstraße 73.

visits.text: Few mining town squares look as geometric as Marienberg’s Marktplatz: a square covering about one hectare, part of the grid plan drawn up by Ulrich Rülein von Calw for the town’s founding in 1521. Nearby, St. Marien lost its interior in the fire of 1610. Finish at the Roter Turm and Zschopauer Tor, remnants of the town walls.

The Museum sächsisch-böhmisches Erzgebirge occupies the Bergmagazin, a granary built for the mining community between 1806 and 1809 and converted into a museum in 2006. Three stories intersect here: the mining town, Germans and Czechs living as neighbors, and the building’s own history. Exhibits are in German and Czech; open Tuesday through Sunday until 4 p.m., so arrive before 3 p.m.

If you visit on a weekend, aim for 1 p.m. or 2:30 p.m. at the Rudolphschacht horse whim in Lauta: horses turn the mechanism that hauled ore from 1838 to 1877. Restored in 2006, the site also offers access to the shaft down to a depth of 20 m. On weekdays, guided tours run at 1 p.m. and 2:30 p.m.

Vaults that bear no weight and an altarpiece donated by miners: St. Annenkirche, completed in 1525, is Saxony’s largest hall church built entirely in the Late Gothic style. On the back of the Miners’ Altarpiece of 1521, Hans Hesse depicted work in Annaberg’s mines. On Sundays, the church opens at noon; the tower is open to visitors from May through October.

“Das macht nach Adam Riese”: Germans still invoke the name of this master, who arrived in Annaberg in 1522, to confirm a calculation. The Adam-Ries-Museum occupies the house on Johannisgasse where he ran his school; here you can try calculating on lines using the method in his 1518 textbook. Open Tuesday through Friday from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., and Saturday from noon.

At the Manufaktur der Träume, you will encounter Erika Pohl-Ströher again, the patron behind Freiberg’s terra mineralia. Her collection here comprises more than 1,000 objects of folk art from the Ore Mountains, spanning four centuries. Step-free access is through the tourist office, with an elevator; allow 1 hour in the early afternoon.

activities.text: Rediscovered during construction work in 1992, the tunnels of the Besucherbergwerk Im Gößner date to around 1500 and extend beneath the old town, opposite St. Annenkirche. The network includes 260 m of tunnels following the ore veins, with shafts reaching depths of up to 24 m. The combined ticket includes the neighboring Erzgebirgsmuseum, founded in 1887.

practical_info.tip: Underground visits are by guided tour at set times: ask for the day’s schedule at the Erzgebirgsmuseum reception desk as soon as you arrive.

visits.text: Crisp air and sweeping views toward Bohemia: at the 1,215 m summit of Fichtelberg, you stand at Saxony’s highest point, facing Klínovec in the Czech Republic. The weather station has recorded conditions here since 1916. Climb the Fichtelberghaus’s 31 m tower on a clear day; spotting the Brocken, 220 km away, is still rare.

Oberwiesenthal deserves more than a passing visit from skiers: at over 900 m, it is Germany’s highest town. On the square, the Postmeilensäule of 1730 indicated distances to travelers; the Martin-Luther-Kirche, rebuilt from 1863 to 1866, houses a nativity scene carved in 1896. It is displayed only from Advent through the end of February.

You can watch for the Fichtelbergbahn’s arrival at Bahnhof Oberwiesenthal, Saxony’s highest train station, at nearly 894 m. This 750 mm gauge railway has operated since 1897, with steam trains running daily on a fixed schedule. The full round-trip journey to Cranzahl takes about 2 hours 30 minutes.

activities.text: The Fichtelberg-Schwebebahn, in service since December 1924, is Germany’s oldest cable car. Its cabins climb 303 m from Oberwiesenthal in about 3 minutes 30 seconds. Buy a one-way ticket, €12 per adult in 2026, if you plan to walk back down.

practical_info.tip: Departures run from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., approximately every 15 minutes; service stops during thunderstorms or strong winds. Maintenance closures: November 2–17, 2026, then April 5–23, 2027.

activities.text: Walk down from Fichtelberg via the Kammweg and Sachsenbaude, then through the Zechengrund along the Pöhlbach. This route follows the second half of the 10.9 km loop described by Bergwelten, starting at Oberwiesenthal station. Cross the B95 carefully at Neues Haus; the Zechengrund requires sure footing.

practical_info.tip: In wet weather, take the Alte Poststraße, which runs parallel to the Zechengrund. The route offers little shade: avoid the hottest hours in summer.

seo.h1_title: The Ore Mountains in 3 Days: Mines, Toys, and Fichtelberg
seo.intro_paragraph: In 3 days, this route connects Freiberg, Seiffen, Marienberg, Annaberg-Buchholz, and Oberwiesenthal, in the heart of the Ore Mountains mining region, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2019. You descend into two silver mines, watch Seiffen’s wooden toys being made, and finish at Fichtelberg, Saxony’s highest peak at 1,215 m.
seo.seo_hook: The Ore Mountains in 3 days: Freiberg’s silver mine, Seiffen’s toys, St. Annenkirche in Annaberg, and the Fichtelberg cable car.
featured_list: Freiberg: tour a silver mine 150 m underground
Freiberg: terra mineralia displays more than 3,500 minerals
Seiffen: the Bergkirche, reproduced millions of times in miniature
Marienberg: a grid plan laid out as early as 1521
Annaberg-Buchholz: Saxony’s largest late Gothic hall church
Fichtelberg: Germany’s oldest cable car, in operation since 1924

places_taglines.DE::freiberg: A silver mining town since 1168, with a teaching mine and Silbermann organs.
places_taglines.DE::seiffen: A wooden toy village born from the decline of tin mining.
places_taglines.DE::marienberg: A mining town founded in 1521 on a grid plan.
places_taglines.DE::annaberg-buchholz: Adam Ries’s town, dominated by the imposing St. Annenkirche.
places_taglines.DE::oberwiesenthal: Germany’s highest town, at the foot of Fichtelberg.

highlights: Freiberg: descend 150 m underground at Reiche Zeche
Freiberg: the great Silbermann organ from 1714 and its 2,574 pipes
Seiffen: ring turning in a water-powered workshop from 1760
Marienberg: a one-hectare square laid out for the town’s founding in 1521
Annaberg-Buchholz: the Miners’ Altarpiece from 1521 and mine tunnels dating to around 1500
Fichtelberg: 1,215 m, the highest point in Saxony

itineraries.title: Stuttgart and Ludwigsburg in 6 Days: Art, Cars, and Baroque
itineraries.subtitle: In 6 days, explore the heart of Stuttgart, its automotive museums, Baroque Ludwigsburg, and the Swabian Jura.
itineraries.notes: Start on a Tuesday: most museums on the itinerary close on Mondays, so a Tuesday-to-Sunday trip finds them all open. The first three days are spent walking and using public transportation; a car becomes useful from the fourth day onward.
itineraries.climate: Best time to visit: May, June, and September, with average highs of 20 to 23 °C in Stuttgart. July and August reach around 25 °C, but July is also the wettest month, often with thundery showers: keep an umbrella handy. From November to March, highs stay between 5 and 11 °C, and Blühendes Barock does not open for the season until spring.

visits.text: Nothing beats Schlossplatz for taking in Stuttgart at a glance. In the center, the Jubiläumssäule, about 30 m tall, commemorates the jubilee of William I’s reign in 1841; a statue of Concordia crowns it because the king refused to have his own statue placed there. Opposite, the Neues Schloss, built from 1746 to 1807 and rebuilt after the 1944 bombings, now houses government ministries. Come early, when you still have the fountains and Baroque flower beds to yourself.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Schlossplatz Stuttgart to Altes Schloss Stuttgart
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

visits.text: Beneath the arcaded galleries of the Altes Schloss, the noise of Königstraße suddenly fades. This medieval moated castle began its transformation into a Renaissance palace in 1553, and an equestrian statue of Eberhard im Bart, who became the first Duke of Württemberg in 1495, presides over the courtyard. The Landesmuseum Württemberg occupies the upper floors: the royal crown treasury on the second floor, and the wheeled bench of the Celtic prince of Hochdorf and Aztec feather shields on the first. Closed Mondays; the Dürnitz, with its café and shop, remains free to enter.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Altes Schloss Stuttgart to Stiftskirche Stuttgart
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

visits.text: Lopsided but endearing, the Stiftskirche has two mismatched towers: the Reformation halted work on the western tower’s spire, leaving it with a flat roof at around 61 m. Against the choir wall, eleven armored counts of Württemberg, commissioned from sculptor Sem Schlör in 1574, stand like an ancestral gallery. The interior, remodeled after the 1944 bombings, reopened in 2003. On your way out, cross Schillerplatz, where the poet’s bronze statue watches over the market on Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday mornings.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Stiftskirche Stuttgart to Markthalle Stuttgart
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

activities.text: The Markthalle came within one vote of disappearing: that was the margin by which the city council decided to preserve it in the early 1970s. Completed in 1914 to designs by Martin Elsaesser, it conceals 33 stalls behind its Jugendstil facade, beneath a glass roof supported by concrete beams without a single pillar. Put together a quick lunch here, then head upstairs for home goods and gifts. Open weekdays from 7:30 a.m. to 6:30 p.m. and Saturdays from 7 a.m. to 5 p.m.

practical_info.tip: No Sunday hours are listed: plan to visit the market hall on a weekday or Saturday.

visits.text: Stuttgart locals call it the Bohnenviertel, the bean quarter: its residents of modest means grew beans in their gardens and draped the stems like garlands across their facades. Completed around 1415 for tanners and dyers who needed the Nesenbach stream, this district outside the old city walls was defended by its residents in the 1970s. Stop by the Leonhardskirche, enlarged from 1463 to 1466, where the humanist Johannes Reuchlin is buried, then wander among antique dealers, used bookstores, and galleries.

activities.text: If you set aside just one evening for wine, spend it in a Weinstube in the Bohnenviertel. These wood-paneled taverns carry on the tradition of the winegrowers’ taverns of old: vineyards once began just beyond Weberstraße. Order a Viertele, the small local measure, and let your hosts recommend a wine from Württemberg. Tables fill up quickly toward the end of the week: reserve that afternoon.

practical_info.tip: Every summer, the Bohnenviertelfest brings the neighborhood to life with music, stalls, and open shops.

to_next_leg.road_type: By rail or public transit: Bohnenviertel → Stadtmitte → U5 → Killesberg
to_next_leg.justification: Marche jusqu’au réseau urbain de Stuttgart puis ligne U5 vers Killesberg ; les 25 minutes excluent l’attente.

visits.text: Take the U5 line to the Killesberg stop: this former quarry became a horticultural exhibition park in 1939, then the Höhenpark, covering about 50 hectares. Its landmark, the Killesbergturm, is a 40 m cable-supported tower designed by engineer Jörg Schlaich in 2001. Two spiral staircases of 174 steps, one for going up and the other for coming down, lead to the upper platform at 31 m. The tower opens at 7 a.m. and has no elevator: come before the heat sets in.

map_keywords: Weissenhofmuseum im Haus Le Corbusier Stuttgart

visits.text: “Arab village”: that was how the Nazis mocked the Weissenhofsiedlung and its flat roofs. Built in 1927 for the Werkbund’s “Die Wohnung” exhibition under the direction of Mies van der Rohe, it brought together 17 architects from five countries. The duplex by Le Corbusier and Pierre Jeanneret, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2016, houses the Weissenhofmuseum: one half tells the story of the project, while the other recreates the 1927 interior. Admission is €6.50; the museum opens at 11 a.m. on weekdays and is closed Mondays.

Pure white, with the hush of a cathedral: the “heart” of the Stadtbibliothek is a void several stories high, lit through the roof, with galleries of books stacked around it. Korean architect Eun Young Yi completed this roughly 40 m cube in 2011 on the site of the former freight station, and it was named “Library of the Year” in 2013. In summer, head up to the rooftop terrace for one of the city’s best panoramic views. Since February 2026, the library has closed at 7 p.m.

Controversial when it opened in 1984, admired today: James Stirling’s Neue Staatsgalerie ranks among Germany’s great postmodern buildings, with Henry Moore’s “Liegende” in front of the entrance. Founded in 1843 by King William I, the museum displays around 800 works, from Rembrandt’s “Paul in Prison” to Picassos, along with Monet, Cézanne, and Oskar Schlemmer, whose archives it holds. Admission to the collection is free on Wednesdays; the museum stays open until 8 p.m. on Thursdays and is closed on Mondays.

Wilhelma began as a royal whim: William I wanted a Moorish-style country house, which Karl Ludwig von Zanth built between 1842 and 1846. Its pavilions, greenhouses, and Moorish garden now form Germany’s only combined zoological and botanical garden, home to around 8,500 plant species. In the pool, a single giant water lily leaf can support up to 70 kg. Arrive when it opens at 8:15 a.m., and keep in mind that the magnolias bloom in March and April.

activities.text: Next, move from the greenhouses to the animals: Wilhelma brings together around 1,200 species across roughly 30 hectares. The great ape house, opened in 2013, gives gorillas and bonobos some 4,500 m², thirteen times their former space, while the Amazonienhaus has recreated a tropical rainforest since 2000. In cold weather, save these heated houses for late morning: they become the park’s best refuge.

practical_info.tip: Opens daily at 8:15 a.m.; closing time is earlier in the low season (listed as 4:30 p.m.). Buy tickets online at wilhelma.de.

visits.text: Here, time unfolds from top to bottom: a visit to the Mercedes-Benz Museum starts on the ninth floor in 1886, then spirals down toward the present. Opened in 2006, UNStudio’s building arranges seven “Legend” rooms and five “Collection” rooms along a double helix, letting you switch between them as you please: more than 160 vehicles across 16,500 m². Admission is €16, with an €8 evening ticket from 4:30 p.m., but ticket counters close at 5 p.m. Take S-Bahn S1 to NeckarPark; the museum is closed on Mondays.

to_next_leg.road_type: B10 along the Neckar

visits.text: The carillon at Esslingen’s Altes Rathaus has chimed several times a day since 1926, beneath an astronomical clock that retains its original mechanism. Built around 1420 as a merchants’ hall and tax office, the building gained its Renaissance facade, designed by Heinrich Schickhardt, between 1586 and 1589, while its south side displays exposed timber framing. Steps away, houses 4 through 10 on Hafenmarkt date from 1328 to 1331. Walk around the building: its two facades tell the stories of two eras.

Next, climb to the Burg via the stairs and Burgsteige, among the vineyards. Despite its name, Esslingen’s Burg is not a castle but a section of the medieval fortifications, with the Dicker Turm dating from 1525 and the Hochwacht, an 18th-century watchtower. The Seilergang wall walk overlooks the old town’s rooftops and the Neckar Valley. Allow 45 minutes for the round trip and wear closed-toe shoes.

Never conquered, but surrendered twice: Hohenneuffen Fortress capitulated in 1519, then again in 1635 after a fifteen-month siege. Perched at around 743 m on the edge of the Swabian Jura, it gained its bastions under Duke Ulrich in the 16th century, served as a state prison, and was then handed over for demolition in 1801. In 1948, a conference of the three German states held here laid the groundwork for the creation of Baden-Württemberg. Admission is free, with a walk of about 20 minutes from the hiking parking lot; on clear days, the view reaches Stuttgart.

Bad Urach’s Marktplatz is lined with 15th- and 16th-century half-timbered houses around the Rathaus, built in 1440 and expanded in 1562. Since 2023, a sculpture by Peter Lenk has celebrated the Schäferlauf, the shepherds’ festival. Continue to the Amanduskirche, a Late Gothic church built between 1475 and 1499, then treat yourself to a coffee on an outdoor terrace before taking the evening drive back to Stuttgart.

activities.text: If you come after a rain shower, the Uracher Wasserfall changes its voice: its flow rises from around 70 liters per second in midsummer to 420 after heavy rain. The water plunges freely for some 37 m, then slides over 50 m of moss-covered tufa, a rock this limestone-rich stream creates itself. Start at the Maisental hiking parking lot; a trail climbs to the plateau on the right side of the falls. Allow a good hour and a half and wear shoes with good traction.

practical_info.tip: The full Wasserfallsteig trail (10 km, around 3 hours 25 minutes) also takes in Güterstein Falls: save it for a longer stay. The best season is April through September.

visits.text: A 36-second elevator ride takes you to the observation deck at 150 m: inaugurated in February 1956, Stuttgart’s Fernsehturm was the first reinforced-concrete television tower. Fritz Leonhardt had persuaded the broadcaster to replace a simple steel mast with a tower featuring a café and observation decks. On clear days, the view stretches to the Swabian Jura you explored earlier in the day. Open daily from 10 a.m. to 10 p.m., with the last ascent half an hour before closing; admission is €12.50. Take U7, U8, or U15 to Ruhbank (Fernsehturm).

More compact than the Mercedes-Benz Museum, the Porsche Museum packs a bigger punch: around 80 cars across 5,600 m², in a structure that seems to float on three supports, designed by Delugan Meissl and opened in 2009. Look for the 1948 356 “Nr. 1” Roadster, weighing 585 kg with a top speed of 135 km/h, then the 917 that won Le Mans in 1970. Arrive before 10 a.m.: the Early Bird ticket costs €12 instead of €15. Free multimedia guide; take S-Bahn S6 to Neuwirtshaus (Porscheplatz). Closed on Mondays.

A single ground-floor room: that was all the Schiller family rented when Friedrich was born here on November 10, 1759. Schillers Geburtshaus, a craftsman’s house rebuilt after the fire of 1693, became a museum in 1859, making it one of the oldest literary memorial sites in the German-speaking world. Inside, you can see a christening cap and a period child’s outfit. Open Tuesday through Sunday, from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. April through October, and from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. in winter.

Next, climb to the Schillerhöhe, developed as a place for celebrations in the 1830s, to visit two neighboring museums. The Schiller-Nationalmuseum, opened in 1903, has presented the “Schiller!” exhibition since 2025, with some 400 items exploring the political poet. Next door, David Chipperfield’s Literaturmuseum der Moderne displays more than 180 manuscripts and objects from the 20th century. Between visits, stroll through the half-timbered old town, rebuilt after the fire set by Mélac’s troops in 1693. Both museums are closed on Mondays.

It is hard to find a more complete example: UNESCO, which listed Kloster Maulbronn in 1993, considers it the best-preserved medieval monastery north of the Alps. The Cistercians settled here in 1147. Step through the Paradies, a porch dating from the 1210s–1220s where Romanesque arches meet the emerging Gothic style, then head to the cloister and the Brunnenkapelle, whose three-tiered fountain retains its original lower basin. Choose the €13 ticket with an audio guide, available in French.

Doctor Faust is said to have stayed around 1516 in the Faustturm, at the southeastern corner of Maulbronn’s enclosure, summoned by the abbot to make gold. Another legend credits the monks with inventing Maultaschen, those Swabian ravioli, though no documents support the claim. On firmer ground: the Protestant seminary that opened in 1556 educated Johannes Kepler, Friedrich Hölderlin, and Hermann Hesse. From March through October, it is open daily from 9:30 a.m. to 5:30 p.m.; in winter, it is closed on Mondays, with last admission at 3:45 p.m.

Four hundred fifty-two rooms across eighteen buildings: even the guided tour gives up on showing all of Residenzschloss Ludwigsburg. Begun in 1704 as a hunting lodge for Duke Eberhard Ludwig and made a residence in 1718, it blends Baroque, Rococo, and Neoclassical styles. Look out for the Schlosstheater and its almost complete original stage machinery. The interiors can only be seen on a guided tour, costing €10, with several departures daily, some in English.

to_next_leg.road_type: Walk from Residenzschloss Ludwigsburg to Bluehendes Barock
to_next_leg.justification: Le parcours piéton est très court ; la distance entière de 1 km est un arrondi majorant imposé par le format, et la durée est harmonisée.

activities.text: Perfectly straight paths on one side, Rapunzel letting down her hair on the other: Blühendes Barock embraces both worlds. These 30 hectares of gardens, surrounding the palace on three sides, opened on April 23, 1954, for Ludwigsburg’s 250th anniversary. The Märchengarten brings more than 40 fairy tales to life, and a boat ride along the Märchenbach is included with admission. In the fall, the pumpkin exhibition takes over the paths: August 22 through November 1 in 2026.

practical_info.tip: The season begins in March (on March 20 in 2026), and the grounds are closed in midwinter; in November, the Märchengarten closes at 4:30 p.m.

visits.text: Two churches face each other across Ludwigsburg’s Marktplatz: the Protestant Stadtkirche to the west and the Catholic Dreieinigkeitskirche to the east, on opposite sides of a square measuring about 110 m by 80 m, designed in the 18th century by Donato Giuseppe Frisoni. At its center, the fountain bears a statue of Duke Eberhard Ludwig, the city’s founder, who was nevertheless reluctant to fund a church. Come on Tuesday, Thursday, or Saturday morning for the market, starting at 7 a.m.

activities.text: End the day beneath the arcades of the Marktplatz, where restaurants and shops occupy the ground floors. This square also hosts Ludwigsburg’s Barock-Weihnachtsmarkt during Advent and its Venezianische Messe. Settle into an outdoor seat facing one of the two churches: the Baroque setting is all you need for an aperitif, and the palace is just a few minutes away on foot.

practical_info.tip: The market runs year-round on Tuesdays and Thursdays from 7 a.m. to 1 p.m., and Saturdays from 7 a.m. to 2 p.m.

seo.h1_title: Stuttgart and Ludwigsburg in 6 Days: Art, Cars, and Baroque
seo.intro_paragraph: Over 6 days, this itinerary devotes three full days to Stuttgart: Schlossplatz and Altes Schloss, the Staatsgalerie, the Weissenhof Estate, Wilhelma, and the Mercedes-Benz Museum. It then heads to Esslingen and the Swabian Jura, followed by Marbach, the UNESCO-listed Cistercian abbey of Maulbronn, and Ludwigsburg’s Baroque palace.
seo.seo_hook: Schlossplatz, the Staatsgalerie, Mercedes and Porsche, Maulbronn Abbey, and a Baroque palace: Stuttgart and Ludwigsburg in 6 days, with time to explore everything in depth.
featured_list: Stuttgart: the Staatsgalerie displays about 800 works, from Rembrandt to Picasso
Stuttgart: the Fernsehturm, the first reinforced-concrete television tower, dates from 1956
Esslingen: the houses on Hafenmarkt date from 1328 to 1331
Marbach: Schiller was born on November 10, 1759, in a craftsman’s house
Maulbronn: a Cistercian abbey founded in 1147, a World Heritage Site since 1993
Ludwigsburg: a 452-room palace surrounded by 30 hectares of gardens

itineraries.title: Thuringian Forest in 3 Days: Wartburg, Rennsteig, and Bach
itineraries.subtitle: In 3 days, travel from Eisenach to Arnstadt via Wartburg Castle, the ridges of the Rennsteig, and Goethe’s trails.
itineraries.notes: Start on a Wednesday or Thursday: the Lutherhaus and Arnstadt’s Schlossmuseum are closed on Mondays, and Ilmenau’s museums are closed on Mondays and, from November through April, Tuesdays as well. Oberhof’s Rennsteiggarten closes in winter; reopening is announced for May 2027. Ice can make the Drachenschlucht impassable in winter.
itineraries.climate: Aim for May through September: along the ridges, average highs range from about 16 °C in May to 21 °C in July (Kleiner Inselsberg weather station, 732 m), with nighttime temperatures of 7 to 12 °C. Avoid October through March for hiking: rain is frequent, with nighttime frost in January and snow and ice on mountain roads. Keep a rain jacket handy even in summer, since July is the wettest month of the warmer season.

visits.text: There is no better place to begin this trip than Wartburg Castle: the first German castle inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List, in 1999, it brings together Luther and Saint Elizabeth on a single rocky spur. In the Lutherstube, Martin Luther, hiding under the name Junker Jörg, translated the New Testament in about eleven weeks; the mosaics in the Elisabeth-Kemenate, however, date only to 1902–1906. Arrive at opening time: the Palas can be visited on a guided tour, and the climb from the parking lot is steep.

According to tradition, the young Luther stayed with the Cotta family between 1498 and 1501 in what is now Eisenach’s Lutherhaus, one of Thuringia’s oldest half-timbered houses. The exhibition “Luther und die Bibel” traces his translation across three floors, followed by a room exploring a darker subject: the church-run “Entjudungsinstitut” of 1939–1945, whose members exploited his anti-Jewish statements. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes, and avoid Mondays, when it is closed.

Stop at the Georgenkirche on Eisenach’s Markt: Johann Sebastian Bach was baptized here in 1685, and Luther preached here on May 2, 1521, while fleeing his pursuers. From 1665 to 1797, four members of the Bach family served here in succession as organists. On your way out, look at the gilded Saint George fountain, designed in 1549, then the Baroque facade of the Stadtschloss on the same square.

Bach’s birthplace? There is no proof, yet Eisenach’s Bachhaus became the world’s first Bach museum in 1907. Every hour, short concerts bring the collection’s historical instruments to life, including two organs built around 1650 and around 1750. Save it for late afternoon, since it is open daily until 6 p.m.; a combined Bach–Luther ticket also covers the Lutherhaus.

activities.text: Water trickles beneath the walkways, and moss-covered walls close in: at its narrowest point, the Drachenschlucht leaves a passage just 68 centimeters wide. This gorge, about 3 kilometers long and south of Eisenach, has been protected as a geological natural monument since 1977, along with the neighboring Landgrafenschlucht. Hike up to Hohe Sonne and take the bus back down; strollers and bicycles are prohibited.

practical_info.tip: In winter, ice can make the gorge impassable: check with the Eisenach tourist office before setting out.

visits.text: It was called “Marienglas,” or Mary’s glass: this transparent gypsum was used in place of glass over pictures of the Virgin Mary. In the Marienglashöhle, between Friedrichroda and Bad Tabarz, the crystal cave discovered in 1784 holds crystals up to 90 centimeters long, preserved since their extraction was banned in 1848. The guided tour lasts about 45 minutes and involves around a hundred steps: bring a fleece, as temperatures stay at 8 to 10 °C even in the height of summer.

to_next_leg.road_type: L1024, then the access road to the summit

visits.text: If the sky is clear, climb the observation tower on the Großer Inselsberg: from its 21-meter height, you can see as far as the Wasserkuppe in the Rhön and the Brocken in the Harz. At 916 meters, this summit is the highest point in the western Thuringian Forest. There is an admission fee for the tower; bring a jacket, even in summer.

activities.text: Follow the Rennsteig across the Großer Inselsberg’s summit plateau, which is about 700 meters long: the ridge trail, marked with a white “R,” shares its route here with the E3 European long-distance path. Running some 169 kilometers between Hörschel and Blankenstein, it marked the former border between Saxe-Gotha and the Electorate of Hesse here. For a longer walk, continue to the Kleiner Inselsberg pass and its 1,000-meter summer toboggan run.

practical_info.tip: A road branches off the L1024 between Brotterode and Tabarz and leads to the visitor parking lot below the summit; there is also a large parking lot at the Kleiner Inselsberg pass.

to_next_leg.road_type: Descent via Brotterode

visits.text: Schloss Wilhelmsburg was inaugurated in 1590, while the construction begun by Landgrave William IV of Hesse was still underway. In the chapel, Daniel Meyer’s organ, with its 252 wooden pipes, was played at the consecration; it ranks among the oldest instruments of its kind still playable in Central Europe. The castle also displays a replica of the Iwein cycle, Germany’s oldest secular murals. From November through March, the museum is open Tuesday through Sunday, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.

Closely packed half-timbered buildings, cobblestones, and two mismatched towers: Schmalkalden’s Altmarkt reveals itself at a glance. The Rathaus dates from 1419, and the town hosted seven of the Schmalkaldic League’s 26 assemblies; in the nearby Stadtkirche St. Georg, a watchman’s dwelling perched about 50 meters up remained occupied until 1935. Walk around the church to compare its two towers, then wander the streets: nearly 90% of the late medieval half-timbered houses have survived.

In February 1537, Martin Luther stayed at Schmalkalden’s Lutherhaus, a house built in 1530, during the assembly of the Schmalkaldic League. He preached at the Stadtkirche, but a bout of kidney stones then prevented him from attending the meeting. Look for the facade as you explore the lanes, then extend your walk to the Siechenteich ponds and the Stadtpark, which provided the setting for the Thuringian Horticultural Show in 2015.

activities.text: Take a sweet break at Viba Nougat-Welt in Schmalkalden: through the factory windows, you can watch nougat being made step by step. The company has produced nougat and marzipan since the 1920s, was known throughout East Germany, and opened this visitor attraction in 2012. The exhibition floor is free to visit and open daily from 9:30 a.m. to 5 p.m.; hands-on workshops require a ticket.

practical_info.tip: Visit Viba before your walk through the historic center: the discovery floor is only open until 5 p.m.

to_next_leg.road_type: Road through low mountains

map_keywords: LOTTO Thüringen ARENA am Rennsteig Oberhof

visits.text: An alpine garden in Thuringia may seem an odd idea, yet this is the stop on the trip that feels most like another world. On the Pfanntalskopf, at 868 meters, Oberhof’s Rennsteiggarten brings together nearly 4,000 species from the mountains of Europe, Asia, the Americas, and New Zealand, including gentians and edelweiss, across 7 hectares of a former quarry. Snow covers the site for about 150 days a year; the garden closes in winter and announces its reopening in May 2027.

activities.text: The LOTTO Thüringen ARENA am Rennsteig hosts biathletes near the Grenzadler, about 2.5 kilometers west of Oberhof. During the 2023 World Championships, 152,000 spectators attended over nine days; nearby, a two-meter boundary marker topped with a Prussian eagle recalls the former border between Prussia and the Duchy of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha. Park in the large Grenzadler parking lot and walk along the Rennsteig for a while.

practical_info.tip: On competition days, access and parking at the Grenzadler change: check Oberhof’s sports calendar before visiting.

visits.text: If Goethe intrigues you more as a government minister than as a poet, start at the GoetheStadtMuseum, in the Amtshaus on Ilmenau’s Markt. Its galleries recount his efforts to revive the town’s copper and silver mines and then its porcelain and technical glass industries; after his first visit in 1776, Goethe returned to Ilmenau 26 times. The museum is open Tuesday through Sunday in summer and Wednesday through Sunday from November through April.

The Jagdhaus Gabelbach, a wooden hunting lodge hastily built in the summer of 1783 for Duke Charles Augustus’s hunts, stands a few hundred meters below the summit of the Kickelhahn. Goethe was a frequent guest; today, the museum explores hunting, his scientific research, and the forest through the exhibition “Der Kickelhahn, Goethes Wald im Wandel.” It follows the GoetheStadtMuseum’s opening hours, and a combined ticket covers three of the town’s museums.

activities.text: Climb the Kickelhahn, at 861 meters, from the Herzogröder Wiesen hiking parking lot on the road to Frauenwald: an uphill walk of about 2 kilometers through the forest. Near the summit, the Goethehäuschen, rebuilt in 1874, recalls the cabin where Goethe wrote “Over all the peaks is peace” in pencil on September 6, 1780; returning in 1831, a few months before his death, he wept as he reread these lines. Finish by climbing the 107 steps of the Kickelhahnturm, which is free to enter.

practical_info.tip: Allow about 2 hours for the round trip, including the tower and the Goethehäuschen; wear hiking shoes, as the forest path gets slippery after rain.

visits.text: Visitors come to Arnstadt’s Schlossmuseum for the dolls, yet its most moving exhibit awaits in the attic: the console of the 1703 Wender organ, played by the young Bach. The 82 miniature rooms of Mon plaisir, created in the 18th century by Princess Augusta Dorothea, are undergoing restoration begun in January 2025, and only a selection remains on display. Take time to explore the mirrored room and its Asian and European porcelain, numbering nearly a thousand pieces.

In June 1703, an 18-year-old musician came to inspect the new organ at Arnstadt’s Neue Kirche and was hired soon afterward: Johann Sebastian Bach. Rebuilt between 1676 and 1683 after the fire of 1581, the church has been known as the Bachkirche since 1935; the Wender organ, modified several times, stands in the gallery above a 1913 Steinmeyer organ. Opening hours vary: check with the tourist office.

“Are there no more Bachs to apply for this position? I absolutely must have another Bach,” lamented the Count of Schwarzburg-Arnstadt upon the death of court musician Johann Christoph Bach. On Arnstadt’s Markt, the statue of the young Bach depicts him as he might have looked at around 18, near the Renaissance Rathaus built in 1586 after the fire of 1581. Continue to the nearby Bachkirche to follow the musician from one site to the next.

Save the Liebfrauenkirche for the end of the morning: built from the late 12th century to around 1330, it transitions from Romanesque to Gothic. Its 1498 altarpiece with double wings depicts Saints Lawrence and Boniface, and the burial chapel houses the tomb of Count Günther XXV of Schwarzburg and his wife, decorated with heraldic lions. The church is a few minutes’ walk from the Markt.

seo.h1_title: Thuringian Forest in 3 Days: Wartburg, Rennsteig, and Bach
seo.intro_paragraph: This 3-day driving tour starts in Eisenach with Wartburg Castle, the Lutherhaus, and the Bachhaus, then follows the Thuringian Forest through the Marienglashöhle, Großer Inselsberg, and Schmalkalden. The Rennsteiggarten in Oberhof, Goethe’s Kickelhahn in Ilmenau, and the church where the young Bach played in Arnstadt round out the route.
seo.seo_hook: Wartburg Castle, the homes of Luther and Bach, a crystal cave, the Rennsteig, and Goethe’s Kickelhahn: the Thuringian Forest in 3 days, from Eisenach to Arnstadt.
featured_list: Eisenach: Wartburg Castle, the Lutherhaus, and the world’s first Bach museum
Friedrichroda: the Marienglashöhle and its crystal cave discovered in 1784
Großer Inselsberg: the Rennsteig crosses this 916 m summit
Schmalkalden: a 1590 organ at Schloss Wilhelmsburg
Oberhof: nearly 4,000 mountain species at the Rennsteiggarten
Ilmenau: the cabin on the Kickelhahn where Goethe wrote his poem
Arnstadt: the church where Bach was an organist at 18

places_taglines.DE::marienglashoehle: A gypsum crystal cave discovered in 1784.
places_taglines.DE::schmalkalden: A Renaissance castle and medieval half-timbered houses associated with the Schmalkaldic League.
places_taglines.DE::oberhof: A biathlon stadium and a garden of mountain plants.
places_taglines.DE::ilmenau: Goethe’s town, at the foot of the Kickelhahn.
places_taglines.DE::arnstadt: The young Bach played the organ at the Neue Kirche here.

highlights: Wartburg: the first German castle inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List, in 1999
Drachenschlucht: a 68 cm passage between the gorge walls
Marienglashöhle: gypsum crystals up to 90 cm long
Schmalkalden: an organ from 1590 at Schloss Wilhelmsburg
Kickelhahn: the cabin where Goethe wrote his poem in 1780
Arnstadt: the console of the organ played by the young Bach
