itineraries.title: From Rosenheim to Burghausen in 3 Days, Between the Inn and Salzach
itineraries.subtitle: Over 3 days, follow the Inn from Rosenheim to Wasserburg, then head to Altötting and the long fortress of Burghausen.
itineraries.notes: Avoid starting on a Monday: Rosenheim’s Städtisches Museum and Holztechnisches Museum, as well as Museum Wasserburg, are closed that day. Altötting’s Schatzkammer and two museums at Burghausen Castle open only during the warmer months, from March or Easter through fall.
itineraries.climate: Aim for May through September: in Rosenheim, average highs rise from around 19 °C in May to 26 °C in July. July and August are also among the rainiest months, so keep a rain jacket handy. From November through March, highs stay below 13 °C, and several museums reduce their hours or wait until spring to reopen.
specialties: Bords de l'Inn et de la Salzach

visits.text: The Lokschuppen alone makes Rosenheim worth a stop. The former locomotive depot of the first train station, which opened in 1858, has hosted exhibitions since 1988 that have drawn up to 280,000 visitors. Through August 1, 2027, RÖMER brings together 1,228 objects from around thirty lenders. Open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.; arrive when it opens.

Max-Josefs-Platz is lined with Inn-Salzach-style facades rebuilt after the great fire of 1641; the square became pedestrian-only in 1984. At one end, the Mittertor is the only one of the market town’s five gates still standing; its core makes it Rosenheim’s oldest building. Allow 30 minutes on foot, continuing as far as the onion-domed bell tower of St. Nikolaus.

To understand the sources of Rosenheim’s prosperity, head upstairs to the Städtisches Museum, housed in the Mittertor. Its 23 rooms display around 4,000 objects covering everything from river shipping on the Inn to trade, and from tiled stoves to popular piety. It opens Tuesday through Sunday from noon to 5 p.m., so save it for early afternoon.

Take the “Himmelsleiter,” the staircase nicknamed the ladder to heaven, to reach the Holztechnisches Museum, which opened in 1990 in the Ellmaierhaus on Max-Josefs-Platz. Across more than 400 m², original objects, models, and tools trace woodworking from the craftsperson to the engineer. Half an hour is enough; the museum opens Tuesday through Sunday starting at noon.

A bright octagon beneath a painted dome: at the Klosterkirche St. Marinus und Anianus in Rott am Inn, start by looking up. Johann Michael Fischer rebuilt the church from 1759 to 1763, Matthäus Günther painted the frescoes, and Ignaz Günther designed the altars. Bring binoculars to view the statues of Emperor Henry II and Cunigunde.

A striking contrast in the shadow of the Rococo: Franz Josef Strauß, Bavaria’s minister-president, who died in 1988, rests in the cemetery of Rott’s former monastery. His wife Marianne, who came from a local brewing family, is buried with him. The grave lies along Franz-Josef-Strauß-Weg; 10 minutes is enough.

Walk across the Innbrücke for the classic view of Wasserburg, with its pastel facades clustered above the Inn. The former wooden bridge was swept away by ice almost every year, for the last time in 1929. At the far end, the Brucktor preserves murals from 1568 on its river-facing side: two armored guards still watch over the entrance to town.

Marienplatz brings two eras face to face: the Gothic town hall, built from 1457 to 1459, whose small hall retains its 1564 decoration, and the Rococo facade of the Kernhaus, the work of Johann Baptist Zimmermann between 1738 and 1740. During the season, a guided tour of the town hall’s rooms takes place on weekdays at 1 p.m.

The lion and tower on Wasserburg’s coat of arms come from the Frauenkirche: its 65 m bell tower served as a watchtower. The city’s oldest church, documented as early as 1324, preserves a Gothic Madonna from around 1420 beneath its Baroque decoration. Fifteen minutes is enough to see the Madonna and the nave.

St. Jakob’s finest feature is its pulpit, carved in 1638 by Martin and Michael Zürn. This 17th-century masterpiece stands out in a Gothic hall church built from 1410 to 1478 by Hans von Burghausen, Hans Stethaimer, and Stephan Krumenauer. On your way out, walk around the choir to find the “tree of life” on its exterior wall.

Four floors, 52 themes, around 8,000 objects: Museum Wasserburg occupies a Gothic patrician house typical of the Inn-Salzach region on Herrengasse. River shipping, the salt trade, and thirteen craft workshops tell the story of the city that served as Munich’s port until the railroad arrived. Open Tuesday through Sunday from 1 p.m.; adult admission is €2.50.

activities.text: Climb for about 20 minutes along Kellerbergweg to Schöne Aussicht, south of the bridge: from up here, Wasserburg reveals its setting in a bend of the Inn that almost completely surrounds it. The Innleiten, slopes on the opposite bank, rise as high as 70 m. Save this climb for clear skies, since the view depends on them.

practical_info.tip: Walk from the bridge over the Inn via Kellerbergweg; the climb takes about 20 minutes.

activities.text: A flood levee turned open-air gallery: along the bend of the Inn, more than 30 sculptures, some very large, line a stretch of about 1.5 km. The AK 68 artists’ association, founded in 1968, began commissioning them in 1988. Look for Leonard Schlögel’s limestone head, “Isis.”

practical_info.tip: A flat walk along the levee, pleasant in the morning before heading to Mühldorf.

visits.text: Mühldorf’s Stadtplatz stretches nearly 500 m from Münchner Tor to Altöttinger Tor. Its Inn-Salzach-style facades rise above the roofs to conceal them, a fire protection measure adopted after major fires. An enclave of Salzburg until 1802, the city retains the air of a small capital. Walk the length of the square, from one gate to the other.

Tree trunks cut straight across mark the mass grave deep in the forest at KZ-Gedenkort Mühldorfer Hart. Beginning in the summer of 1944, thousands of deportees, including many Hungarian Jews, built a bunker here for the aircraft industry in a Dachau subcamp. Open to the public since 2018, the Waldlager and the grave can be explored along paths lined with information panels.

Altötting is nicknamed “the heart of Bavaria,” and the Gnadenkapelle takes the phrase literally: silver urns here hold the hearts of members of the Wittelsbach dynasty, including Ludwig II. Beneath the octagonal structure, which may date from the 8th century, the Black Madonna draws more than a million pilgrims a year. Walk around the ambulatory and its roughly 2,000 votive offerings.

Cross Kapellplatz to the Stiftskirche St. Philippus und Jakobus, built from 1499 to 1511 to accommodate the influx of pilgrims. The tourist office describes it as the last Gothic hall church in southern Germany. On the base of the clock, look for the “Tod von Eding,” a figure of Death dating back to the plague years, then take a look at the cloister frescoes.

Altötting’s finest object is French: the Goldenes Rössl, a 62 cm enameled gold altar made in 1404 by the workshops of the Paris court as a New Year’s gift from Isabeau of Bavaria to Charles VI. It takes pride of place in the Schatzkammer on Kapellplatz. Admission is free from Easter through the end of October; afternoon opening is Monday through Thursday only.

Jerusalem surrounds you: in the Panorama’s rotunda, a canvas 12 m high and 95 m in circumference depicts the city on the day of the Crucifixion. Gebhard Fugel and his team painted it in 1902 and 1903. According to the city, it is the last surviving historical panorama in Germany. In 2026, open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., March 21 through October 31; admission €5.

Neo-Baroque and enormous, the Basilika St. Anna will not appeal to everyone, but its figures command respect: about 83 m long, with room for some 8,000 worshippers. Built from 1910 to 1912 for crowds of pilgrims, it was granted basilica status by Pius X in 1913. Step inside between services; 15 minutes is enough.

Step inside St. Konrad Church, Altötting’s second pilgrimage destination: Conrad of Parzham, a Capuchin friar, served as the friary’s porter for forty years. He died in 1894 and was canonized in 1934; he is venerated here, where his relics are kept. The meeting room is open daily from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m.

activities.text: If you are staying in Altötting on a Saturday between May and October, linger on Kapellplatz after nightfall: a candlelight procession circles the Gnadenkapelle. A more solemn procession takes place on the eve of the Assumption, August 14. For the exact time, check the pilgrimage schedule published weekly during the season.

practical_info.tip: The pilgrimage schedule is published on the city of Altötting’s website weekly from Easter through the end of October, then monthly.

visits.text: Look up inside St. Georg Church in Raitenhaslach: across three bays, Johannes Zick painted the life of St. Bernard in 1743 for the monastery’s 600th anniversary. Established here in 1146 as the first Cistercian monastery in Old Bavaria, it served as the burial place of the dukes of Burghausen in the 15th century. The reception rooms in the Prälatenstock can be visited by reservation.

Burghausen calls it “the pearl of the Salzach Valley”: on its plateau, the Wallfahrtskirche Marienberg raises its twin towers about 3 km from the center. Franz Alois Mayr rebuilt it from 1760 to 1764; Johann Martin Heigl, a pupil of Johann Baptist Zimmermann, painted its ceilings devoted to the Virgin Mary. Stop on your way to Burghausen; 30 minutes is enough.

Burg zu Burghausen stretches 1,051 m along its ridge between the Salzach and Wöhrsee, and Guinness World Records recognizes it as the world’s longest castle. Duke Henry XIII rebuilt it beginning in 1255, and George the Rich expanded it considerably in the late 15th century. Explore the outer courtyards, open at all hours, starting with the sixth and farthest one and working your way toward the Hauptburg.

The Hauptburg is worth the admission price, especially for its upper floors. On the first upper floor, the Staatliches Burgmuseum recreates the apartments of the dukes of Bavaria-Landshut, who kept their gold and silver treasure here; on the next two floors, the Staatsgalerie displays 56 paintings dating from the late Middle Ages to the early 17th century. Tickets are available at the Besucherzentrum in the Dürnitzstock; open daily from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. April through September, and until 4 p.m. in winter.

The daughter of the king of Poland, Hedwig married George the Rich at the famous Landshut Wedding, then lived here with her court from 1475 to 1502. The Stadtmuseum, in the Hauptburg’s Kemenate, devotes its ground floor to this princely life before tracing local history, including the witch hunts. Open from mid-March through fall; a €10 pass covers three castle museums.

A former tax office filled with cameras: the Haus der Fotografie occupies the Rentmeisterstock in the castle’s fifth courtyard. More than 600 cameras from every era trace the history of photography, alongside early photographic processes and old photographs of Burghausen. Founded in 1983, it is open daily from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., from March to early November.

Burghausen’s Stadtplatz, at the foot of the castle, is lined with Inn-Salzach-style screen facades extending to the Taufkirchen-Palais and the Regierungsgebäude, crowned by three Renaissance towers. Nearby, St. Jakob has a 79 m bell tower, and Anton Bruckner played its new organ in 1856. Walk down from the Hauptburg to combine the castle and old town without getting back in the car.

activities.text: Swim at the foot of the ramparts: the Wöhrsee, a former oxbow of the Salzach, has served as a swimming lake for local residents since 1833. In January 2015, its Naturbad even hosted Germany’s first ice swimming championship, followed by the world championship in 2017. Outside the swimming season, walk around the lake; in late November, more than 350 lanterns line its shores.

practical_info.tip: Swim at the Naturbad Wöhrsee in summer; the Liachterlweg lanterns are lit in late November and early December.

activities.text: If the sky is clear, cross the Salzach on the Alte Brücke: on the opposite bank, you are already in Austria. A steep trail climbs to a viewing platform overlooking the old town and the full length of the Burg. The “Über Brücken gehen” loop, 4.3 km and about 1 hour 10 minutes, returns via the Neue Brücke and follows the bronze plaques of the jazz-themed Street of Fame on the Bavarian side.

practical_info.tip: Paved loop with 68 m of elevation gain; the viewing platform has a kiosk and restrooms.

seo.h1_title: From Rosenheim to Burghausen in 3 Days, Between the Inn and Salzach
seo.intro_paragraph: This 3-day road trip connects Rosenheim to Burghausen via Wasserburg am Inn and Mühldorf, two towns with Inn-Salzach-style facades. You spend an evening in Altötting, a major Marian shrine in Bavaria, before a full day at Burghausen Castle, which stretches for 1,051 m above the Salzach.
seo.seo_hook: Rosenheim’s Lokschuppen, the Wasserburg peninsula, Altötting’s Gnadenkapelle, and a 1,051 m castle in Burghausen: the Inn and Salzach in 3 days.
featured_list: Rosenheim: the Lokschuppen, a former locomotive depot converted into an exhibition center in 1988
Wasserburg am Inn: the Kernhaus’s Rococo facade and the view from the Schöne Aussicht
Mühldorf am Inn: the Stadtplatz, nearly 500 m long, between two gates
Altötting: the hearts of the Wittelsbachs in the Gnadenkapelle
Burghausen: the world’s longest castle according to Guinness, at 1,051 m

places_taglines.DE::rott-am-inn: Rococo abbey church by Johann Michael Fischer, consecrated in 1763.
places_taglines.DE::wasserburg-am-inn: Old town almost encircled by a bend in the Inn.
places_taglines.DE::muhldorf-am-inn: Former Salzburg enclave with a square nearly 500 m long.
places_taglines.DE::altotting: Major Marian shrine in Bavaria, centered around the Gnadenkapelle.
places_taglines.DE::raitenhaslach: Former Cistercian abbey established in 1146 above the Salzach.
places_taglines.DE::burghausen: A 1,051 m-long castle overlooking the Salzach and the old town.

highlights: Rosenheim: RÖMER exhibition at the Lokschuppen, 1,228 objects through August 1, 2027
Wasserburg am Inn: old town on a peninsula in the Inn, town hall built from 1457 to 1459
Altötting: Gnadenkapelle, Goldenes Rössl from 1404, and a 1,200 m² panorama
Raitenhaslach: frescoes by Johannes Zick in the Cistercian abbey church
Burghausen: 1,051 m long castle with six courtyards above the Salzach

itineraries.title: North Frisia in 4 Days: Husum, Föhr, Amrum, and Hooge
itineraries.subtitle: Travel from Husum to the islands of Föhr and Amrum in 4 days via Sankt Peter-Ording, Nolde’s garden, and the hallig of Hooge.
itineraries.notes: The Nolde Foundation is only open from March 1 to October 31, and boat excursions from Wyk to Hooge stop at the end of October, so plan your trip between April and October. A car is of little use on the islands: leave it at the island parking lot in Dagebüll, which has a free shuttle to the ferry.
itineraries.climate: Plan your visit between May and September: in Sankt Peter-Ording, average highs range from about 16 °C in May to 21 °C in July and August. Avoid November through February: the Nolde Museum is closed to visitors, excursions to Hooge no longer run, and ferries switch to their winter schedule. Bring a windbreaker and rain gear, even in summer.
specialties: Îles et halligen de la mer des Wadden

visits.text: The Tine-Brunnen, a fountain installed in 1902 on Husum’s Marktplatz, is the town’s symbol. Its bronze statue, by sculptor Adolf Brütt, depicts a young fisherwoman wearing a headscarf and clogs, with an oar in her hand. Behind her stands the Marienkirche, a Neoclassical church completed in 1833. Come on Thursday or Saturday morning, when the square hosts the weekly market.

Step inside the Theodor-Storm-Haus on the narrow street of Wasserreihe. The writer Theodor Storm lived here from 1866 to 1880. Here he wrote poems and around twenty short stories, narratives shorter than a novel. The house, built in 1730, has fourteen rooms, including the living room with its original piano. Storm was the one who dubbed Husum “the gray town by the sea” in a poem. In November and December, the house opens only in the afternoon; admission costs €7.

According to a Husum legend, monks planted the first crocuses in the 15th century to obtain saffron, which they used to dye their robes. Every spring, from February through late March depending on the weather, millions of purple crocuses blanket the Schlosspark, the castle park. Schloss vor Husum was built between 1577 and 1582 for Duke Adolf of Schleswig-Holstein-Gottorf. Its museum opens Tuesday through Sunday and features furnished rooms and 17th-century fireplaces.

In January 1362, a major storm swept the medieval settlement of Rungholt beneath the sea. The Nordfriesland Museum Nissenhaus, a coastal museum in Husum, devotes an entire section to this submerged place. Models, artifacts, and interactive experiments then explain how tides and storms have shaped the shoreline. The museum opens daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., year-round: save it for a rain shower.

Masts, hulls, and the smell of mud: the Binnenhafen, Husum’s inner harbor, reaches almost to the Marktplatz. Along Wasserreihe, small fishermen’s houses face the boats. At the end of the harbor basin, the Schiffahrtsmuseum Nordfriesland, a maritime museum, displays the wreck of a sailing cargo vessel built around 1600. Visit at high tide and again at low tide: the water level completely changes the harbor’s appearance.

activities.text: Walk or bike to Dockkoogspitze, about 2.5 km west of central Husum. This point serves as a swimming area: settle right on the dike, facing the Wadden Sea. The Wadden Sea is the vast expanse of tidal flats, stretches of sand and mud exposed at low tide. Come late in the day for the evening light on the water.

practical_info.tip: The dike is very exposed to the wind: bring a windbreaker, even in summer.

visits.text: Whether the skies are gray or the sun is shining, the Multimar Wattforum in Tönning is the ideal stop for understanding the Wadden Sea. This national park information center, opened in 1999, combines aquariums and exhibits. Its centerpiece is a replica of a 17.5 m sperm whale that became stranded near Denmark in 1997. The largest tank holds around 250,000 liters of water behind a viewing window measuring 6 m by 6 m. The center opens daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., except on December 24.

Tönning’s Packhaus, a former warehouse dating from 1783, stands beside the small harbor on the Eider. This long, four-story building houses the town history museum on its first level. On the quay, flood markers show how high the water rose during the storms of 1362, 1634, and 1962. Then head up toward the Markt, the square dominated by St. Laurentius Church and its Baroque bell tower. The market takes place here on Mondays.

Austere when seen from the road, the Eidersperrwerk becomes impressive when you explore it on foot. This barrier and its gates protect the mouth of the Eider from storms coming in from the North Sea. It was inaugurated in 1973, following the 1962 storm that also flooded Tönning. It is described as Germany’s largest coastal protection structure. Take the pedestrian path above the road tunnel for views of the Eider and the coast.

to_next_leg.road_type: Detour via the Eider Barrier

visits.text: The wind whistles across the planks of Sankt Peter-Ording’s Seebrücke, a 1,095 m pier leading to the beach. It first crosses salt marshes, low-lying grasslands regularly covered by the sea. On the sand, you pass thirteen Pfahlbauten, houses on stilts; the one at the end of the pier houses a restaurant. The beach stretches for 12 km and reaches 2 km in width at low tide. In bad weather, head to the Dünen-Therme, a swimming pool filled with seawater.

activities.text: Park in the paid parking lot at the foot of the Westerhever dike, north of Sankt Peter-Ording. A path of about 2 km then crosses the salt marshes to Leuchtturm Westerheversand. This lighthouse, built from cast-iron plates and set on an earthen mound, was first lit in May 1908. The Stockenstieg, a narrow brick path normally used for the return walk from the lighthouse to the dike from June through September, is currently closed for construction. Return along the main path.

practical_info.tip: You can climb the lighthouse only on a guided tour, which must be arranged at the information booth in the parking lot.

visits.text: One place makes the detour to Seebüll, an isolated hamlet one kilometer from the Danish border, worthwhile: the home of painter Emil Nolde. The artist had this brick house built in 1927 and 1928 to his own specifications. He lived here with his wife Ada from 1930 onward. Today, the Nolde Foundation presents a different selection of his paintings and watercolors here each year. Admission costs €12: arrive when it opens at 10 a.m.

activities.text: In 1926, Ada and Emil Nolde bought a bare warft in Seebüll, an earthen mound raised to protect houses from flooding. Nolde designed the surrounding garden himself. Its central paths form the couple’s two initials, A and E. At the far end are the Seebüllchen, a small thatched-roof pavilion, and the grave of Ada and Emil Nolde. After the museum, allow 30 minutes to walk around the garden.

practical_info.tip: The museum, house, and garden open daily from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., from March 1 through October 31. They are closed to visitors in winter.

activities.text: In Dagebüll, a small harbor at the end of the dike, you will board a ferry operated by W.D.R. The crossing to Wyk auf Föhr takes 50 minutes. Dagebüll Mole station is just a few steps from the ferry terminal, convenient if you arrive by train via Niebüll. If you are driving, leave your car in the island parking lot: a free shuttle takes you to the ferry. From the harbor, a small service railway runs along an embankment toward the islets of Oland and Langeneß; it carries supplies, not passengers.

practical_info.tip: Schedules vary by season and may change due to low water levels or storms: check faehre.de the day before.

to_next_leg.road_type: Ferry crossing, 50 minutes

visits.text: There is no hurry on the Sandwall in Wyk auf Föhr, and that is its charm. This tree-lined seaside promenade looks out toward the halligen, the small, flat islets scattered across the Wadden Sea. In 1819, Wyk became the first seaside resort in the Duchy of Schleswig, the former province to which Föhr belonged. King Christian VIII of Denmark later spent his summers here from 1842 to 1847. Continue your walk to the inner harbor, where shrimp boats are moored.

Whale jawbones arranged in arches form the entrance gates to the Friesenmuseum in Wyk. This museum of Frisian culture was founded in 1908 by physician Carl Haeberlin. Its section on whaling and seafaring is the highlight. In the garden, the Olesen House, a farmhouse from 1617 relocated from the village of Alkersum, is considered the oldest dated house in North Frisia. Buy the combined ticket that includes the Museum Kunst der Westküste.

If you visit just one art museum on the coast, choose the Museum Kunst der Westküste in Alkersum on Föhr. Opened in 2009, it displays paintings created between 1830 and 1930 depicting life along the North Sea. Works by Max Liebermann, Emil Nolde, and Edvard Munch are among those on display. The restaurant occupies Grethjens Gasthof, a former inn where artists visiting the island used to gather. The museum is open Tuesday through Sunday; Alkersum is about 5 km from Wyk by bike or bus.

Nicknamed the “Friesendom,” or Cathedral of the Frisians, St. Johannis Church in Nieblum is described as the largest village church in Schleswig-Holstein. It dates from the first half of the 13th century. Inside, look for the altarpiece from 1487 and the granite baptismal font, carved around 1200 from a single block of stone. Outside, the cemetery preserves about 250 Baroque gravestones. Nieblum lies on the road between Wyk and Borgsum.

to_next_leg.road_type: Ferry to Wittdün, then bus to Nebel

visits.text: The view from Leuchtturm Amrum, the island’s lighthouse, amply rewards the climb. The brick tower is 41.8 m tall and stands on a 25 m dune. Its light shines 63 m above the sea, making it one of the highest on Germany’s North Sea coast. The lighthouse has been operating since January 1, 1875. It stands about 2 km from Wittdün, the island’s port, and is open to visitors only during the summer season.

They are called the “sprechende Grabsteine,” or talking gravestones. In the cemetery of St. Clemens Church in Nebel, these old gravestones bear carved ships and brief accounts of the lives of the deceased. The church itself, with its thatched roof, is the largest on the island and dates to the 13th century. Take time to read a few gravestones before going inside.

The Öömrang Hüs in Nebel is a Frisian farmhouse built around 1751 that remains almost in its original condition. Its rooms show what domestic life on Amrum was like in the past. In the same village, the windmill built in 1771 operated until 1962. It is described as the oldest windmill in Schleswig-Holstein and now houses a small museum. Allow 1 hour for both visits.

Between 1906 and 1969, 32 bodies that no one could identify washed ashore on Amrum. They rest in the Friedhof der Heimatlosen, the cemetery of the nameless, across from Nebel’s windmill. Each grave bears a simple wooden cross engraved with the date the body was found. Be discreet: this is a place for reflection, not an attraction.

activities.text: Follow one of Amrum’s Bohlenwege, the boardwalks laid across the dunes, to reach the Kniepsand. This enormous sandbank borders the island’s west coast. It is about 15 km long and up to 1.5 km wide. Its area alone is close to half that of the island. Stay on the boardwalks in the dunes to avoid damaging the vegetation, and bring water: there is very little shade on the sand.

practical_info.tip: The walk between Föhr and Amrum across the tidal flats, about 8 km at low tide, must be done with a guide.

activities.text: If your legs are up to it, continue north of Norddorf to Amrumer Odde, the island’s northern tip. This headland has been a nature reserve since 1936. Along the way, the 32 m A Siatler dune offers a viewpoint over the island. Stay on marked trails to avoid disturbing birds nesting in the reserve.

practical_info.tip: From April through October, a reserve warden offers guided tours; bring binoculars.

to_next_leg.road_type: From Amrum, reach Wittdün and take the seasonal boat to Hallig Hooge.
to_next_leg.justification: Depuis l'intérieur d'Amrum, rejoindre l'embarcadère de Wittdün par voie terrestre, puis emprunter uniquement en saison la liaison maritime vers Hooge ; horaires et possibilité de trajet simple à vérifier.

visits.text: On July 2, 1825, a storm prevented King Frederick VI of Denmark from leaving Hooge. He spent the night in the Königspesel, the 18th-century Frisian parlor on Hanswarft, the island’s main inhabited mound. Right next door, the Sturmflutkino, the storm cinema, screens a 15-minute film about flooding on Hooge, a hallig: an islet without a high dike that the sea covers during storms. Screenings take place every 20 minutes: fit one in as soon as you arrive, since time ashore is limited.

Modest on the outside, St. Johannis Church on Hooge stands on Kirchwarft, the church mound, and houses furnishings from a vanished parish. It was consecrated in 1637. Its pulpit, bricks, and baptismal font are said to have come from the church in Osterwohld, destroyed by the storm of 1634. Services are sometimes held in Low German, the regional language of northern Germany. Enter quietly if a service is underway.

activities.text: Rent a bike near Hooge’s harbor or board the Pferdebus, a horse-drawn carriage that tours the inhabited mounds. The islet covers less than 6 km² and is protected only by a low dike more than 11 km long. On average, storms flood its meadows two to six times a year. Only the warften, the earthen mounds on which the houses are built, remain above water. Allow about 3 hours to walk around the island.

practical_info.tip: In 2026, Adler excursions from Wyk run through October 31, departing at 12 p.m. and returning around 5 p.m. A W.D.R. ferry also connects Hooge with the port of Schlüttsiel year-round. Day visitors pay a small fee at the harbor.

to_next_leg.road_type: Boat from Hooge to Schlüttsiel, then by road to Dagebüll.
to_next_leg.justification: Le ferry relie réellement Hooge à Schlüttsiel en environ 75 à 95 minutes, puis une liaison terrestre conduit à Dagebüll ; il ne faut pas inventer de ferry direct Hooge–Dagebüll.

activities.text: Dagebüll Mole, the terminus of the short railroad line from Niebüll, is just a few steps from the ferries to Föhr and Amrum. From Wyk, the crossing to Dagebüll takes 50 minutes, but boats departing from Hooge serve Schlüttsiel among other destinations: do not confuse these two ports when planning your return. In Niebüll, some Intercity cars are detached to continue to Dagebüll, connecting the port to long-distance rail services. Leave some extra time between your boat and train, since ferry services depend on sailing conditions. If you left your car at Dagebüll’s island parking lot, a free shuttle takes you back there from the ferry terminal.

practical_info.tip: Check your ferry schedule on faehre.de the day before departure.

seo.h1_title: North Frisia in 4 Days: Husum, Föhr, Amrum, and Hooge
seo.intro_paragraph: This 4-day itinerary starts in Husum and follows the Eiderstedt peninsula to Sankt Peter-Ording. It then heads north to painter Emil Nolde’s house in Seebüll, before the ferry from Dagebüll takes you to Föhr, from where you head to Amrum to spend a day on its large beach. On the last day, an excursion boat drops you off for a few hours on the hallig of Hooge, an islet submerged by the sea during storms.
seo.seo_hook: North Frisia in 4 days: Husum harbor, Sankt Peter-Ording beach, Nolde’s house, ferries to Föhr and Amrum, and a stop on the hallig of Hooge.
featured_list: Husum: writer Theodor Storm’s house and crocuses in the castle park
Tönning: a 17.5 m sperm whale replica at the Multimar Wattforum
Sankt Peter-Ording: a 1,095 m pier and houses on stilts
Seebüll: painter Emil Nolde’s house and garden
Föhr: Friesenmuseum and Museum Kunst der Westküste
Amrum: Kniepsand beach and the lighthouse built in 1875
Hallig Hooge: the King’s Room and inhabited earthen mounds amid the meadows

itineraries.title: East Frisia in 4 Days: Ports, Tea, and the Island of Norderney
itineraries.subtitle: Travel from Leer to Jever in 4 days via Frisian harbors, tea in Norden, and a night on the island of Norderney.
itineraries.notes: Several museums close on Mondays, and the Bünting Teemuseum in Leer also closes on Sundays, so preferably set out on a Tuesday or Wednesday. For Norderney, leave your car in a parking lot in Norddeich; the crossing takes about one hour. Book it online in summer.
itineraries.climate: Aim for May through September: on the coast, average highs range from about 16 °C in May to 22 °C in August, and May and June are the sunniest months. Avoid November through February for the island, when highs stay below 10 °C, sunshine is scarce, and museums open fewer days. Keep a windbreaker and rain gear in the trunk, as October is the wettest month.

visits.text: Red brick, a tall tower, and a carillon: Leer’s Rathaus immediately hints at the nearby Netherlands. Inaugurated on October 29, 1894, and designed by Karl Henrici, it combines German and Dutch Renaissance styles. Then head down to the Alte Waage, a former Baroque public weigh house dating from 1714 beside the Handelshafen. To climb the town hall tower, book a guided tour at the Tourist-Info.

A wine shop on the ground floor and a bourgeois interior upstairs: Haus Samson blurs the lines. The core of the house dates from 1570, while its 1643 facade echoes Amsterdam’s gabled houses, complete with carved acanthus leaves. The furnished rooms tell the story of Frisian life in the 18th and 19th centuries. Visit during the wine shop’s opening hours, when the museum is accessible.

In 1806, Johann Bünting opened a small grocery store selling colonial goods on Brunnenstraße in Leer; two houses down, the Bünting Teemuseum has been telling the story of what that business became since 2001. Tea cultivation, trade routes, and the Frisian tea ritual lead up to a tasting. The museum is open Tuesday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.; the public tea ceremony takes place on Tuesdays at 3 p.m., with advance registration.

Step inside the Heimatmuseum Leer, housed in two 18th-century merchant houses on Neue Straße. The museum covers approximately 1,000 m² across five levels; the visit begins in vaulted cellars devoted to prehistory and moves upstairs to seafaring and herring fishing. From April through October, it is open Tuesday through Sunday from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.; leave time for the maritime floor.

Coming to Emden for painting may seem unlikely, yet it is the best reason to spend the afternoon here. The Kunsthalle Emden, which opened on October 3, 1986, at Henri Nannen’s initiative, brings together Expressionism, New Objectivity, and contemporary art, with paintings by Franz Marc and August Macke. Closed on Mondays, it opens at 10 a.m. on weekdays and 11 a.m. on weekends.

On September 6, 1944, bombing destroyed approximately 80% of central Emden; the Rathaus am Delft reopened on September 6, 1962, exactly eighteen years later. It houses the Ostfriesisches Landesmuseum, whose Rüstkammer displays suits of cavalry armor. Climb to the platform beneath the carillon for views over the city; admission is €8 and free for visitors ages 17 and under, and the museum is closed on Mondays.

The Johannes a Lasco Bibliothek opened in 1995 within the ruins of the Große Kirche, which was damaged by bombing during World War II. It is named after the reformer John a Lasco, who served as a pastor in Emden from 1542. This is a working library: enter quietly and check visiting hours before coming.

Walk along the Ratsdelft, the harbor basin at the foot of the town hall, where two museum ships are moored. The Feuerschiff Amrumbank, a lightship built in 1915, became a museum in 1984; beside it, the rescue cruiser Georg Breusing reached its final berth on December 23, 1988. To see Emden from the water, seasonal canal cruises depart from the Ratsdelft: book them at the Tourist-Info.

to_next_leg.road_type: Roads through Krummhörn via Pilsum

visits.text: Colorful hulls, winches, and nets: Greetsiel’s harbor is more than a backdrop; fishing is still its business. First mentioned in 1388, it is home to approximately 27 Krabbenkutter, shrimp fishing boats representing just over a tenth of Germany’s shrimp fleet. Since the completion of the Leybucht engineering works in the 1990s, boats have been able to enter at any tide. Walk around the basin and watch the catch being unloaded if a boat comes in.

Twins, but not the same age: Greetsiel’s Zwillingsmühlen were built 150 years apart. The red windmill dates from 1706 and was reassembled in 1921 using parts from Aurich’s Wallmühle; the green one dates from 1856. Exhibitions are held here regularly. Step back along the road to capture both silhouettes together.

Greetsiel’s Reformed church began as a private chapel: the chieftain Haro Edzardsna had it built in brick between 1380 and 1410. Look up at the three-masted ship weather vane, installed around 1730; inside, the pulpit dates from 1669 and the organ case from 1738. Its bell tower stands separately: walk around it before going inside.

If this little striped lighthouse looks familiar, thank Otto Waalkes. The Pilsumer Leuchtturm, completed in 1890 on the dike near Pilsum, serves as the comedian’s home in the movie “Otto, der Außerfriesische.” Approximately 12 meters tall, it has sported its red and yellow stripes since 1973 and hosts weddings. Put on a windbreaker and climb onto the dike for views of the Wadden Sea.

Approximately 300 liters of tea per person per year, according to the Deutscher Teeverband: in Norden, the Ostfriesisches Teemuseum explains how tea became a Frisian tradition. Discover Chinese porcelain, Stövchen—small warmers that keep the teapot hot—and “Dresmer Blau,” a blue pattern on a white background. The visit then introduces the ritual of Kluntje, rock sugar, and the cloud of cream that is never stirred. Open daily from April through October, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., and on weekends only from November through February; tea ceremonies take place on Tuesdays, Wednesdays, and Saturdays at 2 p.m. and Fridays at 11 a.m., by reservation.

Norden’s Ludgerikirche, the largest church in East Frisia, stretches for 80 meters. It houses the Arp Schnitger organ built between 1686 and 1692: 46 stops and 3,110 pipes, making it the second-largest surviving Schnitger organ in Germany. Its bell tower, dating from around 1318, stands alone across the street. Then cross the Marktplatz, which covers more than six hectares and is planted with trees over 250 years old.

“Heuler,” or “howlers,” is the local name for orphaned seal pups, referring to their cries for their mothers. At the Seehundstation in Norddeich, between 80 and 180 young seals are raised each year before being released. The center is open daily from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m.; aim for the feeding session with commentary at 11 a.m. or 3 p.m., and buy your ticket online to avoid the wait.

to_next_leg.road_type: Ferry from Norddeich; leave the car in the parking lot

visits.text: From the harbor, walk or take the bus to Norderney’s Kurplatz to get a sense of the resort’s long history. On October 3, 1797, the island became the first royal Prussian seaside bathing establishment on Germany’s North Sea coast; the baths opened in 1800. The Neoclassical Conversationshaus, built in 1840, houses the tourist information office: pick up a map, then look for the Napoleonschanze, an old defensive earthwork hidden in the Kurpark.

An unusual setting for a museum, but a perfect fit: Norderney’s Bademuseum occupies the former seawater swimming pool built in 1974 near the Weststrand. Opened in 2007, it traces the origins of sea bathing, from Heiligendamm in 1793 to Norderney in 1797. Outside, the 1931 wave machine could generate waves 1.80 m high. Check opening hours before visiting, especially in the off-season.

Climb the roughly 250 steps of the Leuchtturm Norderney, standing in the middle of the island on a dune about 10 meters high. First lit on October 1, 1874, its light sits nearly 60 meters above the sea; on clear days, the view stretches to neighboring islands and the mainland. You can climb it from April through late October, from 2 p.m. to 4 p.m., and from 11 a.m. in good weather.

If wind or rain drives you off the beach, take shelter at Watt Welten, the Wadden Sea World Heritage visitor center at Norderney’s harbor. Aquariums, a large diorama, and a small movie theater show how the tides reshape this landscape, listed by UNESCO since 2009. Plan your visit just before your ferry departure: the center is at the harbor, steps from the docks.

activities.text: The salty wind lashes your face from your first steps along Norderney’s Weststrand promenade, beside the family beach on the edge of town. Above it, Georgshöhe, a lookout topped with a monument, overlooks the sand and sea. King George V of Hanover held court on the island every summer starting in 1851. Come late in the day, when the low sunlight glides across the water.

practical_info.tip: Bring a windbreaker, even in midsummer: the promenade is very exposed.

activities.text: Rent a bike in town and head east across Norderney: beyond the last houses, the bike path enters the Wadden Sea National Park, which covers about 85% of the island. The path leads toward Weiße Düne and its long beach; in this area, Walter-Großmann-Düne rises to 24.4 meters, the island’s highest natural point. Stay on marked trails and return in time for the ferry.

practical_info.tip: In peak season, reserve your bike ahead of time with an island rental shop.

to_next_leg.road_type: Ferry from Norderney to Norddeich, then drive to Aurich.
to_next_leg.justification: Depuis Norderney, la traversée en ferry vers Norddeich dure environ une heure, puis le trajet routier mène à Aurich ; la durée exclut attente et embarquement.

visits.text: In 1561, the Cirksena counts left Emden and moved their court to Aurich, which remained their residence until 1744. The Historisches Museum Aurich, housed in the Alte Kanzlei built around 1530 under Count Enno II, tells this story through six themes, from the Stone Age to the present. It opens Tuesday through Sunday from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.: save it for the morning before heading back toward the coast.

“Tauchsieder,” meaning immersion heater, is one of the nicknames of the Sous-Turm, a 25-meter sculpture erected in 1990 on Aurich’s Marktplatz. Around it, the town preserves the memory of its court: the Schloss, rebuilt from 1851 to 1855 on the site of the old castle, now houses judicial offices. Nicknamed the secret capital of East Frisia, Aurich can be explored on foot: park once for your entire visit.

Aurich’s Stiftsmühle, a Dutch-style windmill with an exterior gallery dating from 1858, rises 29.95 meters over five stories. The Heimatverein turned it into a milling museum in 1977, and the gallery offers views over the town’s rooftops. Hours vary by season: check them before visiting.

If Frisian history interests you, take a detour to Upstalsboom in Rahe, west of Aurich. Delegates from the Frisian lands gathered on this mound between 1216 and 1231, then from 1323 to 1338, traditionally on the Tuesday after Pentecost. The stone pyramid dates from 1833; an avenue of beech trees leads to it, perfect for stretching your legs.

Small, compact, and highly photogenic, Neuharlingersiel’s Kutterhafen draws the whole village together around its basin, with eight fishing boats still in operation. TV fans will recognize the setting of “Doktor Martin.” Walk around the basin, then take a look at the Sielhof, a manor house built in 1755 that now serves as a visitor center.

Neuharlingersiel’s Buddelschiffmuseum displays more than 100 models tucked into bottles ranging from 0.7 to 60 liters. The models range from a ship dating to around 200 BCE to a nuclear submarine. Get close to the display cases to appreciate the details, and ask the tourist office about opening hours before visiting.

Founded in 1730 and named after Princess Sophie Karoline, Carolinensiel was East Frisia’s second most important trading port in the 18th and 19th centuries. The Deutsches Sielhafenmuseum tells the story of port life in three buildings: the Groot Hus, a grain warehouse dating from 1840, the Kapitänshaus, and the Alte Pastorei. In season, it opens Tuesday through Sunday; a combined ticket costs €12, with free admission for visitors under 18.

activities.text: Stroll around Carolinensiel’s Museumshafen, where traditional flat-bottomed sailing vessels are moored along the docks. The harbor has had no direct connection to the sea since 1765, when a new dike and the Friedrichsschleuse sheltered it; it came back to life as a museum harbor on September 9, 1987. The docks are freely accessible at all hours, and the museum cutter GEBRÜDER offers boat trips.

practical_info.tip: There is no parking directly at the harbor: park on nearby streets.

visits.text: One ceiling alone makes the Schlossmuseum Jever worth visiting: the carved wooden coffered ceiling in the audience chamber, commissioned by Fräulein Maria von Jever during the renovations of 1560 to 1564. Later, Catherine II of Russia owned the castle from 1793 to 1796 without ever living there. Open daily from May through October, 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., and Tuesday through Sunday in winter until 5 p.m.; free admission for visitors under 18.

Sixteen bells ring out over Jever’s Alter Markt as the Glockenspiel, inaugurated in 1983, parades figures of former rulers several times a day. In the old town, the Stadtkirche, rebuilt in 1964 after the fire of October 1, 1959, retains the monument to Edo Wiemken in its apse. Ask at the Tourist-Info for the carillon schedule to time your walk.

activities.text: Book a tour online of the Friesisches Brauhaus zu Jever, which has been brewing here since 1848. The roughly 2-hour tour takes you to the brewery’s historical museum before a tasting reserved for visitors over 16; the bottling line can fill around 60,000 bottles an hour. There are no tours on Sundays or public holidays, and bottling is often stopped on Friday afternoons and Saturdays.

practical_info.tip: Groups of no more than 20 people, adult ticket €24.90; the brewery is not wheelchair accessible.

seo.h1_title: East Frisia in 4 Days: Ports, Tea, and the Island of Norderney
seo.intro_paragraph: This 4-day road trip starts in Leer, the gateway to East Frisia, follows the coast through Emden, Greetsiel, and Norden, then leaves the car in Norddeich for a night on the island of Norderney. Back on the mainland, it passes through Aurich, the former seat of the counts, and the harbors of Neuharlingersiel and Carolinensiel before ending at Jever Castle.
seo.seo_hook: East Frisia in 4 days: Leer’s old town, Greetsiel’s harbor, tea in Norden, seals in Norddeich, a night on Norderney, and Jever Castle.
featured_list: Leer: Haus Samson and its Amsterdam-inspired facade dating from 1643
Emden: Kunsthalle opened in 1986 at Henri Nannen’s initiative
Greetsiel: twin windmills dating from 1706 and 1856
Norden: Arp Schnitger’s 46-stop organ in the Ludgerikirche
Norddeich: 80 to 180 young seals raised each year
Norderney: lighthouse dating from 1874 and national park dunes
Aurich: Upstalsboom, a Frisian assembly site in the Middle Ages
Jever: Fräulein Maria’s castle and a brewery founded in 1848

places_taglines.DE::leer: Brick-built old town, Baroque weigh house, and Bünting Tea Museum.
places_taglines.DE::emden: Kunsthalle, Landesmuseum, and museum ships moored in the Ratsdelft basin.
places_taglines.DE::greetsiel: Shrimp boat harbor documented as early as 1388, flanked by twin windmills.
places_taglines.DE::norden: Tea museum, Schnitger organ, and Norddeich’s orphaned seals.
places_taglines.DE::norderney: Seaside resort dating from 1797, a lighthouse on the dune, and national park beaches.
places_taglines.DE::aurich: Former seat of the Cirksena family, a windmill with a gallery, and the Upstalsboom mound.
places_taglines.DE::neuharlingersiel: Small shrimp boat harbor and a ships-in-bottles museum.
places_taglines.DE::carolinensiel: Former harbor with a lock, founded in 1730 and turned into a museum harbor in 1987.
places_taglines.DE::jever: Renaissance castle, carillon on the Alter Markt, and a brewery dating from 1848.

highlights: Norden: Frisian tea ceremony at the Ostfriesisches Teemuseum
Norddeich: young seal feedings with commentary at 11 a.m. and 3 p.m.
Norderney: royal Prussian sea bathing since 1797, lighthouse dating to 1874
Greetsiel: about 27 shrimp boats in a harbor documented as early as 1388
Carolinensiel: museum harbor sheltered from the sea since 1765
Jever: Renaissance coffered ceiling in the castle’s audience chamber

itineraries.title: Holstein Switzerland, Lübeck, and the Island of Fehmarn in 3 Days
itineraries.subtitle: In 3 days, travel from Lübeck to the lakes of Holstein Switzerland, then along the Baltic Sea beaches to Fehmarn.
itineraries.notes: Kalkberg Cave is open for visits from April to September, the five-lake cruise operates mainly from April to October, Flügge Lighthouse is open from April to the end of October, and Wallnau Nature Reserve is open from March to October. Special boat trips are also offered during the off-season: check the schedule. Fehmarn has had no rail service since 2022: replacement buses connect the island to Lübeck, but driving remains the easiest option.
itineraries.climate: Aim for May through September: in Lübeck, average highs rise from 18 °C in May to 24 °C in July. Avoid November through March: it is cold (an average high of 3.7 °C in January), and several attractions close, including Kalkberg Cave and Flügge Lighthouse. Bring a windbreaker for the Baltic Sea piers and beaches.

visits.text: Leaning, sunk into the ground, yet still standing: the Holstentor is Lübeck’s great fortified gate. It was built between 1464 and 1478 on marshy ground. The soil was so soft that the south tower began to sink during construction. Since then, the gate has sunk further: its lowest arrow slits are below ground level. On the side facing out of the city, the Latin inscription “Concordia domi foris pax” means “harmony within, peace without.” The museum inside, open daily from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., displays model ships and armor.

If you visit just one museum in Lübeck, choose the Europäisches Hansemuseum, the European Hanseatic Museum. The Hanseatic League was an alliance of trading cities in northern Europe, with Lübeck as its leading city. Opened in 2015, the museum combines period artifacts with scenes that bring the League’s former trading ports, such as Novgorod, Bruges, Bergen, and London, to life. Admission also includes the Burgkloster, a 13th-century Dominican friary. Allow 2 hours: the museum opens daily from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., except on December 24.

A brick facade with lace-like openwork borders the Markt, the market square: it belongs to the Rathaus, Lübeck’s city hall. Its oldest sections date from the 13th century. Light-colored Renaissance arcades were added in the 1570s. Inside, the audience chamber retains a door carved in 1573 depicting the Judgment of Solomon. Its inscription in Low German, the regional language of northern Germany, reminds judges to hear both sides before making a ruling. The rooms can only be visited on a guided tour.

To understand Lübeck’s layout, nothing beats the viewing platform in the tower of St. Petri, St. Peter’s Church. An elevator takes you up 50 m, with no spiral staircase to climb. From the top, you can see the old town, built on an island, and the church towers that earned Lübeck the nickname “city of seven towers.” On a clear day, the view reaches the Baltic Sea. Another distinctive feature: St. Petri has no parish in the traditional sense. It describes itself as “a church for the whole city” and hosts exhibitions and performances.

The “Kabäuschen” are tiny wooden rooms lined up in the great hall of the Heiligen-Geist-Hospital, the Hospital of the Holy Spirit. This charitable foundation, established in the 1220s, took in the sick and elderly. Its building was completed in 1286. The cubicles date from 1820 and were intended to give each resident a room of their own. Under the porch, look up at the Gothic frescoes. For about ten days before Christmas, the building hosts a craft market.

activities.text: Head up to the third floor of Café Niederegger, across from the Rathaus, to see its small museum devoted to marzipan, the sweet almond paste that made Lübeck famous. Admission is free. Twelve famous figures are modeled there in life-size marzipan, including the writer Thomas Mann, a Nobel laureate from a local merchant family. Niederegger was founded in 1806. As early as 1901, it chose the Holstentor as its brand emblem. Then head back downstairs for a snack at the café on Breite Straße.

practical_info.tip: The café and museum are open from 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. Monday through Friday, 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. Saturday, and 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Sunday.

activities.text: In the 14th century, space was scarce within Lübeck’s city walls. Property owners therefore built small, low houses in their back courtyards, renting them to laborers, craftspeople, and sailors. These are the old town’s Gänge und Höfe, its “passageways and courtyards.” There were once 180; about 80 remain, still inhabited. Start at the Füchtingshof, a Baroque courtyard dating from 1640 on Glockengießerstraße, founded for the widows of merchants and sailors. Keep your voice down: these are people’s homes.

practical_info.tip: The Füchtingshof can be visited from 9 a.m. to noon and 3 p.m. to 6 p.m. Elsewhere, enter only passageways that are open and respect the residents’ peace and quiet.

activities.text: If your legs need a break, take a boat tour around the Altstadtinsel, the old town island. Lübeck’s historic center is indeed surrounded by water. The cruise follows its shores for 1 hour. It departs from the An der Obertrave landing, near the Holstentor. Before boarding, look across at the Salzspeicher, former salt warehouses. Like the nearby gate, these buildings are part of the area inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1987.

practical_info.tip: Departures every half hour from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. In the off-season, check the schedule with the tourist office.

visits.text: Kalkberg means “limestone hill,” but this 91 m rock in central Bad Segeberg is made of gypsum, the rock used to make plaster. Centuries of quarrying reduced it from around 110 m to its current height before operations ended in 1931. Beneath it, a salt dome—a buried mass of salt that slowly rises—still lifts it by one to two millimeters a year. A paved path leads to the summit. From late June to early September, the former quarry hosts the Karl-May-Spiele, outdoor plays based on writer Karl May’s adventure novels.

The Kalkberghöhle, a cave discovered in 1913 at the foot of the Kalkberg, extends for 2,360 m through the gypsum. It is Germany’s second-longest gypsum cave. Around 25,000 bats of eight species spend the winter here. A tiny insect, the Segeberg cave beetle, lives nowhere else in the world. The cave visit can be combined with Noctalis, an exhibition devoted to bats. The cave is only open to visitors from April through September; for the rest of the year, it is left to the hibernating animals.

It took just three years, from 1633 to 1636, to build Plöner Schloss, Plön Castle, overlooking Großer Plöner See. This is Schleswig-Holstein’s largest lake, covering 28 km² and containing more than twenty islands. Much of the castle is now occupied by the Fielmann Akademie, a school for optical and hearing care professions. Walk up to the courtyard terrace for views of the lakes. The ducal rooms in the east wing can only be visited on a guided tour, on Saturdays and Sundays, by reservation.

“House of Princes”: that is the meaning of Prinzenhaus, the name of a pavilion in the grounds of Plön Castle. It was built between 1744 and 1751 for Duke Friedrich Karl. Its reception rooms have regained their Rococo decor, an 18th-century style characterized by curves, with stucco moldings (shaped plaster) by Bartolomeo Bossi. From 1896 to 1910, Emperor Wilhelm II had his sons housed and educated here, hence the name. Visits are by guided tour only, at 3 p.m. on Wednesdays and Sundays from May through September, then on Sundays for the rest of the year, except during the closure from mid-December to mid-January.

Climb the Parnassturm, a 20 m observation tower built in 1888 by Plön’s tourism association. Its viewing platform stands 85 m above sea level. From here, the view takes in the town and the lake-dotted countryside. After the castle, it is the best place to grasp the region’s geography at a glance. The climb is free, daily from 9 a.m. to 7 p.m., from Easter through the end of October.

Malente’s Kurpark, a park for spa visitors, was designed in 1962 by landscape architect Karl Plomin. It is protected as a historic monument. Malente has been a Kneipp spa resort since 1955, offering the water-based treatment named after Sebastian Kneipp. Follow the spa visitors’ lead: take off your shoes, walk through the park’s Kneipp pool for a few minutes, then splash water over your arms. On selected Thursdays at 7:30 p.m., Feierabendmusik, a series of free concerts held about once a month, brings music to the park or its indoor hall, depending on the season.

activities.text: A “Switzerland” whose highest point, the Bungsberg, reaches just 168 m? The name Holstein Switzerland originated here in Malente. In 1885, when trips to Switzerland were fashionable, a merchant from Eutin opened an establishment on the shores of Kellersee called “Holsteinische Schweiz.” The train station, then the whole region, adopted the name. To see these lakes, board the 5-Seen-Fahrt, the five-lake cruise: Dieksee, Langensee, Behlersee, Höftsee, and Edebergsee. The round trip from the Malente-Gremsmühlen landing takes about 2 hours and costs €15 per adult.

practical_info.tip: The landing is near the train station. Departures every hour from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., from May to early October; in April and from early to mid-October, there are only three departures: 11 a.m., 1 p.m., and 3 p.m.

visits.text: A moat surrounds Schloss Eutin, which stands on a small island at the edge of the Großer Eutiner See. This four-winged castle first belonged to the prince-bishops of Lübeck, bishops who also ruled a territory. It later became the summer residence of the dukes of Oldenburg. Converted into a museum after the ducal family left in 1918, it displays its drawing rooms and a collection of paintings. It is open Tuesday through Sunday from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m., and daily from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. in July and August. Admission is €10, free for visitors ages 17 and under.

Eutin’s Schlossgarten deserves almost as much time as the castle. Starting in 1788, Duke Peter Friedrich Ludwig had the old Baroque garden, with its geometric paths, replaced by an English landscape garden designed to imitate untamed nature. The park covers 14 hectares and is protected as a historic landmark. The castle also maintains a Historischer Küchengarten, a historic kitchen garden. The gardens close at night, from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m., and on Ascension Day.

Eutin has been nicknamed the “Weimar of the North,” a comparison with Weimar, Goethe’s city. The title comes from the painter Johann Heinrich Wilhelm Tischbein, who painted the famous portrait “Goethe in the Roman Campagna.” Appointed court painter, he lived in Eutin from 1808 until his death in 1829. The composer Carl Maria von Weber was also born here, in 1786. Start at the Marktplatz, the old town’s market square, then step inside St.-Michaelis-Kirche, a church dating from the late 12th century.

Supported by 48 steel piles, Heiligenhafen’s Erlebnis-Seebrücke is a promenade pier that opened in 2012. It extends into the Baltic Sea in three sections pointing in different directions, partly on two levels, with a playground and a swimming platform. No boats dock here because the water is too shallow. The town also holds wedding ceremonies in a glass-enclosed room called the Meereslounge. On your way back, stop by the Fischereihafen, the fishing harbor, where some of the catch is still sold directly from the boats.

activities.text: Walk along the Graswarder, a 2.5 km sand spit separating Heiligenhafen Bay from the Baltic Sea. It has been a nature reserve since 1968. Waterbirds and shorebirds nest here, including graylag geese, shelducks, avocets, and Eurasian oystercatchers. Along the path stand fifteen seaside villas, built around 1900 by wealthy beachgoers, all protected as historic landmarks. In the reserve, the 14 m observation tower run by NABU, the German nature conservation association, is open from Easter through October.

practical_info.tip: Bring binoculars. You can visit the NABU tower independently or on a guided tour from Easter through October.

to_next_leg.road_type: Crossing the Fehmarnsund Bridge

visits.text: “Kleiderbügel,” or “coat hanger,” is the nickname of the Fehmarnsundbrücke, the bridge across the Fehmarn Strait, whose large arch resembles that shape. Opened on April 30, 1963, it connects the island to the mainland. Its arch crosses 248.5 m in a single span. It is one of the world’s first network arch bridges: its cables cross diagonally like the mesh of a net. It carries a road, a railroad track, and a path for pedestrians and cyclists, so you can walk across.

Burg auf Fehmarn, the island’s main town, was mentioned as early as 1202 under the name “Borch up Vemere.” Since 2003, the entire island has formed a single municipality, the town of Fehmarn. On the market square, the brick town hall opened in 1901. St. Nikolai Church, begun around 1230, retains a bronze baptismal font made in Lübeck and dated 1391. Its Gothic altarpiece, the large three-panel decoration behind the altar, dates from the second half of the 14th century. During Advent, the square hosts a Christmas market.

Around 100 million birds pass through Fehmarn each year, according to NABU. The island lies on their migration route between Scandinavia and Central Europe. The Hamburg–Copenhagen road and railroad that cross the island are in fact called the Vogelfluglinie, the “bird flight line”: they follow the cranes’ migration route. Head to the west coast to visit Wasservogelreservat Wallnau, a 300-hectare waterbird reserve established in 1975. Concealed bird blinds let you watch the birds without disturbing them. Open March through October, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.

activities.text: If you love rock music, walk to Leuchtturm Flügge, the Flügge lighthouse, in the Krummsteert nature reserve. Nearby, on September 6, 1970, Jimi Hendrix played his last full concert at the Love-and-Peace-Festival. He died in London twelve days later. A red granite stone about 2.5 m tall marks the site of the stage. The lighthouse itself, built in 1914–1915, is the island’s tallest: 37 m high, with 162 steps to the top.

practical_info.tip: There is no parking at the lighthouse: park at Hof Flügge, then walk 1.5 km. The lighthouse is open to visitors from April through October, except Mondays.

activities.text: End the day at Südstrand, Fehmarn’s south beach, in the Burgtiefe district, which belongs to Burg. Its sand is white. The beach hosts festivals devoted to surfing, kite flying, and foiling on a board fitted with a fin that lifts it above the water. The three apartment buildings overlooking the beach were designed by Arne Jacobsen, the Danish architect and designer. The island’s tourist office is on the promenade at 4 Zur Strandpromenade.

practical_info.tip: For beach festival dates, check with Tourismus-Service Fehmarn on the Burgtiefe promenade.

to_next_leg.road_type: Fehmarnsund Bridge, then the expressway south

visits.text: Glass floor panels beneath your feet reveal the waves below at the Mikado-Teehaus, an Asian-style tea pavilion at the end of one of Timmendorfer Strand’s two Seebrücken, or promenade piers. Opened in 2014, it now houses a restaurant. The other pier, 427 m long, opened in September 2024. It forms a loop over the water, with benches and two boat landings. Keep a jacket handy: at the ends of the piers, you soon feel the wind off the Baltic Sea.

activities.text: Walk along the promenade beside Timmendorfer Strand’s 6.5 km beach to Niendorfer Hafen. This harbor in Niendorf is among the smallest on Schleswig-Holstein’s Baltic coast. It is home to fishing boats, a sailing club, and a few excursion boats. One unusual fact about the municipality: the bottom of the nearby Hemmelsdorfer See lake reaches 39.6 m below sea level. It is Germany’s lowest natural point, but you cannot see it: it is hidden beneath the lake’s water.

practical_info.tip: Timmendorfer Strand has a train connection to Lübeck, about twenty kilometers away, where you can return a rental car or continue your journey.

seo.h1_title: Holstein Switzerland, Lübeck, and the Island of Fehmarn in 3 Days
seo.intro_paragraph: This 3-day itinerary starts in Lübeck, the great city of the Hanseatic League, the alliance of Northern European trading cities. It then crosses Holstein Switzerland, a region of lakes and hills around Bad Segeberg, Plön, Malente, and Eutin. Finally, it reaches the Baltic Sea at Heiligenhafen and on the Island of Fehmarn, before heading back south to the beach at Timmendorfer Strand, near Lübeck.
seo.seo_hook: Lübeck’s Holstentor, the Kalkberg cave, a five-lake cruise, Eutin Castle, and Fehmarn’s lighthouse: Holstein Switzerland in 3 days.
featured_list: Lübeck: the Holstentor, a gate dating from 1478 that has sunk into marshy ground
Bad Segeberg: a 2,360 m cave carved into gypsum
Plön: a castle dating from 1636 overlooking a 28 km² lake
Malente: the five-lake cruise, a 2-hour round trip
Eutin: a moated castle and a 14-hectare English garden
Heiligenhafen: a 2.5 km sand spit protected for birds
Fehmarn: the Fehmarnsund Bridge, opened in 1963
Timmendorfer Strand: a 427 m promenade pier opened in 2024
